News.title: Motorist in his 20s arrested for ‘murder’ after man killed on e-bike as cops appeal for witnesses
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MURDER PROBE Motorist in his 20s arrested for ‘murder’ after man killed on e-bike as cops appeal for witnesses







Next

A MAN has died after a horror e-bike crash as a motorist is arrested on suspicion of murder.

Police were called to the scene in Luton on Friday night where they found the seriously injured victim.



The man was believed to have been struck by a vehicle on Dallow Road and tragically died shortly after.

A man in his 20s has since been arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in custody.



A full murder investigation has been launched by The Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit.

Officials have appealed for anyone with information on the incident.

Det Insp Andrew Moralee said: “This was an awful incident which has sadly cost a man his life.

“Our thoughts are with his friends and family who have lost a loved one in such dreadful circumstances.

“Please refrain from sharing any such footage and instead contact police.

“It could also form part of vital evidence in our investigation.”



Anyone with any information has been asked to contact the police website or Crimestoppers anonymously.

News.title: Pilot killed after two planes crash mid-air with one smashing into woodland as urgent probe launched
News.content:
MID-AIR DISASTER Pilot killed after two planes crash mid-air with one smashing into woodland as urgent probe launched







Next

A PILOT has been killed after two gliders crashed mid-air over upstate New York.

One plane plunged into a heavily wooded and remote area, while the other was able to land safely after the collision.



Each aircraft was operated by a single pilot and carried no passengers.

They collided just before 2.30pm on Friday afternoon near Edinburg, a town around 50 miles north of Albany.



It took investigators more than two hours to find debris from the wreck of the Schempp-Hirth Ventus-2B glider.

Helicopters were seen overhead as they scoured the area for traces of the plane.

The crash site was roughly six miles from where the other aircraft, exactly the same model, landed safely at Plateau Sky Ranch Airport.

The body of the pilot, who has not been identified, was found at the scene.

Footage from the crash site showed police surrounding a small plane in a wooded area.

The other pilot escaped without injury, and even went back up in search of the other glider.



Pictures show the survivor‘s plane had some scraping near the nose, but it was otherwise unscathed.

Elayne Wade, owner of the airport where he landed, told the Times Union: “The front end had some damage.

“The pilot is shaken but OK. He just went up in a plane with my husband to find the other glider.”

It is not yet clear what caused the crash, but an investigation has been launched by the National Transportation Safety Board.

They will analyse flight track data, recordings, maintenance records, the pilot’s license and flight history, witness statements and surveillance video.



A preliminary report is expected within 30 days and a final report will follow in the next one to two years.

News.title: Terrifying moment car crashes head-on into another vehicle after driver veers onto wrong side of road
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a car crashes head-on into another vehicle after the driver lost control and veered into the opposing lane.

Ethan Loveridge smashed into the unsuspecting car after losing concentration while behind the wheel.



The terrifying moment was captured by dashcam footage of one of the victims.

The 20-year-old Loveridge was driving in his Kia Sorento in Caerphilly in August of 2024 when the crash took place.



Loveridge lost control of the car and veered into the wrong lane where he clipped one car and smashed head-first into Martin Howells’ vehicle.

Newport Crown Court heard how Howells was left suffering from broken bones and fractures which left him out of work for months.



After the smash, Howells was left injured inside his car while passerbys attempted to help him.

He was left dealing with eight broken ribs, a broken nose, a detached bicep, injury to his left shoulder and a rotator cuff, and nerve damage to his neck and shoulder.



In a victim personal statement read to the court, Howells said: “It was a horrific crash that has changed my life forever… I had difficulties with my fingers which has prevented me from playing guitar which is something I love to do.

“I have been diagnosed with PTSD and underwent eight months of psychological therapy.”

Howells added his injuries have left him with extreme weakness in his arms and is now permanently unable to lift anything above shoulder height.

He said: “I was unable to sleep properly and woke up in the night thinking about what could have happened. I was unable to work for 10 months after the collision which had massive financial implications on my wife.

“We had to take a pay holiday on our mortgage for six months and had to use our life savings to make ends meet.



“We had to sell our family home where we have lived for 33 years and our children grew up in that house, we have lifelong memories there. We had to downsize to afford to carry on living.”

Loveridge pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, possession with intent to supply a class B drug, being concerned in the supply of class A and B drugs and possession of criminal property.

He was sentenced to five years in prison and was disqualified from driving for four years.

News.title: MPs leap from vintage WW2 plane over Arnhem in stunning tribute to heroes involved in biggest air assault in history
News.content:
Next

TWO MPs leapt from a World War Two plane over Arnhem to commemorate the biggest airborne assault in history – that inspired the film A Bridge Too Far.

Ex Special Forces commando Al Carns and Para reservist Bayo Alaba joined veterans, serving troops, firemen and civilians in the act of remembrance.



They jumped from a vintage Dakota C-47 like the ones used Operation Market Garden in 1944.

Some 41,000 allies troops jumped into Nazi occupied Holland to capture a series of bridges from Eindhoven to Arnhem.



Britain’s commander General Bernard Montgomery hoped it would clear the path for an armoured assault and end the war by Christmas.

But the 10,000 troops from UK’s 1st Airborne Division and the Polish 1st Parachute Brigade faced unexpectedly fierce resistance from a Nazi Panzer Corps in Arnhem.



Paras led by Lt Col John Frost secured the northern end of the Arnhem bridge held it for several days – but eventually ran out of ammo before reinforcements arrived.

Carns, a former armed forces minister, said: “A generation ago people sacrificed their lives for everything we have today.

“We never thought we would have war in Europe and now we are seeing the same casualty rates as the Second World War.

“What you are seeing from Russia is an Arnhem every month.”



Bayo, an independent MP, said: “We are paying respect to our forebears.

“I jumped on the 50th anniversary – 32 years ago – with a lot of veterans who were still nimble enough to jump.

“Now we’re are doing it to honour them. We are carrying that baton and remembering that sacrifice.”



Two Dutch firemen from Renkum – the drop zone where the paras landed – also joined Friday’s jump.

Frank Van Rhijn, 33, and Lex Stegink, 33, said they wanted “to remember the guys that jumped in Renkum”.

Frank added: “Renkum is our hometown so this means a lot to us.”

John Todd, 81, from the Pathfinder Parachute Group that organised the jumpers, said: “We have got to keep the memory alive, it should never be lost.

“This is not just a parade, we are doing what those soldiers did all those years ago.”



The former Parachute regiment reservist who made his last jump aged 79, added: “We have got Belgians, Polish, a couple of Australians, Dutch, an American and a lot British.

“We are using the same planes and the same drop zone that the 1st Airborne Division used – the difference we don’t have any flak being thrown up at us and there is no one on the DZ shooting us.”

Terence Millar, a retired airborne sniper, jumped with his late father’s ashes and scattered them in Renkum the drop zone when he landed.



Terence, a former 2 Para sergeant, said he had promised his dad “one last para descent” before he died aged 90.

Terrence, who served 22 years in the regulars and two in the reserves, said: “My father was Sgt Maj Thomas Millar.

He was 90 and served 9 years in the Irish Army and then was 4 Para from 67 to 76.” Terence, who is known as Moose added: “He was the reason I joined. I stayed with him in hospital till he passed away and promised him one last para descent.”



One of his sons had planned to jump but was ill and another son, who is serving in 3 Para, met him on the drop zone.

Moving body-cam footage captured the moment Terence bid his father a final farewell.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He removed paper packet from his smock and scattered the ashes on the grass in front of his parachute.

He said: “Farewell dad. Airborne dad. Airborne”

News.title: Rape suspect ‘allowed to flee UK while owing taxpayers £200,000’ – as he could still be claiming benefits
News.content:
FREE TO FLEE Rape suspect ‘allowed to flee UK while owing taxpayers £200,000’ – as he could still be claiming benefits







Next

A RAPE suspect who owes £200,000 in taxpayer money was allegedly allowed to flee the UK after police failed to stop him leaving.

Ndumbe Achile Ndumbe claimed hundreds of thousands of pounds in housing benefits despite being a landlord for six houses in Manchester.



The 41-year-old fraudulently claimed £180,000 and was fined another £26,000 in 2025 by the courts after failing to obtain a HMO license.

It is believed Ndumbe flew to Cameroon in January once being released under investigation after being arrested on suspicion of rape in 2024.



It was also revealed that he was allegedly claiming £200 a month in Pip payments.

He pinned this down to mental health struggles and back pain.



An inquiry source told The Times: “This case represents and highlights multiple failures in the system, across the police, the border and Department for Work and Pensions. How was he allowed to leave the country in the first place while being investigated for rape?

“There was evidence he had made previous trips between the UK and Cameroon. He should never have been allowed to keep his passport and leave the country while on bail over a rape complaint.”

When the benefit fraudster was initially arrested in July of 2024 on suspicion of rape, his electronic devices were seized.

His phone, laptop and a camcorder were all confiscated by officials, and possible evidence of further sexual offences was alleged to have been found.



Police expanded their investigation in response to the findings, despite Ndumbe being on police bail for the past two years.

He was also managing six HMOs in Greater Manchester and the freehold owner of two of those properties despite the housing benefit claims.

It was revealed that rent of between £500 and £800 was paid into his account each month.

Ndumbe failed to register the two properties correctly, landing him the £26,486 fine.

Greater Manchester police said in a statement: “Detectives investigating reports of rape have arrested a suspect who remains under investigation and inquiries are actively continuing.



“Specialist agencies continue to provide the victims with support.”

The Department for Work and Pensions and the Home Office have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Madeleine McCann prime suspect Christian Brueckner ‘plans tell-all book’ as sick plot sparks fury: ‘It’s abhorrent’
News.content:
Next

MADELEINE McCann prime suspect Christian Brueckner is reportedly planning to write a tell-all book, sparking fury.

The paedophile – suspected of snatching and killing the missing toddler – is said to be penning his story just a year after he was released from prison for rape.



Retired British police detective Kevin Moore told The Mirror: “I won’t be buying it.”

Furious Germans told the outlet: “It’s a disgrace.”



Brueckner, 49, has never been charged with Madeleine’s 2007 disappearance and maintains his innocence.

The creep has now started drafting a book and has approached at least one professional writer to help him craft and translate it, sources told The Mirror.

One said: “Brueckner is desperate to tell his side of the story. He believes that writing about his innocence will help him.

“He wants the book to be published in both German and English.

“Ultimately he also sees it as a way to help him financially as he has been unable to find any work since getting out of jail and is living on benefits.”

Brueckner has reportedly told friends he believes he could make a seven-figure sum, although the true earnings would be far less.



Criminals in Germany have more avenues to make money from writing about their crimes than in the UK.

In Britain, courts can issue an exploitation proceeds order that effectively ensures they cannot profit from a memoir.

The state cannot as easily seize royalties in Germany, although victims can sue for damages.



It comes as Brueckner is set to appear in court again after Germany’s top prosecutor secured a hearing to tell an appeal judge that he should not have been cleared of rape in 2024.

Crucial evidence with the power to put Brueckner behind bars for good was revealed to have been left out of the trial by The Sun – and could now finally be used against him.

The hearing announcement, set for January, has been hailed by Maddie investigators in Europe as “a game changer” as they realise a retrial will almost certainly follow under the German system.

A second trial is seen as crucial for the McCann case as it could put fiend Brueckner in jail for good. That is when investigators have said they would finally charge the sex offender over Maddie.

A source close to the case in Germany said: “This is a case with very little good news – and no prospect of a happy outcome.



“But for those who want to see Brueckner charged over Madeleine, this new court date is a gamechanger.

“The way the German system works means every part of the original trial will be considered – and the judge overseeing it is incredibly sharp. She will miss nothing.

“Maddie investigators realise for the first time, there is a genuine will to see a retrial and for something to be done about Brueckner.”

Drug dealer Brueckner was cleared of the rape of Irish holiday rep Hazel Behan in 2024 allowing him to sensationally be freed last year.

Prosecutors in Germany still believe he kidnapped and killed Madeleine, three, in 2007 – while British cops have also stepped up their enquiries into the paedophile and are looking at the possibility of extraditing him to the UK.



Their tactic has been to secure a second rape conviction against the sicko that would allow a court to cage him for life – and embolden German cops to prosecute him over the McCann case.

Brueckner has been laying low since publicly declaring he “f***ing hates Maddie” in a vile video outburst published on YouTube.

Three-year-old Madeleine, of Rothley, Leics., vanished from the Ocean Club, in Praia da Luz, Portugal on May 3 2007 while on holiday with her family.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Brueckner was named as the prime suspect in the disappearance and murder of the tot in 2020 by German cops.

Police have been able to confirm his phone was near Ocean Club, where the McCanns were staying, around the time Madeleine disappeared on May 3, 2007.

News.title: Labour slammed as hypocritical over massive political donations from trade unions
News.content:
Next

LABOUR has been slammed as hypocritical over massive political donations.

The Government has said £72million given to Reform by two crypto billionaires is a bid to buy influence.



But Labour has received nearly £43million from unions since 2020 — and introduced laws those organisations had campaigned for.

Labour’s Employment Rights Act 2025 makes it easier for unions to recruit, ballot for industrial action and call rolling strikes.



This week, senior minister Louise Haigh told unions that Labour will make it harder for firms to block requests to work from home.

The announcement was hailed by Trades Union Congress chief Paul Nowak.

But Reform’s Robert Jenrick said the Government’s “hypocrisy is off the charts”.

Shadow Business Secretary Julia Lopez said: “Unions are back pulling the strings, dictating policy.”

But Labour and the TUC said their funding is the “cleanest money” in politics.

Labour added: “There’s a world of difference between money donated by hundreds of thousands of nurses, cleaners and teaching assistants through unions, and millions of pounds donated to Reform by a handful of crypto billionaires.



“Labour will never shy away from standing up for working people.”

News.title: Girl, 2, dies after being pulled from neighbour’s swimming pool as devastated family mourn ‘unimaginable tragedy’
News.content:
POOL TRAGEDY Girl, 2, dies after being pulled from neighbour’s swimming pool as devastated family mourn ‘unimaginable tragedy’







Next

A TWO-YEAR-OLD girl has tragically died after being found in a pool in Texas.

The child was found in a pool by paramedics at Pine Trace Court, in the Atascocita South area of Harris County but it remains unclear how she ended up there.



Her grandmother was in the backyard with the children when she got distracted briefly, an investigator said to KHOU 11.

The family began looking for the little girl after the grandma had lost sight of her.



Just a few minutes later the family checked the garden next door because they knew there was an open swimming pool.

Unfortunately when they reached the pool, the girl was submerged in the water.

Her family repeatedly attempted CPR whilst waiting for emergency services to arrive.

The pool was reportedly in the backyard of a vacant home that was being remodelled.

Constable Mark Herman shared on social media that authorities responded to reports of a child found in a pool around 6pm on Friday afternoon.

Authorities closed the West Lake Houston Parkway, near FM 1960, to allow a Life Flight helicopter to land safely and rush the toddler to Memorial Hermann Hospital.



Locals were advised to avoid the area and expect delays.

Herman wrote on X for everyone to pray for the child and the family.

Despite doctors working tirelessly to administer life-saving treatment, the child sadly died several hours later.

Herman wrote on X: “It is with heavy hearts that we share the tragic update that the 2-year-old child has been pronounced deceased following an incident…where the child was found in a swimming pool.

“This is an unimaginable tragedy, and our hearts are with this child’s family during this incredibly difficult time.



“We ask our community to keep the family, loved ones and everyone affected by this heartbreaking loss in their thoughts and prayers.”

Harris County officials have not publicly identified the 2-year-old.

News.title: M60 traffic: Motorway blocked after two crashes cause four-mile tailbacks
News.content:
Drivers faced long delays on the M60 in Greater Manchester on Saturday afternoon after two crashes led to closures on the motorway in Swinton and the Stockport area

Two sections of the M60 in Greater Manchester were closed on Saturday afternoon after two separate crashes.

The first collision happened on the anticlockwise carriageway at junction 15 (Swinton Interchange) in Swinton, Salford, shortly before 2.30pm, according to traffic monitoring service Inrix. The road was partially blocked, but traffic returned to normal shortly afterwards.

A second crash led to two lanes being closed on the clockwise carriageway between junction one (Stockport Pyramid) and junction two (Cheadle Heath) in the Stockport area. It caused tailbacks of around four miles. National Highways reported the closure at about 3pm, and the lanes reopened just over half an hour later.

News.title: Northern Quarter: Air ambulance lands on top of Manchester car park and street is shut off
News.content:
An air ambulance seen on the top deck of the Northern Quarter multi-storey car park

Emergency services attended an incident at the Northern Quarter car park in Manchester city centre, with an air ambulance seen landing on the top deck

Northern Quarter: Air ambulance lands on top of Manchester car park and street is shut off

A large emergency services presence was reported at a multi-storey car park in Manchester city centre.

An air ambulance was seen landing on the top deck of the Northern Quarter car park on Saturday evening. Cordons were put in place on Church Street, near the car park entrance, and on Turner Street, outside the Abel Heywood pub.

Pictures from the scene showed several police cars and ambulances in attendance, the Manchester Evening News reports. Officers remained at the scene at around 9pm on Saturday.

The Mirror has contacted Greater Manchester Police for further information.

News.title: Deadly West Nile virus spreads across Europe with doctors issuing urgent warning
News.content:
Deadly West Nile virus spreads across Europe with doctors issuing urgent warning

Experts have issued a warning after West Nile virus, which could be deadly in some places, has been recorded in more places in Europe

View 2 Images Experts have issued a warning on West Nile virus (Image: Getty Images)

The potentially deadly mosquito-borne West Nile virus has spread across more of Europe, as experts issue a warning on the concerning rise.

‌



Italian health authorities said they have seen evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons have helped mosquitoes spread the disease across a wider area, during more months of the year. More than 650 infections have been reported in Italy so far this year, according to local health authorities.

‌



This virus is spread mostly through the bites of infected mosquitoes and can cause symptoms like a fever, headache and muscle aches. However, around 1 in 150 cases develop serious disease affecting the brain and nervous system, according to the NHS.

‌



British tourist claims holiday 'ruined' and asks hotel for refund after mosquito bites in Crete READ MORE :

View 2 Images Worker sprays bushes to kill mosquitoes to limit the spread of West Nile virus, near Athens (Image: AP Photo/Thanassis Stavrakis)

This is around half of all the cases of this virus recorded across Europe this year. Antonino Bella, researcher at Italy's National Institute of Health shared a warning on how the changing climate could lead to a greater spread of the virus.

Bella said: "Higher temperatures linked to climate change help mosquitoes reproduce and extend the transmission season, increasing the chances that infected mosquitoes will spread the virus to people."

‌



West Nile has been considered endemic in Italy since 2020, when cases started to surge, and is now reported every summer and early fall. About 80% of infected people develop no symptoms.

Experts say this year's case numbers are broadly in line with recent seasons. However, warmer temperatures favour mosquito reproduction and can mean the transmission season sometimes lasts as late as November, Bella explained.

Areas once mostly unaffected by West Nile virus are increasingly reporting infections. The Netherlands this year has reported more than two dozen West Nile cases, the first since 2020, as well as several deaths, according to its public health institute.

‌



A Belgian research team travelled to study Italy's research and surveillance system, last May, after the country began recording locally acquired West Nile cases.

Marc-Alain Widdowson, who leads the Pandemic Threats, Communicable Diseases, and AMR Division at the World Health Organization's Europe office said: "There's no doubt that warming weather will expand the period of replication for the virus and the vector in more countries."

He added: "You've got to be careful not to say that climate change is all of it, but certainly a warming climate means that we have a longer mosquito season, so that the vectors can survive for longer. Warm temperatures also mean that the virus itself will survive better."

Article continues below

Experts shared that Italy's extensive monitoring network, which tracks mosquitoes, birds, blood donors and human infections, also helps explain why the country detects so many cases.

In June, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control warned that the changing weather in Europe - with heat waves and more flooding - were more favourable for invasive mosquito species.

West Nile Virus was first identified in Uganda in 1937. It is now endemic in parts of Europe, the United States, Canada and the Caribbean.

News.title: Folkestone hotel fire: Sleeping guests evacuated as fire rips through hotel in overnight chaos
News.content:
An overnight fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone has led to hundreds of guests being evacuated and the local council opening a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park

Fire crews battling a blaze at a Kent seafront hotel this morning have issued an "avoid the area" warning to the public.

Hundreds of guests staying at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone have been evacuated from the site following the overnight blaze, according to Folkestone and Hythe District Council.

The fire is believed to have started at around 1am on Saturday, with locals taking to social media to share images of the incident from afar. The cause of the fire has not yet been established.

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said 26 fire engines were used at the height of the blaze while crews wearing breathing apparatus worked to extinguish the fire.

A spokesperson for Folkestone and Hythe District Council said: "A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin Hotel. We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected.

"We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety."

News.title: Earl Spencer's war with King Charles takes fresh turn as Palace braces for new interview
News.content:
Earl Spencer's war with King Charles takes fresh turn as Palace braces for new interview

Princess Diana's brother is set to make fresh revelations in another TV interview on Sunday, after a bruising week of bombshell allegations against King Charles

View 5 Images Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, has spoken in a new interview set to be aired on US TV

Princess Diana’s brother insists he is “not bitter” towards King Charles despite wild claims in his book triggering anger from Buckingham Palace.

‌



A war of words broke out in the wake of Earl Charles Spencer’s allegation Charles told him Diana would be forgotten “soon enough” after her death. Earl Spencer accused the then Prince Charles of launching into a furious tirade during a phone call in the days after the princess was killed in a Paris car crash, alongside her lover Dodi Fayed, in 1997.

‌



However, in a new interview set to air on Sunday in the US, the aristocrat insisted: “I’m absolutely not bitter. I can tell you. If I was bitter, this book would be... more bitter.”

‌



View 5 Images Prince Charles And Princess Diana pictured during their final royal tour together in Seoul in November 1992 (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Asked if he has any resentment towards the King or the royal family, including the late Queen, he added: "I'm not really in the business of resentment. I'm at the stage in my life where the past is the past, and some of it's worth recording.

"But I don't hold resentments, primarily because I don't think it's good for the person to do that themselves. I've let a lot go. I'm not a vengeful, resentful, person. I'm just an eyewitness to history."

‌



The Earl, 62, gave a sitdown interview to the US TV station CBS at his home at Althorp, Northamptonshire, ahead of the publication of his new book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, on Tuesday. The publication of extracts this week led to Buckingham Palace issuing a strongly worded rebuke just over an hour after the Earl’s claims were made public.

The extraordinary royal statement denied the claim and said the King is “mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”. In the new memoir, Earl Spencer also claims Charles had “sounded giddily elated” when he called him after Diana’s death. And he even alleges that he sounded like he had won the lottery.

View 5 Images Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry And Prince Charles watching Princess Diana's coffin depart Westminster Abbey on September 6, 1997 (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

‌



The book also includes the Earl claiming he hung up the phone on the then future King after telling him how he strongly disagreed with the royals' decision to have princes William and Harry – then aged just 15 and 12 – walk behind their mother’s coffin. He also claims in the tome that a lack of obvious care for Prince Harry at his mother’s funeral allowed him to “spin out of control” and that immediately after Diana's funeral he was told Queen Elizabeth had offered to restore his sister's Her Royal Highness title, which he rejected.

Asked by CBS Senior Foreign Correspondent Mark Phillips during the interview if he has any remaining relationship with King Charles, Earl Spencer said: "No, I don't actually. Look, he came into my life as a brother-in-law and that relationship ended.

"And so, you know, he's still my King. I respect the Crown, and that's it, but there's no personal relationship. He's a former brother-in-law to me, really, and he's my monarch and that's it." Earl Spencer added: "I always think people are amazed by how little I follow the royal family 'cause it's just not me. I have so many interests, but I'm not being rude about them... I'm not interested in the royal family."

‌



Speaking about his claims in a separate interview with BBC TV presenter Laura Kuenssberg this week, Earl Spencer said: "I’m telling the truth." He also alleged he had told friends and family "straight away" about an alleged outburst by the then Prince of Wales "because it wasso monstrous".

5 View 5 Images Prince Charles arm-in-arm with Diana on the day they announced their engagement in February 1981 (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images) 5 View 5 Images Earl Spencer's book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister will mark the first time he has spoken at length about his sibling, almost three decades after her death (Image: Penguin Random House/PA Wire)

Article continues below

Meanwhile, veteran journalist David Dimbleby today spoke about the ongoing row and claimed Princess Diana is "still deeply resented" inside Buckingham Palace. Mr Dimbleby, who spent decades covering royal events, told BBC Radio 4: "Diana was the prime example of someone who didn't act like the rest of the Royal Family - she was fresh, new and exciting to the public and they really adored her.

"And that was deeply resented in the palace. And still is. And this kind of tit for tat over who said what, and only two people know what was actually said just reignites all that."

Mr Dimbleby went on to describe the Royal Family as "a bit of a soap opera", but warned against the monarchy becoming "trapped in this cycle of gossip". He added: "People are fascinated and I think whenever any tittle tattle reaches the public domain, people sort of think about it in terms of their own families. "They all have problems and then suddenly... this family that is set up on a pedestal of being leaders of the country - they have problems too."

News.title: Tributes paid to London 'Millionaires' Row' victim, 28, stabbed to death with manhunt underway
News.content:
Tributes paid to London 'Millionaires' Row' victim, 28, stabbed to death with manhunt underway

Tributes have been paid to Reece Salmon, 28, who died after being stabbed in central London on Wednesday night

View 2 Images Reece Salmon, 28, died after being stabbed in Islington, London (Image: Metropolitan Police)

Tributes have been paid to a 28-year-old man who died after being stabbed on a central London street dubbed 'Millionaires' Row'.

‌



Reece Salmon was found with stab wounds on Lloyd Baker Street in Clerkenwell, Islington, on Wednesday night.

‌



The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at 11.20pm following reports of a stabbing. No arrests have been made in connection with the incident.

‌



Mr Salmon was taken to hospital by the London Ambulance Service and sadly died on Thursday. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specially trained officers.

View 2 Images The stabbing happened on Lloyd Baker Street in the Islington borough (Image: Google Maps)

In a statement, Mr Salmon's said: "We are utterly devastated by this loss. Reece was a loving partner and son, and he leaves behind many friends and loved ones. It is impossible to put our loss into words."

‌



Lloyd Baker Street is one of the more affluent residential addresses in Clerkenwell, featuring Grade II-listed Georgian terraced houses. Floral tributes have been placed on the street by the victim's loved ones.

A murder investigation has been launched and police were granted special stop and search powers in the area following the incident.

The Section 60 order enabled officers to search people without the usual requirement to have reasonable suspicion.

‌



It was in place in the Caledonian Road, Clerkenwell and Hoxton areas from 4pm on Friday until 6am on Saturday.

Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart, who leads policing in the area, said: "This is a tragic incident, and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young man who has lost his life.

"You can expect to see additional officers in the area providing visible reassurance and working with partners to keep the public safe.

Article continues below

"The victim was found in a residential street, and members of the public may have information of vital importance to our investigation. If you can help, please come forward."

Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101, quoting reference CAD 8475/16SEP.

Information can also be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or via the Crimestoppers website.

News.title: Tabby Stoecker's incredible life in a circus before starting new career due to Instagram ad
News.content:
Tabby Stoecker's incredible life in a circus before starting new career due to Instagram ad

Winter Olympics hero Tabby Stoecker is one of the stars taking part in the new series of Strictly Come Dancing

View 3 Images Tabby Stoecker will be on this year's Strictly Come Dancing (Image: BBC/Ray Burmiston)

Skeleton star Tabby Stoecker will hit the dance floor on Saturday night as she begins her stint on Strictly Come Dancing. Stoecker, 25, made history with teammate Matt Weston after winning mixed team gold at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics earlier this year.

‌



The highly decorated Team GB athlete only made her international debut in the sport five years ago and was turned on to the discipline by an Instagram advert.

‌



Speaking to BBC Breakfast in February, she elaborated: "I saw an advert on Instagram for Discover Your Gold Talent ID process and got selected for skeleton." Prior to that, Stoecker had a life in the circus, training in such activities as juggling and clowning.

‌



Stoecker told Olympics.com in November 2025: "When I was about 11, one of my friends was doing an open day at the National Centre for Circus Arts in London, and I just went along with her.

"And having a background in gymnastics as a very young kid, I was really up for this whole circus skills thing. One of the coaches asked me to audition for a scheme they have, which was to help kids get really, really good circus training basically, and it was a very holistic approach."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Stoecker trained from ages 11 to 17, with around 20-25 hours of training in addition to school. She added: "Someone does your schedule for you and helps you with managing school and all the training.

"To be honest, it was one of the most incredible things. It was an incredible opportunity for me and just the people that you were surrounded by. It was this massive community and they really cared about your well-being as well as your training. I think that just gave me a very well-rounded level of athletic ability."

View 3 Images Great Britain's Matt Weston and Tabby Stoecker with their gold medals (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire.)

‌



Her favourite circus act was the flying trapeze, which she believes helped her adjust to the dangerous and high-speed world of Skeleton.

"I had an incredible coach with that," she said. "You have to let go of a bar and fly around in the air and the adrenaline rush was incredible.

"I didn't know what skeleton was at that point, but I just wasn't sure I saw a career for myself in circus, and you're at that age where you're not sure about things, and I wanted to test some other stuff out.

‌



View 3 Images Olympic champion Tabby Stoecker opened up on his career (Image: Getty Images)

"I got accepted for skeleton and they taught me how to run, how to lift, and when I went out on the ice for the first time, that feeling of adrenaline was quite familiar, I guess. I had good spatial awareness and body awareness, and I just picked it up, and I guess the rest is history."

Ahead of joining Strictly, she said: "I am over the moon to be joining the cast of Strictly 2026. I’ve had the wildest year of my life so far, so to be rounding it off with a childhood dream of dancing in the Strictly ballroom is surreal and I can’t wait to get stuck in."

Article continues below

News.title: Man dies after falling from building in Liverpool city centre with police referred to watchdog
News.content:
Man dies after falling from building in Liverpool city centre with police referred to watchdog

A man in his 20s died after falling from a building in Liverpool city centre, Merseyside Police said

View Image Emergency services were called to Low Hill in Islington, Liverpool, on Friday afternoon (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A man in his 20s has died after falling from a building in Liverpool city centre.

‌



Emergency services were called to Low Hill, Islington, shortly after 1pm on Friday to reports of concern for the safety of a man on the roof of a building.

‌



Merseyside Police said the man subsequently fell and was taken to hospital, where he sadly died on Saturday. His family are being supported by specialist officers.

‌



Police said there are no suspicious circumstances surrounding his death.

"Due to police attendance at the scene shortly before the man sustained his injuries, a mandatory referral has been made to the IOPC [Independent Office for Police Conduct], which is standard practice in such events," the force said.

Article continues below

Paramedics and fire crews also attended the scene, where a large cordon was put in place to block traffic, the Liverpool Echo reports.

News.title: Major seaside hotel fire that evacuated guests during night treated as suspicious
News.content:
A fire at a seaside hotel where about 280 people were evacuated is believed to have been caused deliberately, police have said.

A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said.

Kent Police said that the fire was being treated as suspicious and is appealing for witnesses.

"Inquiries into the circumstances are under way," police said.

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.

A fresh cohort of famous faces â including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips â also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

News.title: The deadly new drugs reshaping Scotland's fight against addiction
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Davey says Lib Dems are 'firewall against Farage' as conference begins
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.

The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance.

On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state".

Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs.

Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak".

In an essay, external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"

She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".

Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that.

"If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives."

He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world.

"I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration."

Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government.

"One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said.

"Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well.

"We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform."

He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away".

Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union.

The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems.

"An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said.

"Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency.

"A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass."

Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink".

Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.

News.title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he is telling the truth about a phone call with Charles after Diana's death
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother said King Charles "went ballistic" during a phone call with him in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer spoke exclusively with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg about claims he has made in a new book, alleging the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly-worded response to the book claims, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Read more about Laura Kuenssberg's interview with Earl Spencer.

News.title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
News.content:
August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House.

It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance.

In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa.

Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued.

Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will."

Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does.

News.title: 'People forget we exist': Why older LGBTQ+ community fears losing identity
News.content:
As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.

But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.

She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.

The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.

Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation.

"It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says.

"In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."

He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.

Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.

News.title: Sex and dating for the sandwich generation - Sharon Horgan on her latest comedy Youth
News.content:
Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.

Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.

The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too.

And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.

I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters.

"We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, anâ¦ autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"

The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.

The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son".

Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent".

"And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"

But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work.

"I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says.

"I try to put all that in thereâ¦ and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."

She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.

The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy.

"This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
News.content:
One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".

The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.

In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK.

"In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."

He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.

Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.

Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."

Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.

Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.

Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".

Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, told the BBC: "Reforming parenting orders in this way risks being ineffective at best and counter-productive at worst.

"Criminalising parents is unlikely to help children who need support, and putting them behind bars would only put further strain on a failing prison system that is already bursting at the seams."

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum Â£1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all".

In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response".

The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14.

On Thursday, ministers met with local leaders and experts in Manchester to discuss how devolution could help reform youth justice.

Additional reporting by AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul & Shelley Phelps, political correspondent

News.title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
News.content:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
News.content:
Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief.

She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases.

"We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture.

"There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so.

"Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it."

Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve.

She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more.

"In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could."

For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said.

"The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say.

"People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'.

"It can mean even more coming from a stranger."

Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies.

"But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said.

Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do.

"So if anybody can find the way of looking at themselves and just thinking, this hurts right now because I'm decent, because I'm caring, because I have a heart. And I think that's a way of easing ourselves through it."

If you, or someone you know, have been affected by child bereavement, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
News.content:
Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them.

The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city.

"It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said.

Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates.

One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre.

"I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said.

"People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check.

"They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens."

News.title: Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice
News.content:
Reform UK's deputy leader has accused the party's former Senedd Member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd of lying to them about her political beliefs before she defected to Plaid Cymru.

Richard Tice was speaking after a chaotic week for his party in which its Welsh leader resigned after being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Helen Jenner, the party's deputy leader in Wales, is favourite to take over next week.

Tice insisted the events had not distracted the party from the issues it was tackling, saying there were good days and bad days in politics.

Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been "honest about her political beliefs" and had acknowledged her views had changed.

Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, made the dramatic political move to Plaid Cymru, claiming Reform UK was "far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions".

As well as saying she was now a supporter of Welsh independence, she also revealed she had voted to Remain in the EU referendum a decade ago.

News.title: UFC 331 LIVE: Fight card, start time, Van vs Pantoja updates and results tonight
News.content:
UFC 331: Joshua Van, Alexandre Pantoja get heated at press conference

Tonight, Alexandre Pantoja will try to wrest the UFC flyweight title from Joshua Van, after losing the belt to the young star in their first fight.

In December, Pantoja suffered a shoulder injury 26 seconds into his title defence against Van, as the latter became the second-youngest champion in UFC history – under bizarre circumstances.

Pantoja, 36, has not fought since then, while Van, 24, retained the gold against Tatsuro Taira in May. In the eyes of many fans, the Myanmar native legitimised his title reign with that win, surviving great adversity to ultimately stop Taira in a fight of the year contender.

But to really mark himself as the ‘true’ flyweight champion, must Van overcome Pantoja – a pound-for-pound star and divisional great – in emphatic fashion? Tonight, he gets the chance to do so when he defends the strap against the Brazilian at UFC 331.

News.title: No. 9 Texas A&M loses at home to Kentucky, meaning SEC will have two top-10 teams tumble
News.content:

The powerhouse Southeastern Conference will have at least two top-10 teams lose in Week 3.

It could be three if No. 10 Alabama doesn’t beat pesky Florida State.

Kentucky stunned No. 9 Texas A&M on the road Saturday, winning 31-21 behind three transfers: quarterback Kenny Minchey, running back CJ Baxter and safety Jordan Castell.

Minchey, a Notre Dame transfer, completed 14 of 18 passes for 252 yards and two touchdowns. He connected on his final 11 throws. Baxter, a former Texas standout, ran for 87 yards and two scores. Castell, a three-year starter at Florida, finished with a team-high 13 tackles and an interception.

“I’m not shocked,” first-year coach Will Stein said on the field afterward. “This is how these guys practiced every single day. This is what Kentucky football is supposed to look like. So proud of our guys coming on the road, the eye of the storm. How freaking cool is this? Let’s go!”

Stein, 36, replaced longtime Kentucky coach Mark Stoops in December and became the third first-year Wildcats coach to beat a top-10 team — first since Joker Phillips in 2010.

“We knew it was going to be a bar fight, a fistfight, old school,” Stein said. “We were the tougher team tonight. That’s how we won the game.

“This is what we wanted, BBN. Let’s freaking go!”

No. 7 LSU and eighth-ranked Ole Miss will finish later Saturday and provide another top-10 loss.

Alabama led Florida State 26-21 at halftime, rallying after trailing 21-6 early in the second quarter. It was an eye-popping deficit for a Crimson Tide team that shockingly lost at home to the Seminoles to open last season.

LSU-Ole Miss game is the one to watch

Lane Kiffin was wildly booed long before he arrived at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium on Saturday for the LSU-Ole Miss game.

Kiffin appeared remotely on ESPN's “College GameDay," and Mississippi fans still angry about how he left the Rebels for LSU late last season greeted him with a chorus of expletive-laced chants. It was a clear sign of what Kiffin and the Tigers should expect when they play at Ole Miss later Saturday.

“I really appreciate you guys gaslighting them with this,” Kiffin said from the team hotel.

It was the latest in a growing buildup for the first top-10 matchup between No. 7 LSU and eight-ranked Ole Miss since 1962.

It started when Kiffin left the Rebels to take the LSU job and a $91 million contract just as the team he had coached for six years was days away from its first appearance in the College Football Playoff. Kiffin wanted to stay through the playoff, but Ole Miss moved on to coach Pete Golding and advanced to the CFP semifinals. LSU finished 7-6, capped by a loss in the Texas Bowl.

The off-field storylines haven't stopped since. Kiffin's comments about whether Black players could be recruited to Ole Miss, lawsuits alleging Ole Miss transfers owe big money for reneging on their NIL deals and LSU’s now-abandoned defiance of rules against rostering former pro players have only brightened the spotlight for this one.

LSU threw another wrinkle into the mix by saying midweek that quarterback Sam Leavitt was “doubtful” to play, sparking immediate fan accusations of gamesmanship. He's been upgraded since and is expected to start.

Kiffin himself acknowledged there could be “hatred” in the stands Saturday. Security has been dramatically increased as authorities expect 100,000 people in Oxford, a town whose school-year population of about 25,000 is virtually all students.

The winner improves to 3-0 on the season — and gets savory bragging rights.

The undercard

There is a good one in the ACC: No. 16 SMU at No. 23 Louisville, the league leaders in total offense featuring SMU's Kevin Jennings (402.5 yard per game) and Louisville’s Lincoln Kienholz (375.0).

Both are eager to keep pace with No. 5 Miami, which beat Wake Forest 33-20 on Friday night as Darian Mensah completed 30 of 34 passes, including his first 24 attempts, for 220 yards and three touchdowns.

In the Big 12, two of the favorites opened league play with a terrific game Friday night in Lubbock, where No. 13 Texas Tech held on for a 28-26 win over No. 22 Houston. Cougars QB Conner Weigman came up just short of a 2-point conversion in the final minute, a play that went to the Big 12 replay review room — the broadcast audience was able to watch and listen to the analysis — before it was upheld.

Best of the rest

There also are several intriguing matchups pitting 2-0 teams that can be best viewed as measuring stick games, including Virginia Tech at Maryland, Mississippi State at South Carolina and these:

— Florida at Auburn. Gators QB Aaron Philo, who will make his first road start, has completed 76% of his passes with five touchdowns. Byrum Brown, who has been new Auburn coach Alex Golesh's starting QB for all or part of four seasons, was a 1,000-yard rusher last year.

— No. 25 Virginia vs. West Virginia in Charlotte, North Carolina. The Mountaineers, 2-0 for the first time since 2018, are playing their border-state rival for the first time since 2002.

A dog in a parachute briefly brought a London Fashion Week show to a standstill as British label Chopova Lowena sent canine models down a bowling alley runway.

The four-legged guest appeared reluctant to cross the gutter between the lanes, holding up the next model, who eventually had to overtake.

It was an unusually unscripted moment in a show that already featured dogs wearing capacious puffer jackets, futuristic headpieces and protective outfits that evoked a scene from science fiction more than a leafy park walk.

Another model carried a tiny dog bundled into a bright green inflatable coat, its head peeking out from the padded fabric.

open image in gallery A Chopova Lowena model holding the smallest canine model in a green puffer jacket (Jason Lloyd Evans/PA)

The dogs did not reappear for the final walk, leaving the human models to close the spring/summer 2027 show to a heavy metal soundtrack, with spectators packed along both sides of the bowling lanes.

The canine cast was part of an unlikely collaboration between Chopova Lowena and Lloyds Bank to raise awareness for the importance of insuring pets.

Designers Emma Chopova and Laura Lowena-Irons took the idea of dressing dogs to its logical extreme, creating a series of elaborate outfits inspired by everything from accidents to pet theft.

open image in gallery The dog’s seemed bemused by the set up (Jason Lloyd Evans/PA)

One dog wore a neon green airbag-style puffer jacket with black piping and an avant-garde headband, while another was dressed in an anti-theft outfit covered in protruding details, complete with a small security camera and flashing red light.

A third sported oversized goggles and a colourful parachute suspended above its back.

open image in gallery The three dogs who appeared on the runway in their outfits during a photoshoot before the show (Karl Hugill/PA)

The tongue-in-cheek designs were intended to demonstrate the lengths owners might have to go to protect their pets if clothing were their only defence against accidents.

For Chopova and Lowena-Irons, both dog owners themselves, the project was an opportunity to take the idea of keeping their pets safe to absurdly fashionable lengths.

Speaking ahead of the show, they said: “Our dogs are our worlds, so we know just how special pets are and how important it is to keep them safe.

“We felt passionately about finding a way to bring that feeling to life, letting our imaginations run wild and turning the idea of pet safety into an exciting visual representation.”

open image in gallery The smallest dog in the show getting dressed backstage (Karl Hugill/PA)

The label said the outfits were developed in consultation with veterinarians, who were also present during fittings and at the show, and that the dogs taking part were trained.

But the canine couture was only one part of a collection that embraced the sort of organised chaos Chopova Lowena has made its trademark.

Titled X/LUCKY SPIRIT LOST STRIKE/X, the spring/summer 2027 show took place on a bowling alley, with models walking along the wooden lanes as guests watched from either side.

The setting suited a collection that looked as though it had been assembled from the wardrobes of several varying subcultures.

There were checked skirts, oversized collars, graphic prints, layered jersey, brightly coloured tights and heavy footwear, with silhouettes drawn from school uniforms, vintage sportswear and Victorian dress alike.

open image in gallery Models doing the final walk for the Copova Lowena show (Jason Lloyd Evans/PA)

The brand’s characteristic clashing colours and textures appeared throughout, with green emerging as a particularly prominent shade, from the dog’s clothes to the models’ dresses and accessories.

A green floral dress with puffed sleeves and a row of oversized white buttons was paired with black lipstick and tousled hair, while other looks featured striped tops, red sequined trousers and patterned headscarves.

The styling was deliberately confrontational, with belts slung low over layered dresses, colourful socks worn with chunky shoes and fabrics that seemed to have been pulled from entirely different outfits.

open image in gallery Designers Copova and Lowena on the runway (Jason Lloyd Evans/PA)

Yet beneath the apparent disorder was the familiar Chopova Lowena formula, filled with folkloric references, punk styling and a willingness to make clothes push the confines of mainstream silhouettes.

Nearly a decade after launching their label, Chopova and Lowena-Irons have built a recognisable fashion vocabulary around upcycled textiles, kitschy prints and their distinctive carabiner-fastened skirts.

This season suggested they are still finding new ways to make it feel unexpected.

And while the human models offered plenty of outfit inspiration, it was difficult to compete with a tiny dog wearing what appeared to be an entire inflatable sofa.
