World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Independence Day fireworks give way to trade deal hopes
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s Independence Day on Sept. 16 was the focal point this past week, even as less celebratory news circulated. Over the weekend, 21-year-old Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, attending the Autonomous University of Morelos (UAEM) in Cuernavaca, Morelos, was stabbed and killed in Cuautla — the fourth femicide of a UAEM student just this year. On Thursday, Morelos authorities announced the arrest of a suspect, Francisco Javier “N,” but the attack on Tacoronte and the emergency medical response were met with indignation both locally and in Spain.

Also on Sept. 12, Pemex admitted it had contained another oil spill off the coast of Campeche, which the Navy and the state oil company moved quickly to seal and clean up — a contrast to the government’s slower handling of a major spill in February. Meanwhile, the peso spent most of the week trading above 17 to the dollar, weakening toward its worst week since March as markets digested the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, narrowing the Mexico-U.S. rate differential.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Industrial activity posts best growth in years

Mexico’s industrial sector delivered its strongest annual performance in nearly three years in July, with industrial activity up 2.4% in seasonally adjusted terms, according to INEGI — triple June’s 0.8% reading and the best showing since November 2023.

Construction led the gains, climbing 6.7% annually, while mining rose 1.6% and manufacturing grew 1.3%. Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, a second straight month of sequential gains. Still, industrial activity is up just 0.4% for the first seven months of 2026, a modest rebound after a 1.3% contraction in 2025, with manufacturing down 0.7% year-to-date. Economists at Grupo Financiero Monex expect only “moderate” growth ahead, citing USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

Coahuila is Mexico’s safest state

For the first time, Coahuila topped INEGI’s national safety perception survey, the 2026 ENVIPE, with just 27.8% of residents calling the state unsafe due to crime — a 9.9-point improvement that pushed Baja California Sur out of the top spot.

Coahuila registered only 100 homicides in 2025, a turnaround from more than 1,100 killings in 2012, when cartels such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel dominated large swaths of the state. Analysts credited beefed-up federal forces and prevention programs. Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, in office since December 2023, credited “great teamwork.” Nationally, the picture is less rosy: 74% of adults still consider their state unsafe, and México state overtook Morelos this year as Mexico’s least safe state, with 90% of respondents reporting security concerns.

Mexico’s independence is celebrated at home and abroad

On Tuesday night, President Sheinbaum delivered her second Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony before a crowd the Mexico City government estimated at more than 300,000 in the Zócalo, marking 216 years since Miguel Hidalgo’s original Cry of Dolores.

Sheinbaum issued 21 arengas honoring independence heroes including Hidalgo, Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario and Vicente Guerrero, alongside Mexico’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and migrants abroad, several of whom were included in a national Grito for the first time.

Abroad, Iran marked the holiday by lighting Tehran’s Azadi Tower in green, white and red, the first time the landmark has been illuminated in tribute to Mexico — an occasion the Mexican ambassador to Iran called “a great gesture of friendship.” In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani served as grand marshal of Brooklyn’s Mexican Independence Day parade, days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance mocked a Mexican flag-carrying protester at a Dallas rally.

Antitrust regulators probe Liga MX

Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has opened an investigation into whether Liga MX operates as a monopoly, examining whether a small group is unfairly controlling “affiliation, organization and access” to professional soccer competitions in violation of federal competition law. The probe follows Liga MX’s 2020 decision — upheld through the 2026-27 season by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — to scrap promotion and relegation with the second-tier Liga Expansión and end payouts to lower-tier clubs, a move Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed. No defendants have been named; the probe can run up to 120 business days and be extended. If wrongdoing is found, Liga MX and its clubs could face fines of up to 10% of annual income.

CFE advances Project Oasis in Baja California Sur

The Federal Electricity Commission unveiled Project Oasis BCS, a solar, battery and green hydrogen initiative meant to bring reliable power to the isolated Mulegé region, which has no direct connection to the national grid and has historically relied on fossil fuels.

The project pairs a 72-megawatt photovoltaic plant with a battery system, electrolyzers to produce hydrogen and fuel cells to convert it back into electricity for use when sunlight is scarce. CFE projects the initiative will serve 40,000 households and cut emissions equivalent to taking more than 31,000 vehicles off the road annually. If completed, it would be CFE’s first-ever green hydrogen power generation project.

Democracy index shows modest gains

According to International IDEA’s annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, Mexico’s democracy score edged up slightly in 2025 — Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — rising to 1.778 out of 4 from 1.770 the year before. The country improved in rule of law and participation, held steady in rights and declined in representation, its best-ranked category at 83rd out of 173 nations. Mexico ranked in the top 100 in only one of the four measured categories. The report’s authors flagged rising political polarization and “us versus them” identity politics as threats across Latin America, while separately noting democratic backsliding tied to the Trump administration’s consolidation of executive power in the U.S.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump cartel pressure

Responding to a Trump “presidential determination” pressuring Mexico to take “additional action” against cartels and arrest complicit officials, Sheinbaum turned the spotlight on U.S. drug consumption, asking what Washington is doing to curb domestic drug demand, money laundering and the flow of American-made weapons into Mexico.

“We don’t need to be judged from the outside,” Sheinbaum said, insisting “we know what Mexico’s problems are and we act against them every day.” Trump’s determination, submitted to Congress on Tuesday, named Mexico among 23 countries as major drug producers or transit points and singled out Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — on leave amid U.S. accusations of cartel collusion but still free — as an official Washington wants arrested. The exchange came a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mexico isn’t doing enough against cartels, even as he acknowledged Mexican efforts had increased.

Record fuel bust in Guanajuato

Authorities announced on Thursday that they had seized 59 million liters of stolen fuel at a property in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato — the largest single-site fuel bust in Mexican history and roughly five times last year’s record seizure in Tamaulipas. The operation traces to a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, which led investigators to the storage facility, capable of holding up to 80 million liters. No arrests had been made as of Friday, and officials say specialized personnel will be needed to safely handle the seized hydrocarbons. Guanajuato’s security minister said the bust would help choke off a funding source for organized crime in a state that has seen four smaller fuel-theft busts this year.

Trade talks hover ahead of US midterms

The fourth round of formal USMCA-related trade talks between Mexico and the United States is tentatively set for next week, with officials on both sides eager to hammer out a deal before U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework deal would benefit both governments: Trump wants an economic win as he risks losing control of Congress, while Mexico is contending with investor unease and a cooling economy. The push follows the collapse last month of parallel U.S.-Canada trade talks, making the Mexico-U.S. track an effort at an interim bilateral deal.

According to José Medina Mora, president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus.

Pups in the news

Rollo, an adopted mixed-breed puppy, is the National Palace’s newest resident, officially tasked with supporting “the emotional well-being of everyone,” per government videos; his brother Theo still awaits adoption, and the palace’s resident cats, including Coco and Zeus, remain in place.

In Morelia, a dog named Maple dressed as a taco stand won the city’s inaugural Patriotic Pup Contest, beating roughly 40 costumed competitors, with runners-up dressed as an elote-and-pork-loin vendor and a pozole bowl nearly twice their size.

Looking ahead

Next week brings a busy convergence of bilateral trade and security missions as well as the potential for currency swings.

The fourth round of USMCA-focused trade talks in Washington, D.C., could yield either a resolution or more setbacks. According to reporting by Politico, a preparatory call between Trump and Sheinbaum on Wednesday may have placed more topics on the discussion table than just Section 232 tariffs. However, Sheinbaum said after the call that “we’re making progress on trade issues.”

Any signs of progress or friction on tariffs are poised to move the peso. Meanwhile, 139 U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division are scheduled to land in Chihuahua on Sept. 20 for 11 days of joint training exercises with Mexican forces at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento, the military’s largest training facility.

World.title: Junípero Serra: A complex character with a controversial legacy
World.content:
Standing in the plaza of Jalpan de Serra, a town in Querétaro’s remote, mountainous Sierra Gorda, I gazed up in awe at an enormous, intricately designed mission. Having lived in California for 30 years, I was familiar with the missions, designed by the Franciscan priest Junípero Serra, and for whom one of the busiest freeways in the Bay Area is named. But none of the California missions I’d visited were anywhere near as elaborate and baroque as this structure. In fact, I later learned that the style of the five Sierra Gorda missions is known as “mestizo baroque.”

Junípero Serra, a priest from the island of Mallorca, achieved his dream of becoming a missionary in the Americas at the age of 36, in 1749. After disembarking in Veracruz, he refused to ride horseback to Mexico City, instead journeying on foot the entire 270 miles, despite a severe leg injury. Five months later, he walked another 175 miles from Mexico City to the Sierra Gorda. He used the motto siempre adelante (always forward) to drive his missionary zeal.

In the Sierra Gorda, he evangelized the local population and used the sweat of the Pame, local Indigenous people, to build the five missions that, 250 years later, would become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There are several reasons for the dramatic difference in style between the two sets of missions, those in the interior of Mexico and the later ones on the Pacific coast, from Baja California to present-day San Francisco.

Location

The Sierra Gorda missions were close to rich colonial centers, like Mexico City, Querétaro and Guadalajara, which served as supply hubs, as well as to well-established trade routes and ample financial backing from New Spain.

On the other hand, the missions in Alta California (now the U.S. state of California) were built in remote, isolated outposts, thousands of miles from supply ports. Few overland routes existed, which forced Serra to rely on infrequent supply ships.

Skilled labor

In Mexico, the local Pame and other Indigenous artisans had been carving stone for centuries. After being converted, they blended Catholic iconography with Indigenous symbols, creating a hybrid of rich, intricate facades that look as if carved from stone filigree rather than masonry.

In contrast, unskilled workers in Alta California used local sun-dried adobe bricks, timber and river stones, resulting in a much simpler style.

The goal of the missions

In Mexico, the imposing mission architecture was designed to convey permanent control over wealthy interior mining and agricultural zones, whereas in Alta California the missions were built as a military strategy. International law at the time required actual physical settlement to hold a region. Placing missions next to military forts along the coast created a visible barrier against Russian fur traders moving south from Alaska and British explorers from the Pacific Northwest.

Leadership style differences

In addition to architecture, Serra’s way of governing also differed. While he used the same forced Catholic conversion and paternalism in both areas, his treatment of the locals differed. In the Sierra Gorda, he spent nine years learning the Pame language, translating catechisms, teaching European farming techniques and helping the Pames defend their agricultural plots from predatory Spanish soldiers and landowners. And he allowed the well-integrated Pames a high degree of freedom.

In California, however, Serra’s treatment of the Indigenous people was very mixed. On one hand, he wrote letters and reports condemning the violence, rape and mistreatment of native women by Spanish military officers, even walking hundreds of miles to Mexico City to meet directly with the viceroy to secure a “bill of rights” for Indigenous people.

But he was a harsh disciplinarian. Indigenous people were subjected to confinement in crowded, unsanitary conditions; forced labor; and corporal punishment if they tried to leave. Tragically, the isolated missions in Baja and Alta California also became vectors for European epidemic diseases, to which the local population had no immunity, leading to huge population decline, whereas the Pame had already developed relative immunity.

Reactions to Serra’s canonization

Pope Francis canonized Serra in 2015, during a visit to the United States. After such a complicated life, it’s no wonder that his canonization was greeted with very mixed reactions, especially in the U.S. Many traditional Hispanics cheered the decision, seeing it as a long-overdue acknowledgment by the Church of the role the Spanish-speaking missionaries played in bringing the faith to the Americas.

Others condemned the canonization, protesting at the archdioceses in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., and dubbing Serra the “saint of genocide.” They were also disappointed that Pope Francis canonized Serra when only a few months earlier he had apologized for the “grave sins” committed against Indigenous peoples during the conquest of the Americas.

Mexicans were ambivalent. Because most Mexicans are mestizo — a mix of Spanish Catholic and Indigenous — people wrestled with practicing a deep faith that they loved, yet with the painful awareness that it was introduced through brutal colonial subjugation.

Clearly, Junípero Serra was a complex character. On one hand, he went out of his way to defend Indigenous and women’s rights, yet at the same time betrayed a lack of respect for their human dignity and agency. I suspect he will always be viewed as a complicated historical figure with a controversial legacy.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: The story of Hotel Mocambo, Mexico’s original luxury beach resort
World.content:
When it comes to tourism in Mexico, one of the most popular options for international visitors is to spend a few nights at a majestic beach resort. From Cancún to Los Cabos, Mexico has established itself as a premier destination for world-class beach getaways, with Mexico’s Ministry of Tourism reporting that nearly half of Mexico’s visitors opt for ritzy coastal areas — where sprawling luxurious properties abound.

The shift toward Mexico’s coastline

The numbers show just how vital Mexico’s top-tier beaches are to its national tourism economy: Despite an overall lower number of visitors this year and a massive blow from U.S. airlines this summer, Cancún still leads the nation in international flight arrivals, accounting for 45% of Mexico’s airport activity as of June, with 4,844,588 reported flight arrivals.

Besides Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey, which are among the 10 most active airports in Mexico, every other visit is largely due to Mexico’s beaches. This year, Los Cabos, Puerto Vallarta, Tulum, Cozumel and Mazatlán have generated the most airport traffic, respectively, with roughly 66% of Mexico’s inbound flights touching down near those beaches.

And yet, Mexico’s identity as a destination for opulent beach resorts originated in a region that is nowadays overlooked, particularly by international visitors. But if you know where to look, a time-travel beach experience awaits along the Gulf Coast, with its own kind of grandeur and charm.

Hotel Mocambo: Mexico’s first grand luxury resort

It’s impossible to overstate the historical significance of Veracruz and its port city, where the Spanish colonization of continental Latin America began in 1519. Over centuries, many of the country’s earliest contributions can be traced back to its Gulf Coast origins, including coffee, jalapeños, vanilla and more.

Add to that list: Mexico’s first grand luxury beach resort.

In 1938, Hotel Mocambo — named after Playa Mocambo, the beach where the hotel was built, and which originally derived from an Afro-Portuguese word denoting the region’s legacy as a refuge for escaped African slaves — began construction, making it among the earliest (if not the first) major beachfront resort in all of Mexico.

A midcentury haven for Mexican stars and cinema

During its heyday, Hotel Mocambo became a national treasure, with famous Mexican actors, musicians and celebrities — including Agustín Lara, Chavela Vargas and Pedro Infante — becoming regulars throughout the midcentury.

In 1943, “María Eugenia,” starring the iconic Mexican actress María Félix (and featuring a cameo from popular Veracruz singer Toña la Negra, who also personally frequented the hotel in those days), was filmed at Mocambo, demarcating the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.

Mocambo began as a 15-room property with a palm tree-studded view of the coastline to be enjoyed from extensive outdoor terrazas, grand staircases, arched hallways and open-air patios. A large outdoor pool and nearby barroom with high ceilings and jacuzzis can be found on separate levels, with a staircase that connects everything and inevitably descends to the beach.

Spanish influence and architectural expansion

The hotel’s walkways are breezy and bedecked with a combination of maritime decorations and Moorish structural features designed by Jesús Martí Martín, an avant-garde architect who was exiled from Madrid, Spain, after the Spanish Civil War. Martín was commissioned by Gov. Miguel Alemán Valdés to lead the hotel’s design atop the highest coastal hill in Boca del Río — the city just south of the port of Veracruz, which sits on the Jamapa River along the Gulf of Mexico — around the time that other beach hotels were starting to sprout up in the Pacific states of Guerrero and Sonora.

Under the governorship of Alemán Valdés, who would go on to become Mexico’s president, Hotel Mocambo aimed to become the first grand-scale beach resort attraction in all of Mexico.

And for a time, it was.

Just two years after opening, the hotel’s first expansion was overseen by another Spanish architect, Enrique Segarra. At one point, the hotel grew to include 110 rooms, though today that number has dwindled to 70 (for context, Mexico’s grandest beach resorts can now exceed more than 2,000 rooms).

Though it is no longer the nexus of Mexican aristocracy that it once was, Mocambo remains an important historical fixture in Mexico’s development as an attractive beach resort destination.

Preserving the legacy of Mexico’s Golden Age

Before Mocambo and the subsequent rise of beach resorts all over Mexico, the country’s most opulent buildings and high-end tourist attractions were centered in Mexico’s cosmopolitan inland cities. Not until Mocambo in Veracruz — and the rise of Acapulco shortly after — did Mexico gain extreme popularity for its prime coastal real estate and beach resort culture.

Ironically, or perhaps symbolically, the once-tranquil escape of Mocambo is now surrounded by modern buildings, major avenues, parking lots and the nonstop bustle of Mexico’s largest port city on the Gulf Coast. One of the neighboring buildings is a recently built high-rise apartment that juxtaposes interestingly with the dilapidated glory of Hotel Mocambo. And the state’s largest and most glamorous mall is within a short walking distance, as modernity has crept up to overtake Mocambo’s place.

Although the paint is faded and signs of decay are apparent in its grand facades, the resort is still worthy of a visit — simply for the pleasure of reliving Mexico’s Golden Age origins of beachside luxury.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong About the Peso at 37’: An MND podcast
World.content:
Despite the recent weakening from the U.S. Fed interest rate increase, the Mexican peso has been on a tear. Just recently, it was at a multi-year high against the US dollar and below 17.

The peso’s strength has defied just about every single analyst and expert. Even our own MND Peso Index estimates that the peso is nearly 6% overvalued against the dollar.

Recently, I did some analysis and calculated that if the peso had performed since the year 2020 as it did over the previous 25 years, it would currently be at 37 pesos to the US dollar! I wrote about it here: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO.

So how can it be that it is currently trading at less than half of that rate? And can we expect it to devalue again anytime soon?

World.title: The ‘problem’ with Mexico’s 44% growth in exports: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A recent headline took just about everyone by surprise: Mexico’s export revenue in July of this year hit US $81 billion, up 44%. Think about that for a moment — an annualized run rate of nearly $1 trillion of export revenue for the country. Last year, exports hit a record $665 billion on 7.6% growth, up from $417 billion in 2020. So far this year through July, exports are up an impressive 27.7%. As a result, Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, far surpassing No. 2 Canada and No. 3 China. China had been the leader for years until Mexico overtook it in the years following the COVID pandemic.

One would think that a 44% growth in exports would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy … but is it really as good as it sounds? Let’s dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding:

1. Most of the growth has come from the category of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances, which increased by a massive 134% in July. For the first time in that month, Mexico’s exports in that category exceeded the category of auto and auto parts. That category had previously led Mexico’s export revenue figures for decades. I recently wrote about that development here: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO. Automotive exports have been roughly flat year-to-date, and oil exports are actually down. In other words, the vast majority of the export growth is not coming from a diverse set of industries but rather this one segment.

2. Import growth is also booming. Year-to-date, imports are up 25.6%, and in the month of July, imports exceeded exports. Mexico actually had a rare trade deficit in July as imports grew by 45.7%.

3. Mexico has begun to import a massive amount of products from Taiwan, growing by over 200% so far this year and hitting nearly US $40 billion in the first half of the year. For some perspective, Mexico only imported $14 billion from Taiwan in the same period last year. Mexican imports of Taiwanese products increased by only $2 billion in the first six months of 2025, compared to 2024.

4. The massive year-to-date import and export growth numbers are not resulting in an economy that is growing as much as would be expected or hoped. One would think that such a huge increase in exports would dramatically increase production capacity investment and domestic consumption. But neither is happening. Estimates vary, but Mexican GDP is generally only expected to grow in the 1.2%-1.5% range — only half of what is expected in the United States this year.

So what is going on here?

It’s important to look deeper into what is actually happening to these imports and exports, specifically analyzing two measures related to value added:

Domestic value added embodied in the exports (How much Mexican labor is going into the exports?) Mexican-origin content (How much Mexican product is going into the exports?)

What we see is that the rapidly growing electronics category is extremely low in both measures. Said differently, given the high value of the products, the actual amount of Mexican labor and Mexican-origin content going into them is minimal. It is estimated that less than 3% of the exported value of products in this category is Mexican added value — just 3 cents on the dollar! A cynic might say that Mexico is doing little more than receiving the product from Taiwan, adding a “Made in Mexico” sticker and then exporting it — and that cynic wouldn’t be too far from the current reality!

For some perspective, that is barely a tenth of the value that Mexico adds to products in the vehicle segment. Engineering, design, parts manufacturing and assembly in Mexico are all common in that industry. And here is where the real opportunity for Mexico comes in. If Mexico could capture more of the added value in the massive, fast-growing electronics category, it would be hugely impactful on employment in the country. So how can that happen?

Enter the USMCA negotiations. Mexico and the United States have had many rounds of discussions on the updated trade agreement, and despite clear disagreement in certain areas (I’m looking at you, Mexican tomatoes!), increased local content or value added requirements in areas like electronics seems to be an area of agreement and alignment. It is in both countries’ interests to shorten the supply chain and further “de-risk” from China and Taiwan. And it is in both countries’ interests to have more control of the production and supply of such a critical product line.

So will it happen? I am optimistic for a positive outcome given that both countries have similarly aligned interests. Stay tuned to MND as we bring you the developments in this critically strategic area.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Caribbean Reparations Chief Says Slavery Justice Push Is in Final Phase
World.content:
Barbados · Caribbean

Key Facts — The story. Hilary Beckles says the Caribbean reparations movement has entered its final phase. — Why it matters. CARICOM seeks slavery reparations from Britain and other former enslaving nations. — The background. In March, the UN called the transatlantic slave trade humanity’s gravest crime. — The numbers. That UN resolution passed with 123 votes, while three countries voted against. — The catch. The United States says there is no legal right to reparations for such wrongs. — What comes next. Delegates in Barbados are to adopt an action plan for 2027 to 2031.

Caribbean governments have pressed former colonial powers for slavery reparations through a regional commission set up in 2013. Their leading campaigner now says the movement has entered its final phase.

Barbados’s Parliament Buildings in Bridgetown. Photo: Barry Haynes / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Sir Hilary Beckles, who chairs CARICOM’s reparations commission, said on 18 September 2026 that the movement was in its final phase. “This is the final eruption of this movement, and we are not going to retreat,” he told delegates, Barbados Today reported.

Why This Matters

CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, is a regional bloc made up mostly of former British colonies. Its Ten-Point Plan demands reparatory justice from the United Kingdom, other European states and “all enslaving nations”, according to CARICOM.

On 25 March 2026, the UN General Assembly declared the trafficking and chattel enslavement of Africans “the gravest crime against humanity”. Ghana tabled the resolution for the African Group, and it passed with 123 votes in favour, UN News reported.

Three countries voted against and 52 abstained, while the text called reparations claims a concrete step towards remedy. The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against, and Washington said it recognises no legal right to such reparations.

What Beckles Said

“We are now in the fifth wave, and our position is this is it,” Beckles said, Barbados Today reported. Earlier waves ranged from enslaved people seeking pay for stolen labour to land petitions after emancipation, the paper said.

He unveiled a revised Ten-Point Plan that now places the experience of enslaved women at its centre. He said “only an enslaved woman can give birth to a slave child”, explaining how slave law passed bondage through mothers.

He said Barbados imported 600,000 Africans, yet only 83,000 enslaved people remained at emancipation in 1834. For Jamaica, he cited 1.5 million Africans imported and 300,000 remaining at emancipation.

The conference runs from 17 to 19 September under the theme “Reparatory Justice as the Coming Enlightenment”. Organisers said delegates would adopt an action plan for 2027 to 2031 with measurable targets, the Jamaica Observer reported.

What Is Not Yet Known

The full text of the revised plan was not published in the reports reviewed by The Rio Times. It is also unclear how European governments named in the plan will respond to the new push.

The conference’s final declaration and the targets in the new action plan had not been released at the time of writing. The reports reviewed do not say whether leaders will take the revised plan to any specific government.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does CARICOM want from former colonial powers? Its Ten-Point Plan seeks reparatory justice from the United Kingdom, other European states and all enslaving nations. A revised version was presented in Barbados in September 2026. What did the UN decide on the slave trade in 2026? On 25 March 2026, the General Assembly called the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity. The vote was 123 in favour, three against and 52 abstentions.

World.title: US Prosecutors Say Marset Threatened or Killed Police He Could Not Corrupt
World.content:
Uruguay · Security

Key Facts — The story. US prosecutors say Marset threatened or killed officers he could not corrupt. — Why it matters. He is accused of running a cocaine pipeline from South America to Europe. — The background. Bolivian police captured him in March 2026 and handed him to US agents. — The details. Prosecutors link him to a 2020 grenade attack on Uruguay’s anti-drug police. — The catch. He has pleaded not guilty, and none of these allegations has been proven. — What comes next. His trial in a Virginia federal court is set for 11 January 2027.

Sebastián Marset, accused of running one of South America’s largest cocaine networks, faces trial in the United States. US prosecutors now say he met resistance from police with threats or killings.

The port of Montevideo, Uruguay. Photo: Fedaro / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

US Justice Department prosecutors said Marset “threatened or killed” police officers he could not corrupt, la diaria reported on 18 September 2026. The filing answers defence motions in the federal court for the Eastern District of Virginia, where the Uruguayan has pleaded not guilty.

Why This Matters

US prosecutors accuse Marset of leading the Primer Cartel Uruguayo, or First Uruguayan Cartel, which they say shipped cocaine to Europe. He was captured in Bolivia in March 2026 and flown to the US, as The Rio Times reported at the time.

Paraguay has sought him in drug and money-laundering cases and investigates him over the 2022 murder of prosecutor Marcelo Pecci. Uruguay had no open case against him at the time of his capture, Ámbito reported, so it could not seek his extradition.

What the Prosecutors Argue

The filing rejects the defence claim that the case amounts to vindictive prosecution, according to la diaria. Prosecutors called Marset one of the world’s most prolific and violent drug traffickers, the Montevideo daily reported.

They argued that the alleged violence served to advance his organisation, protect his freedom and intimidate others. Montevideo Portal reported in June that prosecutors accuse him of ordering a 2020 grenade attack on Uruguay’s anti-drug police headquarters.

The same filing said he ordered threatening messages to Mónica Ferrero, then an anti-drug prosecutor and now Uruguay’s interim attorney general. In September 2025, attackers fired shots and set off a grenade at Ferrero’s home in Montevideo, Infobae reported.

Investigators suspected a local gang that they said worked in coordination with Marset, according to the same report. A superseding indictment filed in late June added narcoterrorism conspiracy, cocaine and money-laundering charges to an earlier laundering count.

Judge Rossie Alston Jr. has set the trial for 11 January 2027, OCCRP reported. Marset denies the charges, and he has accused DEA agents of trying to extort about US$4 million in cryptocurrency.

What Is Not Yet Known

The public part of la diaria’s report does not say which killings prosecutors attribute to Marset. None of the violence allegations has been tested in court, and Marset is presumed innocent.

The court has not yet ruled on the defence motions that the filing answers. It is also unclear whether Paraguay will pursue its own charges after the US trial.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Sebastián Marset being prosecuted? He faces charges in the federal court for the Eastern District of Virginia, with trial set for January 2027. Paraguay also has cases against him. Has Marset been convicted in the United States? No. He has pleaded not guilty, and the allegations against him have not been proven in court.

World.title: Haiti Police Push Into Kenscoff as Kidnapping Fear Grips Port-au-Prince
World.content:
Haiti · Security

Key Facts — The story. Haitian police launched an operation in gang-hit Kenscoff on 16 and 17 September. — Why it matters. Kenscoff guards the hill route above Port-au-Prince, the capital gangs largely dominate. — The background. Gangs have attacked Kenscoff repeatedly since January 2025, killing and kidnapping residents. — The numbers. A rights group counts at least 164 dead and over 70 kidnapped there. — The catch. The mayor reports advances, but no results of the operation have been published. — What comes next. The UN-backed Gang Suppression Force’s mandate expires on 30 September.

Haiti’s gangs have pushed from the capital into the farming hills of Kenscoff, leaving a trail of massacres. A new police operation there has given the local mayor a glimmer of hope, Le Nouvelliste reported.

The hills of Kenscoff, above Port-au-Prince, Haiti. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Haiti’s National Police began operations in Kenscoff on the evening of 16 September and continued them through 17 September. Le Nouvelliste, Haiti’s oldest daily, cited Mayor Massillon Jean as saying police had made advances on the ground.

Why It Matters Beyond Haiti

Kenscoff is a hillside farming commune above Port-au-Prince, long seen as relatively safe. Gangs have attacked it since January 2025, according to Le Nouvelliste.

In late August 2026, an attack blamed on the Viv Ansanm gang coalition killed at least 47 people, Africanews reported. More than 50 people were kidnapped in that attack, and 25 homes were set on fire.

AP reported on 17 September that rights group RNDDH counted at least 164 dead and over 70 kidnapped in Kenscoff. Its report accused police commanders of passivity and said security in the area had been cut by 60 percent.

Fear in the Capital

A second Le Nouvelliste piece, by Roberson Alphonse, describes rising dread over kidnappings across Port-au-Prince. The article lists schoolchildren seized in Silo, Delmas 33, and a doctor taken with his wife and child in Bourdon.

It also mentions a well-known journalist and three children seized on Friday on their way to school. Juno7 reported that at least five pupils were abducted in Bois-Verna on 18 September, three from one family.

The International Force

UN Security Council Resolution 2793 authorised the Gang Suppression Force on 30 September 2025, capped at 5,550 personnel. Security Council Report said 1,083 military personnel had deployed by 8 July 2026.

The same report said the force began operations on 1 June 2026 but has worked at limited capacity. It expects full operational readiness between October and the end of 2026.

Its mandate expires on 30 September, and Haiti’s foreign minister has called for renewal, Al Jazeera reported. Haiti plans elections on 13 December 2026, its first in a decade.

What Is Not Yet Known

Le Nouvelliste has not reported arrests, casualties or seizures from the Kenscoff operation. It is not clear whether the international force took part or whether police will hold the ground.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Kenscoff? It is a farming commune in the hills above Port-au-Prince. Gangs have attacked it repeatedly since January 2025. What is the Gang Suppression Force? It is an international anti-gang force authorised by the UN Security Council in September 2025. Its current mandate expires on 30 September 2026.

World.title: Panama Audit Office to Send Ex-Public Works Minister Probe to Prosecutors
World.content:
Panama · Politics

Key Facts — The story. Panama’s comptroller will send a probe of ex-minister Rafael Sabonge to prosecutors. — Why it matters. Sabonge ran public works under Laurentino Cortizo, overseeing the Fourth Canal Bridge. — The background. Auditors are examining possible unjustified enrichment, a preliminary finding, not a charge. — The numbers. Auditors cite a gap of US$704,452.61 between his known income and spending. — The catch. The comptroller calls the case preliminary and says the figure may change. — What comes next. The file goes to the Public Ministry once the audit’s procedures are finished.

Panama’s audit office has opened a series of inquiries into officials from the previous government. The most prominent target so far is Rafael Sabonge, the former public works minister.

The Pacific side of the Panama Canal, where the Fourth Bridge is under construction, in January 2026. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

Comptroller General Anel Flores said on 18 September that the Sabonge probe will go to the Public Ministry, Panama’s prosecutors. La Estrella de Panamá reported that the referral will follow once the audit office completes its procedures.

Why It Matters for Panama

Sabonge headed the Ministry of Public Works from 2019 to 2024 under President Laurentino Cortizo. The ministry manages Panama’s largest state infrastructure contracts, including roads, bridges and hospitals.

The best-known project of his tenure is the Fourth Bridge over the Panama Canal. La Estrella reported that design changes, including dropping a monorail component, are under scrutiny for alleged cost overruns.

Panama uses the US dollar, so all amounts here are in dollars. The Contraloría, Panama’s comptroller general, audits public funds but cannot itself bring criminal charges.

What the Auditors Found

According to La Estrella, forensic auditors found known income of US$993,534.05 against spending of US$1,697,986.56. That leaves an unexplained gap of US$704,452.61, which the audit office treats as possible unjustified enrichment.

Resolution 2766-2026-DNAJ/MP of 8 September ordered a precautionary seizure of assets up to that amount. La Estrella reported that it covers two apartments, three bank accounts and registered vehicles.

Flores said the case is at an initial stage and called the figure preliminary, able to rise or fall. He added that his office is also investigating other former and current officials.

Earlier Complaints

Destino Panamá reported that prosecutors admitted a separate criminal complaint against Sabonge and others in May 2025. The current public works minister has also filed a complaint over alleged negligence on the Fourth Bridge project.

Attorney General Luis Gómez said on 15 September he had not been told whether any file had reached anti-corruption prosecutors. He cited the presumption of innocence and the rules that bar him from discussing named people before a verdict.

La Estrella also listed a contract of about US$6.9 million with SmartBrix Centroamérica for modular hospitals among decisions under review. The paper stressed that the asset seizure is a precautionary measure, not a conviction.

What Is Not Yet Known

Sabonge has not been charged, and no statement from him appeared in the reports reviewed by The Rio Times. It is not known when the file will reach prosecutors or whether they will open a criminal case.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Rafael Sabonge? He was Panama’s minister of public works from 2019 to 2024 under President Laurentino Cortizo. He has not been charged with any crime. What does the comptroller allege? Auditors cite a preliminary gap of US$704,452.61 between his known income and spending. The comptroller says the figure may change.

World.title: Panama Runner-Up Lombana Met Convicted Ex-President Martinelli in Colombia
World.content:
Panama · Politics

Key Facts — The story. Anti-corruption politician Ricardo Lombana met ex-president Ricardo Martinelli in Colombia. — Why it matters. Lombana built his brand opposing the corruption Martinelli was convicted of. — The background. Martinelli lives in Colombia under asylum after a money-laundering conviction in Panama. — The numbers. Lombana came second in 2024 with 24.59 percent of the presidential vote. — The catch. Lombana’s party MOCA says the meeting was dialogue, not an electoral alliance. — What comes next. Parties are positioning for Panama’s 2029 election amid a fight over electoral rules.

Panama’s opposition is already manoeuvring for the 2029 election, three years early. Now the country’s leading anti-corruption candidate has met the ex-president he long criticised.

Ricardo Martinelli during an official visit while president of Panama. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

MOCA, the party of 2024 runner-up Ricardo Lombana, confirmed on 18 September that he met former president Ricardo Martinelli in Colombia. El Siglo reported that the party denied any electoral pact for 2029, saying “listening is not making a pact”.

Why It Matters Beyond Panama

Ricardo Lombana leads MOCA, the Movimiento Otro Camino, or Another Way Movement. He finished second in the May 2024 presidential election with 24.59 percent, behind José Raúl Mulino.

Mulino replaced Martinelli on the ticket after his upheld conviction barred the former president from running. Martinelli, president from 2009 to 2014, was sentenced in 2023 to 128 months for money laundering in the New Business case.

La Prensa reported that the Supreme Court rejected three constitutional challenges to the sentence in an October 2025 ruling. He left Panama’s Nicaraguan embassy for Colombia on 10 May 2025 and has lived there under territorial asylum since.

Colombia classed him as politically persecuted, which La Prensa said shields him from extradition there. Those protections end if he leaves Colombian territory, according to the same report.

What MOCA Said

El Siglo reported that MOCA secretary Mario Pinzón confirmed the meeting in a party statement. The statement said the encounter was not a political agreement or an electoral alliance for 2029.

MOCA said its position on corruption and on court rulings “has not changed and will not change”. La Estrella de Panamá quoted the party saying its “sole alliance is with Panamanians”.

MOCA used the statement to criticise proposed electoral changes, including raising party registration thresholds from 2 to 3 percent. It also opposed a financing split of 93 percent for parties and 7 percent for independent candidates.

The Reaction

Eco TV reported on 19 September that the Bancada Seguimos legislative caucus said “we do not make pacts with the corrupt”. The group pledged to oppose any amnesty proposal in the National Assembly.

What Is Not Yet Known

La Prensa reported the visit took place in early August at a Bogotá clinic during Martinelli’s spine surgery. Martinelli’s lawyer Alejandro Pérez told La Prensa the two men have since spoken by phone.

Neither camp has disclosed what the two discussed, and Martinelli has not commented publicly. Martinelli presides over Realizando Metas, the party that carried Mulino to power in 2024.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Ricardo Lombana? He is the founder and leader of MOCA, a Panamanian anti-corruption movement. He finished second in the 2024 presidential election. Why is Ricardo Martinelli in Colombia? He was sentenced in Panama to 128 months for money laundering. Colombia granted him asylum, and he arrived there in May 2025.

World.title: Honduran Critics Call Próspera’s New Officials a ‘Modern Coup’
World.content:
Honduras · Politics

Key Facts — The story. Honduran activists accuse the Próspera zone of a ‘modern coup’ against national sovereignty. — Why it matters. Honduras’s top court declared such private charter zones unconstitutional in 2024. — The background. Próspera named its own civil prosecutor on Roatán island on 15 September. — The numbers. Próspera first sought US$10.775 billion in arbitration, later US$1.63 billion as an alternative. — The catch. The coup claim is the critics’ view, reported by Criterio, not a legal finding. — What comes next. Activists want the Supreme Court and prosecutors to enforce the 2024 ruling.

Próspera, a libertarian-backed private city on a Honduran island, keeps operating two years after its legal basis was struck down. Critics now say its latest appointments amount to a “modern coup” against the state.

The Próspera zone on the Honduran island of Roatán. Photo: ReasonTV / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

On 15 September 2026, Próspera named lawyer Alberto Hernández Franks as “fiscal civil”, a civil prosecutor enforcing its own rules. Honduran outlet Criterio.hn reported on 18 September that civil-society leaders called the move a coup against Honduran sovereignty.

Why This Matters

Próspera is a ZEDE, or Zone for Employment and Economic Development, on Roatán in the Bay Islands. A 2013 law let such zones write their own rules, courts and taxes, with long guarantees of legal stability.

Congress repealed that law unanimously in April 2022, and the Supreme Court declared the zones unconstitutional on 20 September 2024. Criterio reported that eight of 15 justices backed voiding the framework from its origin.

Próspera answered the repeal with an international arbitration claim against the Honduran state. The dispute now falls to the government of President Nasry Asfura, whose National Party created the zones.

What the Critics Say

The appointment was announced on Honduras’s independence day, Criterio reported on 17 September. According to the zone, Hernández Franks will enforce its civil, tax and administrative rules.

Constitutional lawyer Joaquín Mejía wrote on X that Próspera keeps operating and has named a “fiscal civil”. A delegation from the Unidad Popular Hondureña, a civil-society coalition, asked the Supreme Court to enforce its 2024 ruling.

Fernando García, former presidential commissioner against the ZEDEs, described “a type of coup” carried out through international arbitration. Pedro Rafael Alegría of the peasant movement Vía Campesina said the zone acts as a parallel state.

The Arbitration and Próspera’s Position

Próspera filed a US$10.775 billion claim under CAFTA-DR, the US-Central America trade pact, in December 2022. Its October 2025 memorial at ICSID, the World Bank’s arbitration body, seeks restoration of its rights first.

As an alternative, it asks for US$1.63 billion in damages plus US$1 million for moral harm. The company wrote that it “would much prefer a constructive dialogue with Honduras to arbitration”.

After the 2024 ruling, Próspera warned of “a climate of insecurity and uncertainty for investors and employees”, Reuters reported. Honduras’s exit from ICSID took effect on 25 August 2024, and it rejoined from 16 August 2026.

What Is Not Yet Known

Criterio’s report carried no response from Próspera to the coup accusation. It is unclear whether the Supreme Court, prosecutors or the Asfura government will act on the activists’ demands.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Próspera? Próspera is a privately run charter zone on Roatán, created under Honduras’s ZEDE law. It says its rights are protected by legal stability guarantees and CAFTA-DR. Is Próspera legal in Honduras? The Supreme Court declared the ZEDE framework unconstitutional in 2024. Próspera disputes the consequences and is pursuing international arbitration.

World.title: Brazil’s Spy Agency Flags ‘Critical’ US Pressure Before October Vote
World.content:
Brazil · Elections 2026

Key Facts — The story. Brazil’s intelligence agency rated US pressure on the 2026 election as critical. — Why it matters. Brazilians vote on 4 October, and polls show a statistical tie. — The background. Washington has used tariffs, sanctions and terror listings against Brazilian targets. — The details. The confidential report went to the presidency, electoral court and Justice Ministry. — The catch. Published excerpts describe political pressure, not tampering with votes or machines. — What comes next. Lula and Trump both address the UN General Assembly on 22 September.

Relations between Brasília and Washington have soured over tariffs, sanctions and crime policy during the campaign. Brazil’s own spies now describe that pressure as a critical risk to the October vote.

The Palácio do Planalto in Brasília, which received the Abin report. Photo: Senado Federal / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Abin, Brazil’s federal intelligence agency, sent a confidential warning about US pressure on the election in late August. Folha de S.Paulo columnist Mônica Bergamo revealed the report, and Metrópoles and CNN Brasil followed on 19 September.

Why This Matters

Brazil holds the first round of its general election on 4 October 2026. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a race that recent polls show as a statistical tie.

The assessment was classified, so it became public only through a leak to the press. It also lands days before Lula plans to warn Donald Trump at the UN not to interfere in the vote.

What the Report Says

According to Gazeta do Povo and Brasil de Fato, the document is titled “Threats to the 2026 electoral process”. It went to the presidential palace, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) and the Justice Ministry, CNN Brasil reported.

Metrópoles said Abin raised the possibility of US interference to a “nível de criticidade”, or critical level. The agency saw a “selective intensification and reconfiguration” of US pressure on Brazil, according to the same report.

CNN Brasil said Abin drew on Trump administration documents from November 2025 to May 2026. Those papers list goals such as reducing rival powers’ influence in Latin America, the agency noted.

Abin cited US Treasury sanctions of 1 July on two Brazilians and four firms allegedly tied to the PCC gang. It also named Secretary of State Marco Rubio as central to the pressure, Metrópoles reported.

The report recalls a White House draft declaration asking Brazil not to limit “political dissidents” at the polls. Brasil de Fato said the report stresses political, economic and diplomatic pressure rather than direct manipulation of the vote.

How Each Side Has Responded

Lula has called the draft declaration “arquivo morto”, meaning a dead file, Metrópoles reported. Abin, the presidential palace and the US Embassy had not commented publicly on the leaked report in the coverage reviewed.

In August, the State Department said the United States “respects the Brazilian people and candidates chosen in free and fair elections”. Forças Terrestres, a defence news site, cited that statement in its coverage of the Abin report.

What Is Not Yet Known

The full report has not been published, and only excerpts have reached the press. It is not known what measures, if any, the TSE or the government adopted in response.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Abin? Abin is Brazil’s federal intelligence agency, which advises the president on security threats. Its reports are normally confidential. Did Abin say the US will rig Brazil’s election? No. The excerpts reported so far describe diplomatic, economic and political pressure, not tampering with votes or voting machines.

World.title: US Democrats Press Rubio on Venezuelan Tycoon’s Role in Oil Deal
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts — The story. Three House Democrats want answers on Alejandro Betancourt’s role in a Venezuela oil deal. — Why it matters. The deal gives Washington a stake in a firm Betancourt leads. — The background. Betancourt has faced money-laundering probes in three countries but has not been convicted. — The numbers. The US would hold 35% of NABEP and buying rights to 20% of output. — The catch. The administration has no legal duty to answer the letter, Semafor noted. — What comes next. The Democrats asked for documents by 1 October.

Washington’s new oil partnership in Venezuela runs through a businessman who has been investigated in three countries. Democrats in Congress now want to know how he got there and who helped him.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arriving in Guatemala City in February 2025. Photo: US Department of State / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

Representatives Robert Garcia, Gregory Meeks and Jared Huffman wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 17 September 2026. The letter, also sent to Attorney General Todd Blanche, questions the role of Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, Efecto Cocuyo reported.

Why This Matters

After Nicolás Maduro’s arrest in January, the Trump administration moved to take a direct role in Venezuelan oil. Under a deal announced in late August, the US would take a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners.

That company, known as NABEP and led by Betancourt, would give the US preferential rights to buy 20% of production. The deal covers 17 oil fields with estimated reserves of 65 billion barrels, Efecto Cocuyo reported.

What the Democrats Want

The three are the top Democrats on the House oversight, foreign affairs and natural resources committees. Their press release says the administration has shared few details on its handling of at least $13 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue.

Efecto Cocuyo, a Venezuelan news site, reported that they asked for a list of everyone involved in the negotiations. They also want details on the roles of Betancourt and Mauricio Claver-Carone, a former informal US envoy.

The letter seeks records of any US interventions with foreign governments over investigations into Betancourt. Congress “has a right to know who the president has chosen to conduct business with”, the lawmakers wrote.

Meeks asked why Betancourt “is being treated as a business partner instead of the subject of a law enforcement investigation”. Huffman said handing him a stake in another nation’s oil “is exactly how the Trump administration does business”.

Who Alejandro Betancourt Is

Betancourt, 46, runs Venezuela‘s second-largest private oil producer, according to Efecto Cocuyo. He has faced investigations in the US, Switzerland and Spain over alleged laundering of funds from PDVSA, the state oil company.

Axios reported that he was never charged in a 2019 US inquiry into an alleged $1.2 billion laundering scheme. It also reported that US officials, including then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, asked Switzerland in 2026 to pause its case.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither the State Department nor Betancourt had responded to the letter in the reports reviewed. Rubio said on 2 September that no US investigation into Betancourt existed, Infobae reported.

Semafor noted that Democrats could issue subpoenas only if they win control of the House. It is unclear whether the Swiss case against Betancourt remains paused.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Alejandro Betancourt? He is a Venezuelan businessman who leads North American Blue Energy Partners. He has been investigated for alleged money laundering but has not been convicted. What does the US get from the Venezuela oil deal? A 35% stake in NABEP and preferential rights to buy 20% of its output. The deal covers 17 oil fields.

World.title: Costa Rica Data Leak Probe Widens as Prodhab Opens Its Own Case
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Agency for the Protection of Inhabitants’ Data (Prodhab) has opened its own investigation into an alleged mass leak of personal data on people in Costa Rica. It is the third public body to formally examine the case, which came to light a week ago. Prodhab opened case file No. 425-09-2026 on its own initiative and formally requested information to clarify what happened. The agency will examine whether there were failures in how personal information was handled.

Its inquiry runs alongside those already under way at the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (Micitt) and the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The case began on Saturday, Sept. 12, when Micitt’s National Cybersecurity Directorate detected a dark web post from a threat actor claiming to have breached a credit reporting agency. The actor claims to hold more than 400 million lines of data on people in Costa Rica.

According to the actor’s claims, the records include information on the beneficial owners of companies, salaries, home addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, photographs, vehicles, and judicial and marriage records. The actor also claimed to have information on President Laura Fernández.

Micitt has confirmed that a sample of about 10,000 lines released by the actor contains real data. Gezer Molina, the national director of cybersecurity, said the investigation seeks to determine whether a breach actually occurred, when it happened and which system was affected.

Investigators are also trying to establish whether the information comes from a single source or is a compilation of databases obtained earlier. Authorities have not publicly identified the entity the files may have come from. Officials have stressed that the appearance of a database on the dark web does not by itself prove the information is authentic, recent or the product of a single breach.

Micitt said it is coordinating with the Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ), Prodhab and the Directorate of Intelligence and Security (DIS). Molina said authorities are also in contact with counterparts in the Dominican Republic, where the actor has been linked to another incident.

A few days ago, the Public Prosecutor’s Office said its Cybercrime Prosecutor’s Unit had opened an investigation on its own initiative. The investigation will determine whether the crime of violation of personal data was committed. No suspects have been publicly identified. The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) has denied that data in its systems was affected.

The bank issued the statement after reports suggested the leaked information could have come from the Registry of Transparency and Beneficial Owners (RTBF), which the BCCR administers. The RTBF holds ownership information on corporations and other legal entities registered in Costa Rica, including the individuals who ultimately control them.

Micitt has warned that the exposed information could be used for fraud, identity theft, extortion or phishing attacks. The ministry recommends that people distrust unexpected messages, avoid opening suspicious links or attachments, refuse to share personal information and turn on multifactor authentication for their online accounts.

Cybersecurity expert Esteban Jiménez has warned that the leak could lead to a rise in fraud in the coming months. Real details such as names, addresses and phone numbers can make fraudulent calls and messages far more convincing. The case is the latest in a series of cyber incidents in Costa Rica. In 2022, a ransomware attack on the Finance Ministry and other public institutions paralyzed key digital services, including tax and customs systems.

In March of this year, the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) reported that part of its systems had been breached and 9 GB of emails taken. Investigators have not said how many people may be affected or when they expect to release their findings.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría Airport Keeps Highest Passenger Experience Accreditation
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría International Airport has renewed the highest level of an international passenger experience accreditation, placing the country’s main airport among just 12 worldwide holding the distinction in 2026. The airport, operated by AERIS, received Level 5 accreditation for the second consecutive year under the Airports Council International Customer Experience Accreditation program. Level 5 is the highest of five levels in the program.

The distinction does not simply rank airports based on how much passengers like them. Instead, ACI examines how well an airport has built the passenger experience into the way it operates, including how it listens to travelers, trains employees, measures service, uses technology and coordinates the different companies and government agencies working inside the terminal.

Juan Santamaría is one of only 12 airports worldwide currently holding Level 5 accreditation. Quito’s Mariscal Sucre International Airport in Ecuador is the other Level 5 airport in the Americas. “Renewing Level 5 represents for us an achievement as important as reaching it for the first time, because it demonstrates that we have managed to maintain a culture of service over time and that the passenger experience is part of the decisions we make to continue transforming the airport,” AERIS CEO Ricardo Hernández said.

AERIS has expanded its passenger service programs over the past year, including an Excellence Program aimed at improving customer service across the airport community. The airport also strengthened its Customer Experience Committee, which brings together airlines, airport operators, businesses and government agencies to identify problems and coordinate improvements.

About 500 employees from AERIS and other organizations working at Juan Santamaría participated in training, workshops and passenger service activities during 2025. Travelers have also begun seeing more technology designed to reduce waiting times and make moving through the terminal easier.

The airport is using LiDAR technology to anonymously monitor passenger flows around passport control and security in the international departures area. According to AERIS, Juan Santamaría is the first airport in Latin America to use the technology for this purpose. Other projects include automated eGates for immigration, self-service baggage drop systems and new scanning technology at security checkpoints. The airport began operating its first four eGates in the arrivals area on September 8.

Accessibility has also become part of the effort. Juan Santamaría joined the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program, an international system that allows travelers with non-visible disabilities to discreetly signal that they may need extra time or assistance. The airport has also achieved Level 1 in ACI’s Accessibility Enhancement Accreditation program.

Recent passenger surveys indicate that the changes are being noticed. At the end of June 2026, Juan Santamaría scored 4.44 out of 5 for overall passenger satisfaction and 4.38 for overall experience under ACI’s Airport Service Quality program. Its satisfaction score was slightly above the worldwide average of 4.38 for airports handling a similar number of passengers.

The accreditation comes as Juan Santamaría continues a broader modernization program. The airport currently connects Costa Rica with 42 destinations and is served by 26 international airlines and two domestic carriers. For travelers, the Level 5 renewal does not mean every trip through Juan Santamaría will be trouble-free.

Lines, flight disruptions and busy travel periods remain part of airport travel. What the accreditation indicates is that passenger experience has become part of the airport’s formal management system rather than a collection of individual customer service projects. For Costa Rica, that carries added importance because Juan Santamaría is the first and last impression of the country for millions of international visitors each year.

World.title: Video of Orcas Spotted Near Costa Rica’s Cocos Island in Rare Encounter
World.content:
A group of orcas has been spotted near Costa Rica’s Cocos Island, giving park rangers a rare look at one of the ocean’s most recognizable predators in waters where the species is only occasionally reported. Between four and five orcas were observed around midday yesterday near Manuelita Islet, just off Cocos Island.

Park rangers found them while carrying out routine monitoring in the waters surrounding Cocos Island National Park. Several of the orcas appeared to be juveniles, raising the possibility that the animals were traveling as part of a family group. The encounter was captured on video.

While orcas can travel enormous distances and have previously been documented in Costa Rican waters, they are not considered regular visitors around Cocos Island. The remote national park is much better known for marine species that are routinely encountered there, including hammerhead sharks, whale sharks, manta rays and dolphins.

Scientific records show just how unusual an orca encounter around the island can be. A study examining Costa Rican Pacific sightings between 1990 and 2020 identified 31 reported orca encounters involving 105 animals throughout the country’s Pacific waters. Only four of those sightings, involving a total of 10 animals, were recorded around Cocos Island.

The South Pacific accounted for the largest number during the study period, with 17 sightings involving 56 animals. Researchers have not established that the latest appearance represents any broader change in the distribution of orcas around Costa Rica. Orcas are highly mobile animals capable of traveling long distances while searching for food. Their movements can be influenced by prey availability as well as changing ocean conditions.

The waters surrounding Cocos Island provide an unusually rich marine environment. Ocean currents and underwater mountains help concentrate nutrients and marine life around the island, supporting large populations of fish and other animals that can potentially attract top predators.

Orcas are opportunistic hunters with diets that vary significantly between populations. Depending on where they live and the group involved, they can feed on fish, rays, sharks, sea turtles and marine mammals. Their presence in Costa Rica is not unprecedented.

Occasional sightings have been documented for decades along the country’s Pacific coast, with previous reports occurring in the northern, central and southern Pacific as well as around Cocos Island. However, researchers still know relatively little about the orcas that pass through tropical waters compared with populations studied in areas such as the Pacific Northwest, Norway and Antarctica.

That makes individual sightings potentially useful for understanding when the animals appear in Costa Rican waters and where they travel. The latest encounter also highlights the extraordinary marine biodiversity surrounding Cocos Island, located approximately 550 kilometers (342 miles) off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast.

Its isolation and surrounding protected waters have made the island one of Costa Rica’s most important marine conservation areas and an internationally known destination for experienced divers.

For now, yesterday’s encounter appears to be another uncommon visit rather than evidence that orcas are becoming regular residents around the island. But for the park rangers conducting their routine monitoring, it provided a rare encounter with a species that can pass through Costa Rican waters without being seen for long periods.
