Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. Powodem jest plan budżetu bez żadnej przewidywanej redukcji deficytu fiskalnego państwa w relacji do PKB. I totalna blokada decyzji przez… — Ignacy Morawski (@iggnacy) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. World.title: Russia planning “accidental” strikes on eastern NATO states, warns Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems. The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymyr Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly. “Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk. “The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw launches patrols to crack down on improperly parked electric scooters
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. E-scooters, which are currently unregulated in Poland, have been blamed for hundreds of accidents annually, with half of victims being pedestrians hit by riders https://t.co/TcrfPQocfr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 3, 2021 Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. The police have launched a campaign on the legal requirements for using e-scooters, including a warning that riding or parking them on pavements can be illegal. In 2022, accidents involving e-scooters in Poland resulted in 421 injuries and three deaths https://t.co/dMOBiNUBNG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish right-wing opposition MPs call for Independence Day march in Ukrainian city of Lviv
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of MPs from Poland’s main right-wing and far-right opposition parties have jointly called on the government to organise a march on Polish Independence Day in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, which was historically part of Poland. The idea has been firmly rejected by figures from the ruling coalition, who have called it “gross stupidity” and “madness”. It is also unclear to what extent the leadership of the opposition parties support the proposal. Pomysł zorganizowania "polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa" połączył polityków całej prawicy: PiS, Konfederacji, Rozwoju Plus i Konfederacji Korony Polskiej. Odsłaniamy kulisy. Pisze @patrykmichalski, autor programu #NewsMichalskiego ⤵️ 🔵 https://t.co/9L0M5lN0zY pic.twitter.com/1W3YxHdXHT — TVN24+ (@tvn24plus) September 15, 2026 The suggestion was made in a so-called parliamentary interpellation – through which MPs can ask questions and make suggestions to the government – submitted this month and signed by a group of 21 opposition MPs. They called on the government to do more to support the ethnic Polish community that still lives in Lviv, arguing that neither the Polish nor the Ukrainian state does enough to help them preserve and celebrate their identity. By contrast, argued the signatories, Polish state entities provide funding for Ukrainian organisations and events in Poland, including celebrations of Ukrainian Independence Day on 24 August. As such, they called upon the government to “organise official celebrations of [Polish] Independence Day in Lviv, including a Polish Independence March through the streets of the city” on 11 November. This would be “a concrete sign of remembrance and solidarity with Poles living in Ukraine”. Among the 21 signatories, 14 are from the caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and now the largest opposition group. A further three are from Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right opposition group. One is from Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a group that broke away from PiS earlier this year; another is from Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian party led by Grzegorz Braun. The final two are an independent, Janusz Kowalski, who recently quit PiS; and Jarosław Sachajko, who was elected in 2023 on the PiS party list but is part of the small Direct Democracy (Demokracja Bezpośrednia) group associated with Paweł Kukiz, a right-wing, anti-establishment figure. Interpelacja do Prezesa Rady Ministrów w sprawie zorganizowania 11 listopada polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa 11 listopada Rzeczpospolita Polska obchodzi Narodowe Święto Niepodległości. Jest to święto wszystkich Polaków, również tych, którzy mieszkają poza granicami… pic.twitter.com/7m6yUg1iKZ — Dariusz Matecki (@DariuszMatecki) August 25, 2026 It remains unclear to what extent the MPs have the backing of their parties in calling for the government to organise an Independence Day march in Lviv. Indeed, when Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, was asked about the idea on Wednesday, he appeared to know very little about it. Speaking to broadcaster RMF, Bosak said that he had first heard about the proposal on Tuesday and that, after looking into it, he said it appeared to be a “stunt”, and one that he felt was “unnecessary”. “I think the point is to draw attention to the fact that Polish institutions are participating in the celebration of Ukraine’s Independence Day in Warsaw, and that there should be some symmetry,” said Bosak. However, he added that he felt many people would not understand this intention. “The appeal should be directed at Ukrainian institutions, not the Polish foreign ministry,” he said, adding that the MPs who came up with the idea should better explain it. “Frankly, I have more serious matters to attend to.” Czy przemarsz Polaków ulicami Lwowa z okazji Dnia Niepodległości to dobry pomysł? Zdaniem @krzysztofbosak niepotrzebny, a traktować go należy w kategorii happeningu. Ale jeśli się trzymać zasady wzajemności, to już lepiej organizować coś podobnego… w Kijowie. pic.twitter.com/PxdqNKBlCC — Ekonomat (@ekonomat_pl) September 16, 2026 Throughout much of history, Lviv (known in Polish as Lwów) was part of the Polish state, most recently during the period between the First and Second World Wars. However, amid postwar border movements, it became part of Ukraine along with some other former Polish territories. Many in Poland still feel a sense of attachment to the former Polish “borderlands” (kresy) that are now located in Ukraine, Lithuania and Belarus, and which are still home to at least hundreds of thousands of ethnic Poles (though the exact number is a matter of dispute). In Lviv itself, the most recent Ukrainian national census, taken in 2001, showed just under 10,000 people declaring Polish ethnicity in the city (around 1% of the population), though some estimates put the figure higher. Poland's culture minister has condemned Russia's attacks on the historic centre of Lviv in Ukraine, a UNESCO World Heritage site. She noted that Lviv, which was once part of Poland, represents the "shared history of Ukraine, Poland and all of Europe" https://t.co/qPhqXMAZ9r — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 25, 2026 Last year, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, clashed with the mayor of Lviv, Andriy Sadovyi, after visiting the city and criticising a monument commemorating nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, a figure seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland. Followers of Bandera were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians. Poland regards the killings as a genocide but Ukraine rejects that label. The issue has caused renewed tension this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army”, which led the massacres. Any Polish attempt at a state-backed Independence Day march in Ukraine would likely stir further controversy. A leading candidate in Poland’s presidential election has clashed with a Ukrainian mayor after visiting his city and criticising the presence of a monument to Stepan Bandera, who is seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland https://t.co/nA9JzMmBcg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2025 Although the Polish government has not yet officially responded to the opposition MPs’ interpellation, a number of figures from the ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – criticised the idea on Wednesday. Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk called it “gross stupidity” to think of organising such a march in Ukraine, especially at a time of war. He asked how Poles would feel if Germany tried to organise a similar march in Poland (some of whose current territory was part of Germany before World War Two). Both Dariusz Wieczorek, an MP from The Left (Lewica), and Marek Biernacki from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) told broadcaster TVN that the idea was “madness”. Próba zorganizowania we Lwowie prawicowej prowokacji z udziałem PiS-u, Rozwój Plus i Brauna to jednoznaczne działanie na rzecz Rosji i przeciwko polskiej racji stanu. — Witold Zembaczyński🇵🇱 (@WZembaczynski) September 16, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: European Parliament strips Polish far-right leader of immunity to face Holocaust denial charge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years. The decision marks the sixth time that the European Parliament has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial. Braun is already on trial in Poland for an attack on a Jewish religious celebration in parliament and is facing a number of other legal cases. Parlament Europejski w głosowaniu w Strasburgu uchylił immunitet europosła Grzegorza Brauna. Sprawa dotyczy negowania przez niego Holokaustu. Więcej: https://t.co/rB3UPUiS8o pic.twitter.com/icRLEqsWmF — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) September 15, 2026 In a vote on Tuesday, a majority of MEPs voted in favour of a request, submitted in February by Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, to lift the immunity enjoyed by Braun as an MEP. He has sat in the European Parliament since being elected in 2024. In his request, Żurek said that Polish prosecutors wish to charge Braun in relation to “denial of genocide crimes committed by functionaries of the Third Reich in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp and the Lublin concentration camp (Majdanek)”. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has prosecutorial power, also revealed that the accusation relates to the use of gas chambers at those two camps. Neither the IPN nor Żurek confirmed at the time what specific words Braun had said that prompted the planned charges against him. However, the IPN noted that they had come at a live event broadcast online on 27 September 2025. On that date, Braun took part in a discussion with Jan Żaryn, a right-wing historian and former senator for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, titled “The Polish Underground State and the Jewish Issue”. A recording of the event is still available online. During his remarks, Braun referred to the “fake gas chambers of Majdanek and Auschwitz”, calling them “a dark, monstrous fantasy that has no satisfactory historical or academic support”. He suggested that the idea of the gas chambers had been invented as part of “propaganda and black PR operations conducted by the Soviet and Anglo-Saxon security services during World War Two”, and that the false claim continues to be exploited by Jews today. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 In actual fact, historians estimate that around 900,000 people were killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The vast majority were Jews, but victims also included Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and ethnic Poles. Meanwhile, gas chambers at Majdanek were used to kill tens of thousands, again mainly Jews. Today, the ashes of the camp’s cremated victims are preserved in a memorial at the site of the former camp. Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the veracity of Nazi crimes against Jews. Last month, he was charged with denying Nazi crimes in a separate case over earlier comments in which he called Auschwitz’s gas chambers “fake”. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 In December, Braun went on trial over a separate set of charges relating to four other incidents, including his attack on a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament in December 2023 and his disruption of a lecture by a Holocaust scholar. “I am standing before this court because I dared to defend myself against oppression and the ritual manifestation of Jewish supremacy,” declared Braun at the start of the trial, which remains ongoing. Braun is also facing various legal cases relating to his anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT actions. Last week, he posted a video of himself using a hammer to vandalise a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Police are investigating that incident. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a WWII group that fought against the Soviets but was also responsible for massacring Poles https://t.co/oCYRtNRO9N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2026 Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 8-9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next year’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. An MEP from the ruling coalition, Michał Kobosko, welcomed Tuesday’s decision to lift Braun’s immunity, saying that the far-right leader “deliberately and consciously…stokes hatred”. Kobosko said that such actions are particularly dangerous at a time when Russia is “actively waging hybrid and cognitive war against Poland”. He noted that Braun and his party have taken a sympathetic position towards Russia, including calling for Poland to “normalise” relations with Moscow. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Poznej Vltavu Festival Returns to Prague on September 28
World.content:
The second edition of the Poznej Vltavu (Get to Know the Vltava) festival will take place across Prague on September 28, 2026.

For one day, the banks of the Vltava will host a programme exploring the river from a variety of perspectives.

The festival will feature workshops, exhibitions, sports activities, boat trips, and tours of places that are not normally open to the public.



Prague’s riverfront embankments and other locations along the Vltava will offer activities for children, adults, and seniors.

The festival aims to highlight the Vltava as a natural part of Prague’s urban environment and an important ecological feature, while giving visitors the opportunity to spend a day exploring the river and its surroundings.

Experts from a range of fields will discuss the Vltava in its broader context and offer insights into lesser-known aspects of the river.

This year’s programme will involve organisations including the Prague Institute of Planning and Development, Prague City Tourism, the Prague City Gallery, the Vltava River Authority, Prague Waterworks and Sewerage Company, the Prague Water Management Company, ROPID, Prague City Forests, the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic, and many others.

The festival area will extend farther along the Vltava this year, reaching Žluté lázně and the new Dvorecký Bridge, which has quickly become a popular destination for Prague residents since opening.

Most events will be free to attend, although some activities will require advance registration due to limited capacity.

More information is available on the festival’s Facebook event.

World.title: Red Arrows to Fly Over Charles Bridge This Friday
World.content:
Prague will hear the roar of Royal Air Force jets on Friday, September 18, when the Red Arrows aerobatic team stages a flypast over the city.

Ten BAE Hawk T1 aircraft from the British RAF team are scheduled to pass over the Charles Bridge at around 2:00 PM. The jets will leave smoke trails in the colours of the Czech flag during the display.



The formation is expected to approach Prague from the north before reaching the area around Václav Havel Airport. The aircraft will then form an arrow-shaped formation and fly around the western and southern parts of the capital before turning north along the Vltava.

The jets are expected to fly at an altitude of roughly 300 metres above the ground. The engines will be clearly audible across parts of the city, although the flypast itself will last only a short time.

After passing through central Prague, the formation will turn northeast and continue toward Ostrava. The city is hosting NATO Days, one of the Czech Republic’s largest military and security events, this weekend.

The timetable and route could still change because of weather or other air traffic in the Prague area. A similar Red Arrows flypast was held in Prague last September, but poor weather delayed the aircraft by more than an hour.

The flypast is being held in connection with Czech Air Force Day, which is observed on September 15.

The Red Arrows are the official aerobatic display team of the Royal Air Force and regularly perform at air shows and military events in Britain and abroad.

World.title: Groovy Market Fest Returns to Riegrovy Sady on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Groovy Market Fest will return to Riegrovy Sady on Saturday, October 3, bringing together food, independent brands, design and live music for its third edition.

The one-day event will take place at Energy Pub from noon until 10 p.m.

Following two editions held during the summer, the organizers are extending the concept into the autumn, with visitors able to browse local products, eat street food and listen to live music and DJs throughout the day.



The market is organised around three main areas. The Food Garden will focus on gastronomy and street food from local businesses, while Palm Street will feature bakeries, artisanal products and other local goods. The Design Zone will bring together fashion, design and products from independent Czech brands.

Live performances and DJ sets will run from the afternoon into the evening, providing the musical programme alongside the market stalls.

Marek Novák, founder of Groovy Market Fest, said the first two editions helped the team establish the format and identify what visitors respond to.

“After two editions, we know exactly what works at Groovy Market Fest: high-quality local brands, good food, and an atmosphere that keeps people coming back,” Novák said. “This third edition is an opportunity for us to show that Groovy isn’t just a summer event, but a festival that holds a firm place in Prague all year round.”

Visitors can buy tickets for either of the two five-hour sessions. The first runs from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by a second session from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m.

A ticket for one session costs 100 CZK, while an all-day ticket covering both sessions is available for 190 CZK. Tickets are sold through GoOut.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Groovy Market Fest (@groovymarketfest)

From Barcelona street food to a Prague market

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food sector.

One of their main inspirations was Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market, an urban market known for combining food, design, music and independent creative businesses.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing is out: Orbán’s new campaign, motorway deal and a possible break with Russian gas
World.content:
Orbán is back on the political frontline, and Hungary’s new government is moving against some of the most controversial legacies of the previous era.

This week’s Hungary Weekly Briefing by Daily News Hungary looks at Viktor Orbán’s “national resistance” campaign, his claims of foreign intelligence interference in Hungary’s election, and the escalating clash with Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

We also examine the government’s plans to unwind a major motorway concession, high-profile arrests in a Volánbusz corruption investigation, scrutiny of the former residency bond scheme and a new complaint over Szijjártó-era private flights.

But perhaps the biggest long-term shift is happening in energy: Hungary says it could be ready to leave Russian gas behind by October 2027. The briefing explores what that could mean for Hungary’s energy security — and the costs of breaking with a system built up over years.

Plus: new developments in Hungary-Ukraine relations, Austria’s extended border checks, the Budapest-Belgrade railway, Airbnb rules, tobacco taxes and more.

Hungary Weekly Briefing on Substack

Read the full Hungary Weekly Briefing for the political, economic and diplomatic stories shaping Hungary this week.

World.title: Pedestrian brutally attacked at Budapest crossing as bystanders rush to help – VIDEO
World.content:
A pedestrian was knocked to the ground and repeatedly kicked in the head in central Budapest on Friday evening. The attack, which took place near one of the city’s best-known theatres, was captured on video.

The incident happened on 18 September near the Vígszínház theatre, at a pedestrian crossing by Szent István Boulevard and Honvéd Street. According to footage shared on social media, a man was walking across the road when another man suddenly approached him from the side and brought him to the ground.

The assailant continued the attack while the pedestrian was lying on the road, striking him and kicking him several times in the head. The victim appeared to be motionless after the assault.

Police arrest young man after the attack

Police launched proceedings against a young man on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm following the assault on Szent István Boulevard late on Friday evening.

Márton Mérkőy, a press officer for the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK), confirmed on Saturday that officers had apprehended the suspected attacker at the scene. He added that the man’s questioning was still ongoing.

In a response to Hungarian news outlet 24.hu , police stated that the suspect had been detained and that proceedings were underway on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm.

The circumstances and motive behind the assault have not yet been established. The exact extent of the pedestrian’s injuries has also not been officially confirmed.

If you missed it: Legal threats fly as PM Magyar confronts Orbán-linked billionaire over motorway deal

What do Budapest’s latest crime figures show?

The attack comes amid a broader police effort to improve public safety in Budapest. In July, the Budapest Police Headquarters launched a series of targeted checks across the capital, focusing on locations identified through crime data, residents’ reports and consultations with local authorities. During the operation’s first 30 days, officers checked the identities of more than 11,000 people and made 252 arrests.

The latest annual figures offer some wider context. According to the BRFK, the number of registered crimes in Budapest fell by 22% in 2025 compared with the previous year. Police also reported a decline in offences committed in public spaces.

World.title: Budapest lands surprising spot in global quality-of-life ranking – see where it stands
World.content:
Budapest has landed in a surprising spot in a global quality-of-life ranking covering more than 300 cities. The Hungarian capital trails several Central European neighbours, including Vienna, Prague and Bratislava, although it scores higher than some of the world’s best-known metropolises. So what is behind its result, and where does Budapest stand out?

Budapest ranked 209th out of 303 cities, with a quality-of-life score of 142.5, according to a snapshot of Numbeo’s continuously updated index.

The index assesses everyday living conditions using eight indicators:

Purchasing power

Safety

Healthcare

Cost of living

Property prices relative to income

Commuting time

Pollution

Climate

These factors are combined into an overall score, with higher values indicating more favourable conditions under Numbeo’s methodology. The index draws partly on user-submitted data and surveys, meaning its results should be treated as an indicative comparison rather than a definitive judgment on where people should live.

Dutch cities dominate the global quality-of-life ranking

European cities dominate the top of the ranking, with the Netherlands accounting for six of the first ten places. The top 10 cities in the September ranking were:

The Hague, Netherlands Eindhoven, Netherlands Rotterdam, Netherlands Utrecht, Netherlands Ghent, Belgium Luxembourg, Luxembourg Stuttgart, Germany Groningen, Netherlands Amsterdam, Netherlands Gothenburg, Sweden

The Hague led the list with approximately 227.7 points. Its result reflects a combination of high purchasing power, favourable safety and healthcare indicators, relatively short commuting times and low pollution. Other leading Dutch cities also performed strongly across several of these measures.

The ranking illustrates why income alone does not determine a city’s overall result. High purchasing power can be offset by expensive housing, long journeys to work or unfavourable environmental conditions. Conversely, a city can score well by combining economic opportunities with relatively favourable everyday living conditions.

Cost of living in Hungary in 2026: rent, groceries, transport and monthly budgets

How does Budapest compare with other European capitals?

Budapest’s 142.5-point result placed it behind several nearby capitals. Prague received 178.6 points, Bratislava 159.1 and Warsaw 153.6, while Vienna scored approximately 205.

The comparison with major international cities produced a less predictable picture:

Prague: 178.6 points

Bratislava: 159.1 points

Warsaw: 153.6 points

London: 149.3 points

Paris: 143.6 points

Budapest: 142.5 points

New York: 135.9 points

Los Angeles: 131.6 points

While Budapest trails several Central European capitals, it ranks ahead of New York and Los Angeles in Numbeo’s overall index. The figures reflect a combination of economic, environmental and everyday living conditions rather than any single measure, such as wages or housing costs.

Why Budapest falls behind – and where it performs better

Compared with Prague, Budapest received a lower healthcare score: 52.1 points against the Czech capital’s 74.7. Its purchasing-power index was also lower, at 92.1 compared with Prague’s 113.9.

The commuting-time indicator was approximately 38.7 minutes for Budapest and 32 minutes for Prague. Housing affordability, however, was one area in which the Hungarian capital compared more favourably with its Czech counterpart.

Budapest’s safety index also offers a different perspective. At 66.4 points, it exceeded the corresponding figures for London, Paris and New York in the reported snapshot

Is Budapest still an affordable place to live?

Budapest’s cost-of-living index was approximately 54, below the 303-city median of 59. This distinction matters particularly for foreigners considering moving to Hungary. Someone earning a salary from abroad may experience the city’s prices differently from a resident relying on local wages.

Does that make Budapest a bargain? Not necessarily. Numbeo’s cost-of-living index excludes rent, and lower prices do not automatically translate into greater affordability for people earning local salaries. For those considering a move, however, there may be another financial advantage: recent moving data suggests relocating to Hungary can cost significantly less than moving to Spain from the same European countries.

The figures are based partly on user-submitted data and reflect the ranking reported on 19 September 2026. As Numbeo updates its index continuously, scores and positions may change.

World.title: Budapest traffic alert: Iconic bridge closes, three tram lines suspended this weekend
World.content:
Planning to travel around Budapest this weekend? Liberty Bridge is closed to road traffic, three major tram lines are suspended, and several bus services are diverted on 19–20 September. The changes are part of the city’s Car-Free Weekend, which also brings vintage vehicles, street food and family activities to the city centre. Here is how to get around.

While visitors will be able to explore parts of the city centre without cars, the closures also mean significant changes for passengers who usually travel through the area by tram or bus.

Budapest’s Liberty Bridge (Szabadság híd), connecting Fővám Square in Pest with Szent Gellért Square in Buda, is closed to regular road traffic on Saturday and Sunday.

The closure is part of European Mobility Week, with sections of central Budapest temporarily transformed into pedestrian-friendly event areas. However, visitors and residents should expect changes to several important public transport routes.

Which roads are closed in Budapest?

The restrictions affect Liberty Bridge and several surrounding streets, including Vámház körút near Fővám Square, Műegyetem Quay on the Buda side, and sections of the Lower Pest Embankment. The embankment closure began on Friday evening, while the wider restrictions apply throughout the weekend.

Drivers should avoid the area around Liberty Bridge and Fővám Square. For the full list of affected roads, check BKK’s official traffic information .

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Trams 47, 48 and 49 are not running – what are the alternatives?

Tram lines 47, 48 and 49 will not operate on 19 or 20 September. These services normally connect southern Buda with central Pest via Liberty Bridge.

Passengers can use the following alternatives:

To cross between Buda and Pest: Take metro line M4. Tram lines 4 and 6, and buses 7 and 133E, also remain available on their usual routes.

On the Buda side: Tram 61 runs on an extended route to Városház Square, while tram 56A serves Kelenföld railway station. An additional tram 61B operates on Saturday.

Around central Pest: Metro line M3, bus 9 and trolleybus 72 offer alternatives to the suspended trams along the Small Boulevard.

Several other services, including buses 15, 107 and 223E and some night buses, are also affected. Passengers should check individual routes before travelling.

For the most suitable connection, use the BudapestGO journey planner , which provides real-time public transport information.

What is happening on Liberty Bridge this weekend?

The closures are part of Budapest’s Car-Free Weekend on 19–20 September, organised during European Mobility Week. For two days, Liberty Bridge and several surrounding streets are being transformed into public spaces where residents and visitors can explore the city on foot and discover more sustainable ways to travel.

The programme includes vintage trams and buses, cycling and scooter activities, guided walks, family-friendly events and street food. Vehicle displays on Vámház körút run from 10 am to 6 pm on both days, while activities also extend to Fővám Square and Műegyetem Quay.
