World.title: South Ossetia election: as expected, former Moscow official Marat Kambolov becomes new president
World.content:
Kambolov becomes South Ossetia president

As expected, Marat Kambolov, the prime minister and acting president of South Ossetia who previously held senior positions in the Kremlin, is winning the snap presidential election held on 18 September.

According to preliminary results, he is securing a convincing victory over his formal rivals – state security officer Murat Valiev, South Ossetian University rector’s state adviser Kazbek Kodoev, and Unity party chairman Zurab Kokoev.

After 40% of the ballots had been counted, CEC head Emilia Gagieva said Kambolov had received 88.4% of the vote. Valiev had 4.3%, Kodoev 1.1%, and Kokoev 1.0%.

Marat Kambolov is a former Moscow official who first appeared in South Ossetia in May 2026 as an adviser to then-President Alan Gagloev. He was quickly granted South Ossetian citizenship and, within a month, rose from minister to prime minister, and then became acting president after Alan Gagloev resigned.

Polling stations were also open in Russia – in North Ossetia and Moscow. According to Emilia Gagieva, turnout was high at all polling stations and no violations were recorded.

According to the CEC, the election was monitored by 66 observers from 15 countries: Russia, Abkhazia, Nicaragua, Belarus, Armenia, Venezuela, Germany, Zimbabwe, Kenya, Mexico, Serbia, Tanzania, Turkey, Uganda and South Africa.

CEC member Dina Ostaeva said that “no complaints or appeals related to violations of electoral legislation or the organisation of voting” had been received during the day.

After polling stations closed at 8pm, a celebratory concert and lottery were held in the city centre, with household appliances, smartphones, TVs, bicycles, vacuum cleaners and the grand prize – a Russian-made Niva Legend car – raffled off.

As soon as the prizes had been handed out, Marat Kambolov took the stage, thanked the people of South Ossetia for taking part in the election and said that, in terms of voter turnout, the election had broken all records.

“Preliminary data show that we have broken all records. Never before have so many people taken part. More voters participated in this election than in any previous one. Only together can we strengthen our Tskhinvali and our Ossetia,” Kambolov said.

One of the voters who cast his ballot for Marat Kambolov believes that the high turnout and the large share of votes he received were not so much the result of political strategists’ work as of people believing in Kambolov and voting “for his authority, for the authority of Russia”.

Blogger Alik Pukhaev expressed hope that the new president would “finally make South Ossetia a state for all Ossetians”.

By this, he means the possibility for all ethnic Ossetians to obtain a South Ossetian passport.

At present, the law provides for citizenship only for people born in South Ossetia and their descendants. Under previous governments, however, there were repeated scandals over the illegal issuance — and even sale — of passports to residents of Chechnya, Ingushetia and Dagestan.

Russian State Duma MP Kazbek Taisaev, who observed the election, said it had been organised “at the highest level – transparently, fairly and openly”.

He also stressed that Russia would continue to provide South Ossetia with comprehensive support.

And that is almost certainly what will happen, given that Marat Kambolov is a Russian official who was clearly sent by the Kremlin with the specific aim of taking the presidency and governing in Russia’s interests rather than those of local politicians pursuing their own agendas.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: EU does not recognise “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
EU condemns Russia and South Ossetia election

The European Union does not recognise the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). In a statement, the EU Delegation said the results of the election have no legal effect.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the so-called “presidential election”, calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The EU statement says it does not recognise the constitutional and legal framework, including recent amendments, under which the election was held in the Russian-occupied region, which unilaterally declared its secession from Georgia.

“The EU strongly condemns Moscow’s actions aimed at installing a Russian official as the de facto president of South Ossetia, Georgia’s occupied breakaway region,” the statement said.

The EU also expressed concern over the signing of the so-called “Treaty on Deepening Allied Cooperation” on 9 May 2026 and criticised Russia’s attempts to strengthen its control over South Ossetia in the political, military, economic and judicial spheres.

The EU considers these steps contrary to a peaceful resolution of the conflict and paving the way for the future illegal annexation of the Russian-occupied region.

“Such actions systematically deepen divisions, threaten regional security and stability, and constitute a flagrant violation of international law,” the EU statement said.

The bloc reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in Georgia, including through its co-chairmanship of the Geneva International Discussions and the activities of the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia.

The EU called on Russia to respect Georgia’s sovereignty and cease all actions undermining its territorial integrity.

“The European Union reaffirms its unwavering support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

Unlike Kambolov, the other three candidates were residents of South Ossetia. But that was where their advantage ended. Most experts described them as “technical candidates” — people who were not seriously trying to compete for the presidency:

Zurab Kokoev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetia University;

Murat Valiev, a candidate nominated by the Patriots of Alania party and an employee of the state security service.

None of them campaigned among the population. They presented their views on the development of so-called South Ossetia only during live televised debates.

News in Georgia

World.title: Pashinyan’s salary to nearly double as Armenian civil servants set for pay rises from 2027
World.content:
Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

From 1 January 2027, senior Armenian officials will receive higher salaries. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, for example, will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1.5 million ($4,143). Deputy prime ministers’ salaries will rise to 2,163,000 drams ($5,975), from 1,289,000 ($3,560).

The increases will apply not only to the executive branch, but also to the legislative and judicial branches. The state budget will allocate 25 billion drams ($69 million) for this purpose. The government has already approved the draft. Parliament must now approve it.

“How does this public official live? How does he buy a suit and a watch? We never assess the negative impact [of this factor] on the development of our state. But the effect is highly negative. If we do not solve this problem, it will lead to disasters,” Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the draft.

The ruling party views the decision as a reform. The prime minister said he was confident that failing to implement the project would mean “keeping Armenia stuck in place and continuing to subordinate the logic of the state to the logic of corruption”.

However, the opposition warns that such decisions will further deepen the sense of social injustice.

“Citizens often become disillusioned and leave the country not only because of economic difficulties, but also because of a sense of injustice,” former MP Garnik Danielyan said.

Salary increases in figures

Under the proposed amendments to the law “On remuneration for persons holding public office”:

the president of Armenia will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the speaker of the National Assembly will earn 2,496,000 drams ($6,895), up from 1,497,600 drams ($4,137);

MPs will earn up to 1,497,600 drams ($4,137), up from 832,000 drams ($2,311);

the president of the Constitutional Court will earn 2,412,800 drams ($6,665), up from 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the prosecutor general will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 1,248,000 drams ($3,447);

the ombudsman will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 998,400 drams ($2,758).

Governors, deputy ministers and deputy speakers of parliament will also receive higher salaries.

The stated amounts include taxes and other mandatory payments.

Ruling party representative’s assessment and opposition response

Eduard Aghajanyan, an MP from the ruling party, told journalists:

“The public administration system has consistently faced difficulties attracting highly qualified specialists. The issue became particularly acute after the 2018 revolution, when the logic of working within the system changed radically. Systemic corruption was eradicated, and the motivation mechanisms were completely restructured.

At the same time, pay levels made the public administration system unattractive to highly qualified professionals.

We have been at the helm of government for eight years now. I believe that the decision to address this issue is somewhat overdue.

I welcome the government’s decision. I am confident that it will produce the desired results in attracting highly qualified professionals.”

Former MP from the opposition Armenia bloc Garnik Danielyan wrote on his Facebook page:

“According to official data for 2024, Armenia’s poverty rate stands at 21.7%. One in four children lives in poverty, while thousands of families continue to face severe social hardship. People struggle to meet their basic needs. Moreover, in the 21st century, Armenia has recorded cases of people dying from hunger.

In your 2021 election programme, you [addressing the authorities] promised to halve the poverty rate by 2026. Poverty has not declined. But you yourselves are now living better. You no longer buy vacuum cleaners or televisions on instalment plans. Instead, you are accumulating assets.

Of course, no one objects to high salaries for public officials. But given this level of poverty, should the priorities not be addressing social problems, creating new jobs and ensuring decent living conditions for people?

And this is happening while Armenia’s public debt has already exceeded $14 billion. Housing and employment remain critical issues for thousands of Karabakh Armenians. Hundreds of people still live in temporary shelters, and many are forced to buy groceries on credit.

Clearly, political calculations also lie behind this decision — namely, preserving loyalty within the state system.”

Comments from Armenian residents on social media

The decision to raise the salaries of senior public officials has sparked heated discussions on social media. Most users criticised the authorities. Here are some of their comments:

“Of course, raising the salaries of civil servants and public officials is important. But we must not forget a phenomenon that is shameful for Armenia. Librarians receive the lowest salaries [75,000 drams — $208]. Raise them!”

“After spending days and nights thinking about the people, the ‘democratic’ government decided to raise its own salaries by 60–80%. Meanwhile, citizens earning 80,000–150,000 drams ($220–414) can continue entering shops full of goods. As prices rise rapidly, they must painfully choose whether to buy food for their child or shoes for themselves.”

“They are setting their salaries higher than those of members of the British royal family. And they are paying for all this with our taxes. They will bleed us dry. This is only the beginning.”

“The [prime minister] claims that raising his salary and those of other officials is necessary to prevent a catastrophe. According to this passionate speaker, a ‘catastrophe’ is when someone asks where an official got his suit or watch. I wonder who will ask him what he plans to spend those 2,662,000 drams — around $7,400 — a month on, considering how expensive he is for the state. For nine years now, you have paid neither rent nor utility bills, car expenses, petrol or maintenance costs.”

Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

World.title: Tbilisi condemns “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
Georgia condemns Russia over South Ossetia election

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry condemned the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

According to the ministry’s statement, “the opening of polling stations by Russia in the occupied territory without the consent of the Georgian government is a gross violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and another manifestation of Russia’s policy aimed at the de facto annexation of Georgia’s regions.”

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said that holding the so-called election violates fundamental norms and principles of international law and cannot legitimise the occupation regime in Tskhinvali or change the region’s status under international law as part of Georgia.

“Holding any so-called elections in Georgia’s occupied territories, which are under military occupation and the effective control of the Russian Federation, while internally displaced persons and refugees are not given the opportunity to return to their homes safely and with dignity, is illegal and cannot have any international legal consequences,” the ministry said.

Tbilisi also condemned Russia’s decision to open polling stations for the Russian State Duma election in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region from 18 to 20 September.

The Foreign Ministry called on the international community to properly assess and condemn Russia’s actions and ensure an appropriate international legal and political response.

“Georgia continues to call on the international community to firmly protect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and support a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” the statement said.

World.title: Armenia’s anti-corruption campaign: law on confiscating illicit assets takes effect
World.content:
Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

A large-scale anti-corruption campaign is unfolding in Armenia . As part of the campaign, the state is confiscating assets belonging to members of the country’s former financial and political elite.

The authorities say they are moving from high-profile political accusations to a systematic effort to recover illegally acquired property. The list of people accused of corruption whose numerous properties and business assets have been frozen includes former Armenian president Robert Kocharyan , Prosperous Armenia party leader Gagik Tsarukyan, and former finance minister and ex-head of the State Revenue Committee Gagik Khachatryan. Prosecutors accuse those involved in these high-profile cases of money laundering, bribery and abuse of office.

At the same time, the debate in Armenia goes beyond how they managed to amass such wealth. It also concerns whether the process complies with the law, whether the authorities apply the law equally to everyone, and whether the confiscated property is genuinely being returned to the people.

About the law

Armenia’s Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin has been in force since 2020. The authorities adopted it “to strengthen the fight against corruption and restore social justice”. The law applies to assets worth more than 50 million drams ($132,120). It allows the state to confiscate property if its owner cannot prove that the income used to acquire it came from legal sources.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, between 2018 and the first half of 2026, the state and local communities recovered assets worth approximately 304 billion drams (around $840 million). More than two-thirds of that amount — about $562 million — was recovered over the past three and a half years.

Comment from lawyer Aram Orbelyan

“The Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin contains fundamental contradictions. In international practice, confiscation models are clearly separated. One involves checking declarations: if a person cannot explain their income, the state confiscates the property. The other involves confiscation following proof of a crime. Our lawmakers, however, have mixed everything together into complete confusion.

The grounds for an investigation are chaotic. Half of the provisions are linked to criminal cases, including cases that authorities have suspended or closed on non-exonerating grounds. The other half allows officials to launch confiscation proceedings based simply on ‘operational information’. As soon as any intelligence report appears, law-enforcement agencies immediately begin examining a person’s property, going back as far as 1991.”

The factual vacuum of the 1990s

“What political statements describe as ‘plunder’ is often impossible to prove in court because the circumstances of that era were different. In the 1990s, non-monetary transactions, including agricultural exchanges, were widespread. There was no clear system of tax and customs control. Vehicle databases only appeared in the early 2000s, while electronic tax records emerged in 2013.

Moreover, the law at the time did not require businesses to keep documents for more than five years. This has naturally created an information vacuum today. Young prosecutors fail to take this historical context into account, leading to dead ends in court.”

Intrusion into private life and the political context

“The extent of the intrusion into private life raises serious questions. The law allows investigators to examine years of bank statements belonging to any relatives of a person under investigation. As a result, investigators and prosecutors gain access to strictly personal spending unrelated to corruption: where people went on holiday, what they ordered in cafés and what illnesses they received treatment for.

Society sees this mechanism exclusively as a ‘law to recover what former [authorities] stole’. Legally, however, the law should target corruption as such, rather than individuals. To ensure that anti-corruption tools do not appear politically selective, they must operate universally. They should apply to all elites, regardless of their current political status or affiliation with the ruling camp.

Authorities must examine both the past and the present transparently, without politically motivated cases, while taking limitation periods and the economic realities of earlier years into account. The process should objectively target illicit property, rather than serve as a selectively applied repressive tool.”

Comment from Varuzhan Hoktanian, an expert at Transparency International’s Anti-Corruption Centre

“The law sparked legal disputes from the outset, which led to a review of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The court, in turn, sought an expert opinion from the Venice Commission. International experts offered two key recommendations. First, the confiscation of property for the benefit of the state should take place through separate civil proceedings, rather than criminal prosecution resulting in imprisonment. Second, some responsibility for proving the lawful origin of assets should fall on the owner.

It is often extremely difficult to prove that property has a corrupt origin. For example, Kocharyan’s case involves the signing of government decisions. For the charges to stand, the prosecution must prove that he deliberately approved specific decisions in the expectation that the assets would eventually pass to his family. This is extremely difficult to establish, so the evidence often appears unconvincing. The situation is compounded by the absence of a mandatory declaration system in the 1990s. As a result, it is now virtually impossible to confirm that property was acquired legally.”

Discrimination or fight against corruption?

“Applying legal mechanisms exclusively to one group of people discredits the anti-corruption institution itself, turning the law into a tool of political pressure. Attempts to deprive opponents of financial resources by seizing their property create a risk of completely clearing the political field. If this is combined with double standards during elections — harsh punishment, including arrests, for vote-buying while ignoring the abuse of administrative resources — the system of checks and balances itself collapses. Ignoring any of these abuses leads to dictatorship.”

What happens to confiscated property?

“The legal question is only one side of the problem. The question of what happens to confiscated property after the state receives it is no less important.

I recall a similar confiscation from Soviet history — the dekulakisation campaign of the late 1920s and early 1930s. We later learned about the grave consequences it caused, including the Holodomor. As it turned out, the party nomenklatura ultimately received everything that the authorities had seized. Today, these assets could likewise pass to new wealthy individuals or another nomenklatura. Once again, ordinary people would receive nothing.

When people talk about confiscating property, they mean both financial assets and movable and immovable property. For example, someone may have built a luxurious house and live in it. If we return to the Soviet example, after the October Revolution, the authorities seized property from wealthy people and turned luxury homes into communal apartments. That will not happen in our case. No one plans to move an ordinary citizen into someone else’s mansion. This raises the question: who received the mansion belonging to formerprimeministerformer prime minister Hovik Abrahamyan, or the Golden Palace hotel in Tsaghkadzor?

The situation is also problematic here. Even if a new wealthy owner buys these properties, a change of government could lead to their seizure again, with the authorities claiming that the original confiscation was unlawful.

Moreover, the phrase ‘returning property to the people’ sounds somewhat abstract to me. The trend shows that confiscated real estate goes not to the people, but to another wealthy person close to the authorities. And the public will ask: ‘What do we get out of it?’

Let me give you an example. There used to be a kindergarten in our courtyard. A newly wealthy owner acquired it through an illegal transfer. If the state takes the building back today and restores its former status as a kindergarten, then yes, that would mean ‘returning it to the people’.

In other cases, this could become a vicious circle in which each successive government dispossesses the previous one. This is quite dangerous, especially in the context of investment. Investors should not have to fear that the authorities might dispossess them tomorrow.”

How can confiscated funds be used?

“As for monetary confiscations, the seized funds go into the budget, into what is known as a ‘common pot’. It is unclear how the authorities then spend this money. These are not earmarked revenues, so the authorities decide how to use them.

It would be better to classify these revenues as earmarked funds and regulate them by law, directing the money towards social programmes designed to improve citizens’ welfare.”

Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

World.title: Poll: Do Abkhazia residents consider voting in Russia’s State Duma elections important? Video
World.content:
Russia’s State Duma elections will take place on 20 September. As most residents of Abkhazia hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, they can also take part in the vote. In the republic, which has a population of 250,000, as many as 35 polling stations have opened, and campaigning is in full swing.

Ahead of the election, we asked residents of Sukhum whether they planned to vote and whether they believed doing so would make a real difference.

The poll produced highly contradictory responses. Some people do not want to spend their day off voting in another country. Others consider it very important because, “if things go badly in Russia, things will get very hot here in Abkhazia too”.

Rustam: “For some reason, Russia is placing great importance on Abkhazia at the moment, and they really want all residents to take part in these elections. Perhaps it does not even matter how people vote, because there is no alternative. What matters is showing the turnout — that people are actively and collectively going to the polls, thereby acknowledging the assistance Russia provides to Abkhazia.

Personally, I will not vote because I see no point in it. If the [Yabloko party] had not been barred from the election, I would definitely have voted. Or I would have supported the Communists. As things stand, I do not want to spend my day off that way.”

Eliso: “I will definitely go to the polls and vote.

I will not say whom I will vote for. But as a Russian passport holder, I have the right to influence the composition of the State Duma, because the decisions made there directly affect us.

As a woman and a future mother, I want Abkhazia residents with Russian citizenship to be able to receive child benefits. I believe this bill should be among the first issues considered by the new parliamentary term.”

Timur: “I always vote in every election, both ours and Russia’s. My choice may almost never win, but I want to feel involved and have at least some opportunity to influence events. Russia directly affects us, and by voting I make my small contribution to what is happening in Abkhazia today.”

Almaskhan: “I will not vote. I never take part in elections and I am not interested in politics. I do not even know which parties are currently running or what they decide. Everything is done without us anyway. We live in a reality that we simply have to adapt to. It is impossible to change anything with a ‘tick’ on a ballot — everything has already been decided.”

Liana: “I will see how things go on Sunday, but I am not particularly keen. I do not even know whom to choose. The only party I hear about is United Russia, because its s are everywhere. Everyone says it is the strongest party. And Kiriyenko (the Kremlin’s overseer of Abkhazia — JAMnews) is a member, so apparently everything here is done through them. If I go, I will probably vote for them.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Will Abkhaz vote in Russia’s State Duma elections?

World.title: Investigation launched into dozens of children falling ill at Tbilisi nurseries
World.content:
Children poisoned at Tbilisi kindergartens

Fourteen children were taken to hospitals from state-run nurseries in Tbilisi with symptoms of intoxication. The agency responsible for managing the capital’s kindergartens said seven state-run nurseries had suspended operations “to prevent epidemiological risks”.

According to the agency, the children had developed high temperatures, while some also experienced nausea and vomiting.

The Investigation Service of the Ministry of Finance has launched an inquiry into the incident. Searches reportedly continued throughout the night at four kindergartens and three companies supplying food to them. Relevant teams from the Interior Ministry and the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture also took part in the investigative activities.

At this stage, it is unclear what caused the children’s condition or whether the cases were linked to food served at the nurseries. Some parents said their children had eaten a beef cutlet at the kindergarten. However, doctors say investigators will only be able to establish the exact cause through clinical tests.

The investigation is being conducted under Article 198, Part 2 of the Criminal Code. The provision concerns the production and sale of products that pose a danger to human life or health, where this creates a risk to life or health.

According to the information available so far, 55 children and one staff member from 20 Tbilisi kindergartens have sought medical attention. However, the number of children and staff showing signs of poisoning may be higher, as not all of them have visited medical facilities.

Maya Chkhaidze, director of the Tsitsishvili Children’s Clinic, said 14 children from different kindergartens had been brought to the clinic. They had experienced vomiting, abdominal pain and symptoms typical of gastroenteritis.

“This could be a symptom of a viral infection or intoxication. At this stage, it is impossible to determine the exact cause,” Chkhaidze said.

According to her, none of the patients is in serious condition. Several children have already stabilised and are in satisfactory condition, although they remain in the clinic under medical observation.

Saba Buadze, a former Tbilisi City Council member from the opposition Lelo party, wrote on social media that companies which win tenders supply food products to kindergartens, while staff prepare meals directly on the premises.

According to him, the estimated value of procurement in this sector exceeded 100 million lari (around $40 million) in 2024–2025.

Buadze recalled corruption cases uncovered in the sector, including during the investigation into the case of recently convicted former State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. One of the corruption episodes for which authorities charged him involved allegedly taking kickbacks from commercial organisations when awarding kindergarten food procurement contracts, using his official position.

“During my time on the Tbilisi City Council, we summoned officials accused of corruption to the council several times. But they failed to attend the hearings, violating the law. Recently, the quality of food in kindergartens has improved compared with previous years,” Buadze wrote.

Children poisoned at Tbilisi kindergartens

World.title: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers urges Russia to withdraw troops from Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
Council of Europe urges Russia to withdraw troops

The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers has again called on Russia to withdraw its troops from Georgia’s occupied regions and end so-called “borderisation” – the installation of border signs along the dividing lines in the Georgian-Ossetian and Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zones.

According to the Georgian Justice Ministry, at its September meeting the Committee of Ministers discussed the implementation of European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) judgments in the interstate case Georgia v Russia.

● The Committee reaffirmed its support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and called on the Russian Federation to fulfil its international obligations.

● Among its demands, the Committee called for the withdrawal of Russian troops from Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region and an end to so-called “borderisation”.

● The Committee also called on Russia to ensure the free and safe movement of the local population, access to property and the opportunity to receive education in the Georgian language in the Russian-occupied regions.

● The Committee of Ministers called for the necessary conditions to be created for the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced people to their homes and for an end to killings, abductions, torture, unlawful detention and other serious violations.

The Georgian Justice Ministry said the government had secured rulings in several major interstate cases against Russia at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, including cases concerning Russia’s deportation of Georgian citizens, the August 2008 war and Russia’s continuing occupation of Georgian territories.

According to the ministry, the Georgian authorities continue to work to secure the full implementation of the ECHR judgments through legal and diplomatic mechanisms.

World.title: Today marks City Day for Khankendi, Khojaly, Khojavand and Aghdere
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. Today marks City Day for Khankendi, Khojaly, Khojavand and Aghdere.

On September 18, 2024, President Ilham Aliyev signed an order amending the order “On establishing City Days in the territories of the Republic of Azerbaijan liberated from occupation.”

Under the order, September 20 was declared City Day for Khankendi, Khojaly, Khojavand and Aghdere.

It should be noted that on September 19, 2023, the Azerbaijani Army launched local anti-terrorist measures in response to provocations and terrorist acts by the Armenian armed forces and forced the separatists to surrender in less than 24 hours.

The anti-terrorist measures were aimed at ensuring the implementation of the provisions of the trilateral statement, preventing large-scale provocations in the Karabakh economic region, ensuring the disarmament and withdrawal of units of the Armenian armed forces from the territory of Azerbaijan, neutralizing their military infrastructure, ensuring the safety of civilians returning to the territories liberated from occupation, as well as Azerbaijani servicemen and civilians involved in reconstruction work, and restoring Azerbaijan’s constitutional order.

On September 28, 2023, separatist leader Samvel Shahramanyan signed a document on the dissolution of the so-called “regime” in Karabakh.

On October 15, 2023, President Ilham Aliyev raised the State Flag of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the cities of Aghdere, Khojavand and Khojaly, in the settlement of Askeran in Khojaly, on the territory of the Sarsang reservoir and in the city of Khankendi.

World.title: Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

In Victoria's tropical north, where the Murray River winds, a select group of houses are selling for half of what you'd expect.

It's got nothing to do with changes in the housing market and can trip up even the most savvy investor.

The unusual house prices are thanks to the 140-year-old legacy of two Canadian engineers who decided education should be the benefactor of their entrepreneurial endeavours.

Mildura's founders set aside one-fifteenth of the town's available land to generate funds for education in the region. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Mildura's college lease scheme is unique.

No other Australian town has one.

In the citrus capital, 184 lots are leased to individuals and organisations instead of being sold freehold.

Basically, someone can own the improvements but not the land itself.

Officially, the land is owned by the Victorian education minister.

Revenue from the lease agreements goes directly to schools in Sunraysia, which use the funds to buy new classroom equipment and technology that they would otherwise go without.

A Department of Education spokesperson said the Mildura Schools Land Trust disburses about $1.95 million annually to 27 primary and secondary schools, providing additional funding that benefits more than 9,000 students.

Canadian engineers William B Chaffey and George Chaffey founded the township of Mildura. (Supplied: Chaffey Trail)

A lofty deal

In 1886, the Victorian government signed a deal with Canadian engineers George and William Chaffey to build the Mildura irrigation settlement.

Historian and former primary school principal Bob Walton said the Chaffey brothers set aside one-fifteenth of available land to generate funds for an agricultural college, although this was never built.

Instead, a local high school became the first to benefit from the lease funds.

"They decided to set aside and not sell some of the allotments in the colony," he said.

"The Chaffeys were very interested in education."

Mr Walton said the Chaffey brothers were inspired by a similar scheme in California, their base before coming to Australia.

'Cheap' prices grab buyer attention

College lease properties often appear in real estate listings for what, at first glance, seem like a bargain price.

One home recently sold for a reported $300,000 on Mildura's Lemon Avenue where, across the road, a similar freehold property fetched almost $550,000 two months earlier.

"Obviously, there's lease land for other things, but not like this. This is very unique," Ray White Mildura managing director Damian Portaro said.

"It's interesting having to explain to a buyer from Melbourne or Sydney exactly what this is.

" It's 100 years old now, this system. It was probably ahead of its time back then, but I haven't seen it or heard of it anywhere else. "

Agent Damian Portaro says investors are drawn to college lease homes. (Supplied: Ray White Real Estate)

Mr Portaro said the property listings appealed to first home buyers, but they often ran into difficulty obtaining finance due to the unusual lease clause.

He said most buyers of college lease land were investors rather than owner-occupiers.

"They might get in for half the price, for example, then they start factoring in 'there's rates, there's insurances, there's a college lease I have to pay.'"

Unlocking housing supply

Mallee Accommodation and Support Program (MASP) has utilised the scheme to build social housing on five college-lease properties with assistance from Homes Victoria.

Charmaine Calis is the CEO of MASP, which has built social housing on five college lease properties. (Supplied: MASP)

"We see it as a really good way to have two social goods out of the one block of land — both continuing to support local schools and also building social and affordable housing onto it," chief executive Charmaine Calis said.

MASP told a parliamentary inquiry last year the Victorian government should look at more ways college leases could ease the housing crisis.

"We do need to increase the supply of housing available, and this is certainly one way we can look at doing that," Ms Calis said.

World.title: Three women killed in suspected DV-related incidents in 24 hours
World.content:
Three women have died in separate suspected domestic violence-related incidents across New South Wales in 24 hours, including a 90-year-old woman who was fatally stabbed in Sydney's east.

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

About 5:15pm on Saturday, emergency services were called to a unit at Bondi Beach, where they found an elderly woman with stab wounds to her torso.

Paramedics treated the 90-year-old but she died at the scene.

A 47-year-old man, who was known to the woman, was arrested at the unit.

He has since been charged with domestic violence-related murder.

The man was refused bail and is due to appear before Bail Division Local Court on Sunday.

A 47-year-old man has been charged with domestic violence-related murder. (ABC News)

Woman found dead at property in northern NSW

Hours later a man was arrested over the death of a 70-year-old woman in NSW's Northern Tablelands region.

Police were called to a property on Ironbark Road at Mole River, west of Tenterfield, following reports of a domestic violence incident about 9:30pm on Saturday.

Officers were told a 37-year-old man had entered the home and attempted to steal a vehicle before assaulting the 74-year-old male home owner.

Following the 37-year-old man's arrest, police located a body, believed to be that of a 70-year-old woman, during a search of a neighbouring property.

She is yet to be formally identified.

A house located on the property was also partially damaged from a fire, according to police.

The man was taken into custody.

Fatal stabbing in Riverina region

In Wagga Wagga, a 31-year-old man was arrested over the fatal stabbing of a 23-year-old woman.

Police were called to a home on Ziegler Avenue at Kooringal about 11:45am on Saturday.

Officers were told a man had left the property before emergency services arrived.

An 18-year-old man was arrested at the scene and taken to Wagga Wagga Police Station, where he was released without charge.

About 8:30pm, police arrested a 31-year-old man at a nearby home on Menzies Avenue.

He has been taken to Wagga Wagga Police Station, where inquiries continue.

Police said all parties are believed to be known to each other.

Police will provide an update at a media conference this morning.

World.title: Emergency helicopters still unable to land at two SA regional hospitals
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Emergency helicopters remain unable to use the helipad at the regional hospitals in Victor Harbor and Murray Bridge.

South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer said the issues at Murray Bridge were close to being resolved, but the situation at Victor Harbor was "complex" and would need a long-term solution.

The Victor Harbor Childcare and Education Centre sits alongside the helipad. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The sites are the final two to reopen after 13 regional helipads were temporarily closed in 2024 because they did not meet new Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) guidelines.

The helipads cannot be used until certified as safe by Babcock, the current operators of the MedSTAR helicopter service.

Issues remain around the required downwash exclusion zone and the proximity of houses at Murray Bridge, and a community-run childcare centre at Victor Harbor.

The centre has a peppercorn lease in place with SA Health until 2030.

The childcare centre is adjacent to the helipad. (Supplied: David Basham)

Mr Boyer told state parliament last month there had been discussions with residents of Murray Bridge who "might be in a home that is in the downwash area" and that he "hoped to have positive news soon".

However, he said reinstating the Southern Fleurieu Health Service's helipad at Victor Harbor would take "longer-term planning".

Independent member for Finniss Lou Nicholson said it was her understanding the minister was trying to find a solution ahead of the lease expiry date.

Lou Nicholson is the independent member for Finniss. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

From her conversations with government, she said she understood that it was not the government's intention to wait until the lease expired.

"If indeed the path ahead is finding a new location for the childcare centre, that work does need to be underway now," she said.

A community and education centre is located adjacent to the helipad in Victor Harbor. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Hor)

One Nation member for Hammond Robert Roylance raised the Murray Bridge helipad in parliament last month.

While happy with indications it was closer to opening, he said his electorate wanted a clearer response.

"Can we expect it in three months, six months? Soon is good, but what is soon?" he said.

Robert Roylance says his electorate needs to know when the helipad will be operational. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Roylance said a 66-metre space was required around the helicopter landing site and he understood several houses were within that area.

In a statement provided to the ABC, Mr Boyer said $23.4 million had been invested to upgrade regional helipads across the state to meet updated CASA requirements, and work continued to bring the two remaining sites back into operation.

"Medical retrieval services remain available for the community and surrounding areas by utilising alternative sites nearby.

"Patient, staff and community safety remain the priority."

World.title: Infertility was incredibly hard. Loving one another got us through
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After three IVF cycles, Susanne and Mike Armour made the difficult decision to stop trying for a baby. While childlessness wasn't something they planned for, the pair, based in Sydney, say their unwavering love for one another meant the future as a family of two was still one to look forward to.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

One or two kids would be nice

Mike: We met on the first day of acupuncture school in 2005 in New Zealand.

I was just quite taken with her. For me, it was love at first sight.

I just assumed that I would have kids, like it was part of growing up — we would get married, have a family.

Susanne: Having children wasn't necessarily high on my list, but once Mike and I were engaged, that was the kind of thing you start talking about. "Oh yeah, maybe it would be nice to have a child or two."

Once you start to think about that as a woman, it's a thought that is quite difficult to turn off.

September 14 to 20 is World Childless Week. If you have a story about childlessness, we'd be honoured to hear from you

The most traumatic experience

Susanne: We started seriously trying for a baby in 2009 with me doing the whole shebang of acupuncture, herbs, temperature checking, et cetera.

I have always had painful periods, but in 2008 I started to have pain outside my period.

I eventually had an exploratory laparoscopy, which found nothing apart from some ''scar tissue' and we ended up doing three cycles of IVF.

The second and third were discontinued as I did not respond to the medications.

Thinking back, going through IVF was one of the most traumatic experiences I've ever had.

I just felt like a number. There was no continuity of care or carer, no emotional support.

It was so distressing.

I ended up with overwhelming grief, anxiety, feelings of loss of control.

Susanne and Mike Armour would have liked to have one or two children together. (Supplied)

Mike: We were obviously in a position where Sus is a midwife and I had a medical background. We had good health literacy, good health contacts.

And we still just felt incredibly unsupported.

The thing that really struck me was just how little support or care there was for me.

I wanted to be there to support Sus, but I didn't feel like there was anyone there to support me.

I don't remember anyone asking me about my feelings or experience at the time, and only one wonderful friend asked me afterwards.

We would not leave each other

Mike: We were having our third cycle of IVF and the nurse came in and she started crying. She said something like: "I'm afraid there is nothing more we can do."

When she left, I remember Sus saying she'd had enough, she didn't want to go through any more, and we'd put our lives on hold, which was very true. And that she didn't have anything left.

And I just thought, "Well, she's the one who is going through all of this, the drugs and investigations." I thought, "That seems fair to me, I understand."

Susanne: I was just done. I just had nothing left at the end. I felt so traumatised and I just wanted to put it all behind me really.

We had no friends who would understand what we were both going through. We pretty much just had us.

We saw several friend relationships break apart from fertility struggles and that was something we regularly talked about.

We started the journey together and whatever the outcome, we would not leave each other.

I remember saying how good we were as a couple.

Having a baby would have been an add-on but us together as the two of us, as a family unit, we were perfect.

Mike: I just remember thinking I had two choices. Either stay with Sus and we don't have children, or if I want children, then it has to be with someone else.

And it was a no-brainer; I would much rather stay with Sus and just be the two of us.

Helping others has been healing

During IVF, the couple say they felt unsupported. (Supplied)

Susanne: My last IVF cycle was at the end of 2013. I was 39.

Eventually, after we moved to Australia, I had a hysterectomy, which showed extensive endometriosis and adenomyosis.

The hysterectomy and the diagnosis came as a relief to be honest.

What probably was the hardest when I was going through infertility was that I am also a midwife and was working in a postnatal facility at the time.

When you work with women and families having babies, seeing the love and joy and still giving your absolute best to them — it is one of the hardest, most selfless things to do.

What helped me heal was shifting out of normal midwifery to supporting women going through grief and loss. That is where my speciality now is. That's really been healing for me.

Mike: Seeing what Sus went through with her pain, and being shocked by what little could be offered to her, triggered me into doing a PhD and working in endometriosis research.

I thought there has to be something we can do about this to make things better for other people.

We're best friends

Susanne: I love how caring Mike is. How compassionate. And I love his sense of humour.

He's the first person I see in a crowd and when he comes around the corner, it still catches my breath.

I'm just incredibly proud of him for who he is and what he does. That he stands up for women and women's health. That makes me love him even more every day.

Mike: Sus is the kindest person I know. No-one is perfect, but she's perfect for me.

She's my best friend even after all these years. I still look forward to coming home so we can talk.

Things like travelling and dating and romance have taken a back seat for us while I've been dealing with some really bad health challenges the last few years.

But we still have so much to talk about and I just enjoy being with her.

World.title: Albanese visits Apple HQ, warns Australia can't sit on sidelines of AI race
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has not ruled out changing copyright laws to attract AI investment from tech giants, warning Australia needs to be "forward leaning" if it is to help shape the development of the increasingly powerful technology.

Paying a visit to Apple's headquarters in Cupertino, California on his way to New York, Mr Albanese also made the case for global rules to regulate the development of AI and said he would be speaking to like-minded leaders at next week's United Nations General Assembly.

Sitting on the sidelines was not an option, he said, describing AI as a "global phenomenon".

"I certainly accept that there are risks and that's why we need to mitigate them," Mr Albanese told reporters.

"There is a need for a discussion about what the global framework is for the rollout of AI, because it is moving very quickly, and we need to make sure that humans remain in control."

Debate over the pace of AI development is reaching an inflection point, with Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI's Sam Altman and Space X's Elon Musk, calling for a coordinated slowdown.

Mr Albanese has made it clear he wants the two major powers, the US and China, to cooperate "in the interests of humanity".

"The truth is they're the big two giants here and so we want to see cooperation," he told the ABC's Insiders program in an interview recorded in Cupertino.

"President Trump, of course, will act in the interests of the United States. But there's a need for all of us to act in the interests of humanity."

But US President Donald Trump has pushed back, arguing any deceleration would give America's biggest competitor, China, the upper hand.

Ahead of his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week, Mr Trump doubled down, declaring he would establish a new "AI Force" to protect against the "decimation or destruction" of AI.

"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful," the president wrote.

"We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"

Australia could help 'shape' technology

Australia is developing national standards for AI and data centres, setting out safety, environmental and industrial rules, which the prime minister said he hoped to legislate early next year.

Separately, the government is consulting on changes to Australia's copyright laws that tech giants including Anthropic and OpenAI have identified as a sticking point over plans to invest here.

They fear their unauthorised use of copyrighted material to create — or "train" — their AI models is breaking the law.

Mr Albanese said meeting with Mr Cook was a "proud moment". (Supplied)

Speaking to reporters in Cupertino, Mr Albanese said writers, musicians and other creatives would maintain control over their intellectual property and be remunerated for any use of their work, but left the door open to an "opt out" model.

If Australia can attract more investment from companies, particularly in cutting edge frontier models, Mr Albanese said it could help shape the development of the technology.

"We think that there is a way through," he said.

"We've actually had constructive discussions to make sure that we can shape the way that that occurs, rather than, be just, if you like, powerless.

"I want to make sure that Australia plays a role in this as forward leaning."

AI firms meet with ministers The leaked plans have sparked backlash from creatives and critics across the political spectrum.

The government is refusing to give AI companies free rein to train their models on copyrighted materials in Australia, but the ABC revealed it is considering other proposals including giving creators the right to opt-out, reversing the existing onus for companies to seek permission to use copyright material.

The creative sector, the Coalition and the Greens have all criticised the proposal suggesting it is more favourable to tech giants and undermines copyright laws.

Apple meeting a 'proud moment'

Mr Albanese was invited to Cupertino by Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook to discuss the tech giant's new parental controls for children, which were partly inspired by Australia's social media reforms.

Mr Albanese was invited to discuss Apple's new parental controls for children. (Supplied)

The new features, to be made available in Australia, give parents the ability to control the apps, content and contacts their children interact with, impose time limits on usage and detect images that contain nudity, gore and violence.

Labor moves to make algorithm a choice Labor wants to make social media platforms proactively reduce foreseeable harms while giving users control over whether algorithms shape their feeds.

Mr Albanese and Mr Cook held a 45-minute closed-door meeting which the prime minister described as a "proud moment".

"I'm not sure it has been recognised fully in Australia is just the way that Australia is seen to have led the world when it comes to protecting children from some of the negative consequences of access to social media and new technology," Mr Albanese said.

"And that was certainly recognised by Mr Cook"

Mr Albanese will use Australia's leadership on digital safety as part of his pitch when he formally launches his bid for a two-year position on the United Nations Security Council from 2029.

Australia last held a temporary spot in 2014 and is vying for one of two seats available this time around.

World.title: Protests in Philadelphia as Ed Sheeran returns to stage
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Protesters have descended on a Philadelphia stadium as Ed Sheeran returns to the stage after becoming embroiled in controversy set off by his opening act's pro-Palestinian comments.

Rapper Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's US Loop Tour on Monday, local time, after the owners of stadiums hosting upcoming shows objected to his shouting "Free Palestine" onstage in New Jersey earlier this month.

Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour's promoter was responsible.

Macklemore donate millions to Palestine Macklemore had challenged Robert Kraft to match his donation to Palestinian charities after the billionaire stadium owner dropped him from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour.

But four supporting acts soon quit the Shape of You singer's tour. They included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.

At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the conflict in Gaza and West Bank settler violence, the 35-year-old British performer has maintained his apolitical stance.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.

Ed Sheeran says the tour promoter was responsible for dropping Macklemore. (AP: Andy Kropa/Invision/File)

However, he said, "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum".

No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced, and it is not known how Sheeran plans to carry out his show in Philadelphia on Saturday night.

Speaking to the ABC outside the Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, protest organiser Adi Chattopadhyay said "there is a right and wrong side of history and [Sheeran's] on the wrong one".

"If he wants to engage with this city, if he wants to engage with the community at a meaningful level, then he needs to take a stance," he said.

"He needs to be more in favour and advocating for a free Palestine, otherwise things like this will continue to happen."

Pro-Palestinian demonstrators gather at a Philadelphia train station prior to the protest. (AP: Allie Ippolito)

Protester Donna Greenberg described the protests as "a cultural watershed moment".

"It gives people who are pro-Palestinian an opportunity to educate other people in a way that we have not been able to do before," she said.

The former busker-turned-superstar, accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners, has been targeted by boycott calls over the controversy.

A pro-Palestinian group has urged artists, fans and crew members to stay away from Sheeran's concerts on three continents.

"We now extend our call for boycotting Ed Sheeran's entire world tour, including the upcoming Latin American dates, and the as-yet-unannounced European leg," the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel said in a statement.

AFP/ABC

World.title: In an outback town, this small venue raised $1 million to save itself
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It might seem unlikely that a volunteer-run venue in one of the country's most remote towns could inspire people from across Australia and the world to help raise $1 million to save it.

But it did.

Over the past month, the founders of popular Alice Springs live music venue The Black Wreath have been fundraising to buy the building and turn the whole block into a creative hub after their landlord put the property up for sale.

Artists and music industry figures came on board, including Amyl and the Sniffers, who played at The Black Wreath's Blacken Open Air festival in 2022, as well as donors who matched pledges dollar for dollar.

Loading Instagram content

The Black Wreath hosts local gigs and offers artists a recording and rehearsal space, helping kick-start the careers of some of the most remote bands in the world.

Before he launched the campaign on August 4, the Black Wreath's founder, who goes by the mononym Pirate, hardly used social media.

But by the end of the appeal, he was posting daily videos, pushing as hard as he could to save one of the creative heartbeats of Alice Springs.

"It's a massive milestone, I'm really proud of the community achievement and everyone that's gotten behind this," he said.

The fundraisers gave themselves until September 13 to reach their $1 million funding goal, but hit the target two days early before a massive weekend of coordinated gigs across the country in solidarity with the cause.

Pirate says he hopes to run The Black Wreath as a foundation. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

It wasn't until the day after the Alice Springs gig, headlined by South East Desert Metal, that Pirate had his first day off in months.

He said the whole town "became a metal head for the night".

"The last month it's been 12 to 15 hours every single day, it hasn't been healthy, but it's been necessary," Pirate said.

" And yesterday I just absolutely collapsed, couldn't do a bloody thing. "

However, Pirate said there was a long road still ahead.

As part of the fundraising campaign, people from across the country made pledges for something in return, which ranged from T-shirts, records, rings and hats to an entire festival, Blacken Open Air, to be held on April 30 next year.

"I'm not celebrating yet just yet; I'm getting back to work," Pirate said.

Loading...

"It's just the beginning of the process, we've raised some money and now we need to negotiate with the owners.

"There's a lot more to do."

Pirate said the grand vision was to turn the entire property into a creative precinct.

"My big hopes and aspirations and dreams are that it's run as a foundation and the income generated goes into local music and arts," he said.

"And touring Central Australian artists outside of here, [as well as] bringing artists to Alice Springs and putting them on stages here as well.

"Fifteen years of doing this, I find that the travel aspect has been the biggest hindrance to connecting us with a wider community."

Ltyentye Apurta/Santa Teresa musicians South East Desert Metal describe themselves as the most isolated touring band in the world, and credit The Black Wreath for success that's seen them perform on the steps of the Sydney Opera House.

The band's lead vocalist and guitarist, Chris Wallace, said there was nothing else like it in Alice Springs.

The fundraiser to save The Black Wreath has been hailed as "an amazing moment for the whole nation". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I really love it, all that comes from Black Wreath," he said.

" Black Wreath was the one that found us, and made us who we are. "

Reflecting on the successful fundraiser, Pirate said it was "an amazing moment for the whole nation, especially for the heavy metal community".

"This is very historic," he said.

"I'm proud to be a part of that community and we're as far away from everyone as you can possibly get, but right now it feels like there's no distance at all between us."

World.title: John Farnham to miss tribute concert due to poor health
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed ahead of the Melbourne event.

The concert, dubbed The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend, will be held at Rod Laver Arena this evening, with funds raised on the night going towards the cancer service that supported Farnham during his cancer battle.

In a statement posted on social media, Farnham's wife, Jill, and sons, Robert and James, wrote that the singer was "deeply moved" by the musical tribute but would be too unwell to attend the arena spectacular.

John Farnham performing his 1986 smash hit You're the Voice at a 2017 charity concert. (ABC News: Kristian Silva)

His family confirmed the 77-year-old You're the Voice singer required continuous oxygen support and was receiving 24-hour nursing care.

"Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending tomorrow night to watch it all happen," the Farnham family statement said.

"Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John's health to help explain why.

"John's health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility.

"It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it."

Farnham's 1986 comeback, Whispering Jack, was one of Australia's best-selling albums and relaunched the singer's career. (ABC)

Some of the biggest names in Australian entertainment are scheduled to take centre stage at the Farnham tribute tonight, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson.

International stars, including Canadian singer Celine Dion and American crooner Richard Marx, are also taking part in the event, which will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia.

"We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John's changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John's fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend," the Farnham family said.

"If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person.

" As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable. "

Farnham is one of Australia's most successful performers, with his 1986 album, Whispering Jack, selling more than 1.6 million copies.

The British-born singer was named 1987 Australian of the Year by then-prime minister Bob Hawke, and has won 21 ARIA awards.

In 2024 Farnham released an autobiography, The Voice Inside, which details the monumental triumphs of his career as well as the immense struggles he has faced.

World.title: Fans condemned for throwing bottles at umpires after prelim heartbreak
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaAFL 2026 Fans condemned for throwing bottles at umpires after prelim heartbreak Alexander Darling Updated September 20, 2026 — 10:03am ,first published September 20, 2026 — 8:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ugly scenes erupted at the MCG on Saturday night when fans threw bottles onto the ground, narrowly missing umpires as they walked off the turf after a pulsating finish to the preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane. Dozens of water bottles and cans rained down on the ground after Brisbane’s nine-point victory, when Hawthorn fans booed the umpires and vented their fury to a series of high-stakes decisions in the match’s dying minutes. Loading Footage showed one field umpire, Jacob Mollison, reacting quickly to protect his colleague from a projectile that appeared to have been thrown from the second level of the stadium. The ugly scenes triggered a blunt reaction from AFL figures: “They should not have things thrown at them. A bottle’s come down from the top tier,” said commentator Luke Hodge, who played for both Hawthorn and Brisbane.



The Lions clawed back the lead moments before the final siren when Hawks defender Jarman Impey was pinged for holding the ball and Lion Hugh McCluggage cooly slotted the resultant set-shot goal. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said he understood the fans’ emotions, but condemned their behaviour. Cans litter the ground after Hawthorn’s loss to Brisbane. Getty Images “The emotion of sport, it’s why we love it so much,” he said in his post-match press conference. “All sports, but ours in particular – the beauty is the emotion it makes you feel. At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears. Part of me wanted to scream with rage. Part of me wanted to throw chairs. “When you’re in the stands, you need to continue to feel that emotion, but we shouldn’t be throwing things on the field.



AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said on Sunday that he was stunned by the spectacle. “I’ve never seen a collective doing what they did like that,” he told this masthead. Cans and bottles on the ground at the MCG. Getty Images “It wasn’t just one or two or five people. It looked like it was a few hundred people around the entire ground throwing stuff onto the ground. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing.” Issko said the sheer number of fans participating in the ugly spectacle made the incident different to previous throwing incidents.



Earlier this year, Hawks star Nick Watson claimed he had a Coke bottle thrown at him in a match against Sydney, while a fan who threw a lemon at Eagles player Reuben Ginbey was banned for five years. “If we can find people that threw it, even though we’re not going to catch everyone, they should face consequences, that’s just not the fans that the AFL fans association represent,” he said. “It’s just not on. If you want to do that to umpires, we won’t have umpires and we won’t have a game of footy.” Issko said the incident would be on the agenda of his group’s next meeting with the AFL, but how to prevent such widespread delinquency happening again he wasn’t sure.



Victorian Premier Ben Carroll also condemned the behaviour on Sunday, telling reporters that throwing projectiles at umpires was “not the Victorian way” and those responsible should be made an example of. “I think this people should be made an example of. This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head,” Carroll said. Umpires dodge projectiles as they exit the ground. AFL Photos via Getty Images “You’ve always got to respect the umpire’s decision. As a North Melbourne supporter, I’ve gone home heartbroken many a time, but that’s just the way it goes.” The MCG said its security team was investigating the incident. “We have zero tolerance for this type of behaviour at our venue,” a spokesperson said.

Washington: US President Donald Trump said he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as an “AI tsar”, and create an “AI force”, though he did not provide details about either initiative or how they would be implemented. Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed by AI technology on humans and property. President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Saturday (Washington time).



“Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘I am the Hoax Buster’: Trump takes on America with seven-post rant promoting AI, data centres If Trump follows through on the pledge, it would be his second AI tsar. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served in the role before stepping down in the spring and moving into an external advisory position. Sacks has echoed Trump’s scepticism of new AI regulation. Speaking at a Politico event on Wednesday, he said AI developers should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products and could be held liable if problems arise, adding that new federal rules are unnecessary.



The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s post. Related Article Analysis

China relations ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’: How the world’s two most powerful leaders can find common ground Trump’s post comes ahead of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in artificial intelligence, which both governments view as vital to their economic and military strength. Trump and technology executives have argued that excessive regulation would slow US AI development and undermine American companies’ ability to compete with Chinese rivals, a claim that safety advocates often refute.



US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent would meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday (New York time) at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York to discuss AI security, trade and other economic issues, a person familiar with the planning said.
