World.title: The Qantas lounge gave her a dressing down for her ugg boots. I’m with the airline on this one
World.content:
LifestyleFashionStyle Opinion The Qantas lounge gave her a dressing down for her ugg boots. I’m with the airline on this one Melissa Hoyer Writer September 20, 2026 — 9:30am

September 20, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Recently, someone got turfed out of the Qantas lounge in Melbourne. Not for being drunk, obnoxious, for gluttonous plate stacking, food smuggling or overstaying their welcome, but for wearing ugg boots. Cassidy Gaiter, a singer and theatre performer, said she’d worn the same slippers into five lounges in the past month without a blink from staff. This time, apparently, she didn’t look “business” enough, so someone made a beeline for her at the door. Cassidy Gaiter needs to move to Thornton in NSW’s Hunter Valley, the home of the giant ugg boots, situated outside Mortels Sheepskin Factory. Maitland Mercury Cue the outrage cycle. “Make it make sense,” she said. Except it does make sense; it’s just not the sense she wanted it to make. Face it: their house, their rules. Here’s the thing nobody wants to hear: airport style has been in freefall for years, and the ugg boot bouncer moment isn’t some kooky overreach. It’s one of the last places still enforcing the idea that how you show up in public matters even slightly. And I’m absolutely here for it.



While Cassidy – who seems a nice human – has since deleted her initial lounge banishment beef from TikTok, it got me thinking. Once upon a time, flying was an event. Not a ballgown moment but it at least involved presentable humans in public spaces. These days, somewhere between boarding-group chaos, delayed flights and neck-pillow couture, we’ve collectively decided the plane – and now, apparently, the airline lounge – is just an extension of the couch. Nobody’s asking for three-piece suits or cocktail attire at 35,000 feet – we’re not resurrecting Mad Men energy – but there’s a wide, comfortable middle ground between “airport chic” and “I rolled out of bed and emotionally gave up”. And lots of fliers, whether frequent or not, have set up camp firmly at the second address. And even though we try to sleep on a plane (whether you turn left or right on boarding) you should no more arrive in PJs for the flight than you would walk into a restaurant with an apron and a baking dish expecting to make some noise in the kitchen. Athleisure did some of this damage. Leggings, hoodies, slides, sock-and-sandal hybrids are all technically functional but at times worn with the enthusiasm of someone who has accepted defeat before gate allocation. “You don’t need couture but just clothes that are clean and look like they were meant to be worn out of the house.” Getty Images



Sure, comfort is king when you fly but it doesn’t mean a bit of spit and polish should get walked out via the emergency exit. The “wellness comfort” movement of soft fabrics, oversized everything, breathable nothing-in-particular is brilliant and something we all love, but while long-haul flights are hard on circulation, spines and peace of mind, comfort doesn’t have to mean visual and sensory chaos. Tailored track pants exist. Clean sneakers exist. So do clipped toenails, underarm deodorant and pumice stones. Uggs, famously, were designed for the walk from the shower to the couch and are a winter-wardrobe staple at my place but they’re not for an airport lounge with a buffet, a bar and a view of the tarmac. Interestingly, this isn’t the first time uggs have caused an airport lounge brouhaha. Nearly a decade ago a Human League singer was also denied entry to a lounge for wearing the sheepskin beauties. Social media hasn’t helped with our haute flying attire either. Airport dressing aspiration – the oversized sunglasses, chic trench, effortless “I travel well” vibe – has split into two lanes. There’s hyper-styled influencer theatre or unbothered realism and, somewhere in between, some travellers decided opting out entirely was the easiest lane of all. And it’s Qantas and all airline lounge staff who are left holding the dress code (and yes, there is one!) nobody wants to read before they board.



The idea that airports are still shared, public spaces where a baseline of effort is a form of respect should be common sense, and before you come at me for being an absolute sartorial tosser, no, you do not have to spend big money on a special airport ensemble. You don’t need couture, just clothes that are clean and look like they were meant to be worn out of the house. There is no question that when you dress slightly better, you feel slightly better. You move differently. You carry yourself differently. An airline lounge dress code is one of the few remaining nudges telling us that leaving the house, even to sit in an airport eating free cheese and pikelets, is still, in some small way, an occasion. So no, we’re not bringing back hats and gloves, but maybe, just maybe, if an airline has to spell out “no sleepwear” for adults boarding flights, that’s less a “little-known rule” and more a referendum on how far the bar has dropped. None of this requires a trust fund or a stylist. Looking pulled together is still free. The lounge, it turns out, is just one of the places brave enough to say so out loud.



Melissa Hoyer is a social commentator and writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital Menna Alaa El-Din and Timour Azhari September 20, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Riyadh: Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city’s main airport. Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks by the Houthis in the kingdom. Video and photographs showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main

terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks. Loading The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub.



The Houthis said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa. Related Article Middle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh early on Saturday (Riyadh time). In a statement, the coalition also said it had foiled attacks targeting civilians in the Saudi cities of Bish and

Farasan in the south-west and Taif in the west, as well as Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. It did not say whether there was any damage. Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj, east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh’s Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent.



Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation with the Houthis began in July. Houthi warning The Houthis, who ⁠control ​the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, ​have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red ​Sea. A large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Reuters The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, creating new threats to global oil

supplies and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded.



Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia might have military needs due to the ongoing Houthi attacks and Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants It was unclear what kind of support Turkey might provide, but Fidan, in an interview with broadcaster NTV, said Saudi needs could include “some technical issues”. The trilateral agreement signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all of them. On Friday Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response.



The Iran-aligned group, which seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning advance earlier this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it ​in recent days. The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. US President Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera in an interview aired on

Saturday that Tehran wanted the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to end, adding that he believed Yemenis also wanted a settlement with Saudi Arabia. Rezaei also said Iran had conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in stalled negotiations with the

United States, including “ending the war on all fronts”. Consultations were continuing with Qatari and Pakistani mediators and Tehran was awaiting a response from Trump, Rezaei said.



The UN Security Council in a statement on Friday “condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children”. In the statement, the Security Council also condemned “Houthi military escalation in Yemen”. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Sharon Horgan’s five-star comedy is for every woman stuck in the ‘sandwich generation’
World.content:
★★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Sharon Horgan’s five-star comedy is for every woman stuck in the ‘sandwich generation’ Kylie Northover September 20, 2026 — 9:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Youth ★★★★★ If you’re a fan of Sharon Horgan (who isn’t?), as both writer and actor, you’ll almost certainly love her new comedy-drama. Something of a spiritual successor to her 2006 series Pulling, which followed the dating lives of women in their 30s, and the brilliant Catastrophe, about a marriage kick-started by an accidental pregnancy after a wild week-long fling, Youth sees Horgan exploring the specifics of middle-aged womanhood. But if that sounds too earnest, be assured that it’s very, often darkly, funny. Sharon Horgan as Alex in the comedy-drama Youth. Horgan is Alex, a recently divorced 50-year-old who is the embodiment of the “sandwich generation”, the term for those (almost always women) juggling caring for ageing parents, teenaged or young adult kids, holding down a career and the onset of invisibility and waning sex appeal. The series is deeply informed by her own life: Horgan, recently divorced herself, describes it as “auto-fictiony”. She recently told Vanity Fair that she wanted to look “through the lens of a divorced woman who has a very specific amount of time left to find happiness,” while feeling like there’s a “big alarm bell going off”.



The first episode opens as a solemn voiceover over a montage of influential older women – Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Gloria Steinem, Margaret Atwood – intones about ageing, telling us that “no decade moves faster than 50-60. You need to make every single second of your time count”, before cutting to Alex laughing at a TikTok video of a parrot having a haircut and blow-dry. Phew. Horgan as Alex and Aran Murphy as her rebellious teenage son Ruari. HBO Max Her scrolling is interrupted by a text from her boss/best friend Sam (Sharlene Whyte) asking where she is. Alex is a literary agent, and working for her friend is just one of many frustrations. She’s excited though, that her rebellious teenage son Ruari (Aran Murphy, son of Cillian), is about to head off to university, even if he has started dabbling in videos from manosphere influencers. Ruari’s self-absorbed dad Lorcan (Owen McDonnell), isn’t exactly the greatest role model – he’s a jobbing actor about to move to Canada with his younger girlfriend for a role in a B-grade sci-fi series, leaving Alex to deal with Ruari as he grapples with young manhood. Then there are her parents: her mum has diabetes and her dad is showing signs of dementia (“mild-ish Alzheimer’s, like Joe Biden second term-level”). These are problems she’s trying to share with her younger sister, who is busy with a newborn baby.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Patrick Brammall’s home-grown thriller, plus five more picks At once thrilled and terrified at her newly emptied nest, Alex is also anxious about her age, studying older women on the bus, constantly buying new fitness equipment, worried she’ll never have a relationship again. She has an ongoing casual hook-up with Patrick (Rupert Friend), but he is definitely not the settling-down type, although Alex keeps going back there. Sam insists he’s entirely wrong for her, and sets her up on a blind date. But when the date, Michael (Tim McInnerny), reveals he’s 67, he might as well have said 97 by the look on Alex’s face. When Sam texts her to ask how it’s going, Alex’s response is, “he’s old as f--- is how it’s going. I told you how I feel about a new penis, let alone an old penis”. Alex feels like an older version of Catastrophe’s Sharon – perhaps inevitable given both series draw from Horgan’s actual life – and this is a glorious thing. Rupert Friend co-stars as the roguish Patrick, a former boyfriend of Alex’s. HBO Max

World.title: Albanese urges US, China to strike AI deal akin to nuclear non-proliferation treaty
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAI Albanese urges US, China to strike AI deal akin to nuclear non-proliferation treaty Rob Harris Updated September 20, 2026 — 9:00am ,first published 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cupertino, California: Anthony Albanese has urged the United States and China to strike a deal on artificial intelligence akin to a nuclear non-proliferation treaty ahead as world leaders meeting at the United Nations General Assembly prepare to tackle the rise of the technology. During a visit to California, the prime minister raised the need for nations to commit to international rules governing AI, declaring humans must “remain in control”, after meeting Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the global tech giant’s executive team. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a press conference at Apple Park Visitor Center in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer Australia will join a collective middle-power effort at the United Nations this week amid an attempt to shape the global response to AI and a growing debate over whether the technology is developing faster than efforts to control its risks. The race is being played out largely between the United States and China, as Washington and Beijing compete for technological and strategic advantage. After doomsday warnings of wiping out humanity, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (US time) he was forming an “AI force,” despite some within the industry recently sounding the alarm about the dangers of artificial intelligence continuing to grow unchecked.



“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump wrote, declaring he would fight any “decimation or destruction of AI”. Albanese told ABC’s Insiders program he hoped there would be progress in a scheduled meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week. “The truth is, they’re the big two giants here,” he said. “We want to see co-operation. We’ve seen that in the past with new technologies, even on nuclear weapons, for example. I think middle powers, such as Australia, have a role to play here as well.” Speaking to reporters outside Apple Park, Albanese also left the door open to an opt-out copyright regime for artificial intelligence companies, despite warnings from Australian writers, artists and other creatives that such a system would undermine fundamental copyright protections. Asked whether there was a danger in handing too much power to tech companies, given warnings about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, Albanese said there were risks.



Related Article United Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat “I certainly accept that there are risks, and that’s why we need to mitigate,” he said. “That’s why we need to act, and that is something that’s recognised by the companies themselves.” He said the international debate was already under way among leaders preparing to attend the UN General Assembly in New York. “What is being discussed this week, and has already been the subject of interaction between leaders who’ll be attending the UN this week, is what’s the international framework as well to take advantage of the benefits but also to mitigate the risks,” Albanese said. Spruiking Australia’s pioneering social media ban for under 16s, Albanese met with Apple executives behind closed doors for an hour at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Media were briefly allowed on site for a product demonstration, including the new foldable Duo phone, but were not allowed to film or take any photos of the meeting, buildings or any Apple employees.



AI giants, including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind, have flagged that Australia’s current copyright regime was a hurdle to their increased investment in the country. When asked, Albanese did not rule out the Australian government considering an opt-out system for copyright material used to train AI models. Instead, he stressed the need for Australia to regulate AI and said legislation establishing Australian AI standards would be introduced before the end of the year. “Part of that will be protecting intellectual property,” Albanese said. “We think that the protection of the creative sector is very important, and we’re engaged constructively. I think there’s a way through this.”



Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The ABC last week reported that AI companies would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one plan put forward. Under Australia’s existing copyright regime, the owner of copyright in a piece of writing, photograph or other creative work generally has the right to control how it is reproduced and commercially exploited. Creators and rights holders have warned that an opt-out model would reverse that principle by allowing AI companies to use copyright material unless individual creators took steps to prevent it. They argue the burden should instead fall on AI companies to seek permission before using protected works to train their models. Booker Prize-winning Australian author Richard Flanagan argued last week that copyright was the foundation of Australia’s creative industries rather than an impediment to AI development.

World.title: ‘Ticking bomb’: Inner-eastern rat run’s days could be numbered
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘Ticking bomb’: Inner-eastern rat run’s days could be numbered Rachael Ward September 20, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ten-year-old Floyd Connor says he remembers his fear when a car mounted the footpath and hurtled straight towards him. Camberwell Primary School parents and students hope a road in between the school’s two campuses will forever shut after a series of near misses. Eddie Jim It was a pupil-free day at Camberwell Primary School, but Floyd went to school anyway to play around on his scooter with mates when he says the car appeared, swerving around the temporary bollards blocking the road to traffic. “It went across the footpath with no number plate and nearly hit us, so we had to jump on the road to stay safe and [the driver] just carried on like nothing happened,” Floyd said. That stretch of road, which runs between Camberwell Primary School’s two campuses, has been shut for the past 18 months by removable bollards after a near-miss involving a young child and a car smashing into a school fence in 2024.



Related Article World golf Women at centre of Camberwell Golf Club stoush make move against president Floyd’s mother, Wendy Trinet, is worried that a car could swerve around the temporary bollard again and no longer lets her son play at the campus outside school time. Trinet is among local parents pushing for a permanent fix after years of close calls. “You can’t drive in the middle of the road, but you can access the side, the footpath, so this is still not blocked,” Trinet said. “An accident is going to happen, it’s just a ticking bomb.” Boroondara Council is considering whether to block the section of Reserve Road, which in the past could be used as a rat-run to avoid Camberwell Junction, but multiple local groups and traders oppose permanently shutting it and are calling for an alternative solution due to the loss of more than 40 parking spots and concerns over traffic.



The death of 11-year-old Jack Davey, who was struck by a car that ploughed into a fence at nearby Auburn South Primary School in late 2024, is front of mind for the school community, Camberwell Primary School Council president Elaine Ko said. Wendy Trinet no longer lets her son play around the school grounds after he described a terrifying encounter with a car, which mounted a footpath near Camberwell Primary. Eddie Jim Students cross the road multiple times a day under adult supervision to attend classes, assemblies or go to the playground. While most of the school’s 550 students patiently line up, Ko said young children were known to bolt across the road unexpectedly and the risk of a serious incident remains too high. “We’ve been very lucky up until now that nothing more serious has happened,” she said.



Reserve Road runs through the heart of an area known as Camberwell Civic Park, which includes the school, three churches with facilities used by community groups, a tennis club, parkland and Camberwell Library. The school’s playground is open to the public outside school hours. Camberwell Centre Association president Di Gillies, who represents hundreds of local businesses, does not support the proposed permanent closure and urged the council to defer making a “hasty” decision on the area’s future. Related Article City life This level crossing is among Melbourne’s most dangerous. Plans to remove it have riled the community “This decision significantly impacts traffic management near a busy junction, reduces local parking, and restricts access for church events and local organisations,” she said. Gillies, whose children attended the school and was previously a councillor, is also concerned about child safety on Reserve Road but questioned whether blocking part of the street even on non-school days was viable for Camberwell.



She called for greater consideration of alternatives, including installing an overpass or gates to stop traffic during school hours. The Camberwell Music Society hosts concerts at the Uniting Church next to the school. President Peter Gray said his organisation had lodged an age and disability discrimination complaint to the Victorian Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission over the temporary closure on behalf of a member with mobility issues. “[The closure] deprives people who come to events at the Camberwell Uniting Church of adjacent parking that involves a short walk and access without having to negotiate steps,” he said. Gray is exploring legal options and said he supported blocking the road on school days only. “I certainly don’t want children to be unsafe, I certainly don’t want that, but there are thousands of school crossings, and every school has a street frontage.”



The number of car spots on Reserve Road dropped from 79 to 36, including four accessible spaces, when the road was temporarily shut, while ticketed parks on surrounding streets were made free. There are more than 100 other fee-free spots on the other side of Camberwell Road behind businesses, in addition to those at the library. Related Article City life The 107-year-old rule at the heart of a legal bid to block a new childcare centre A masterplan for the area developed by council staff, which has not yet been voted on, proposes turning part of Reserve Road into open green space. As a state government activity centre, Camberwell Junction is earmarked for further development, and its population is predicted to more than double over the next 25 years. Bundoora Council will consider closing the road permanently next week, and Mayor Wes Gault said councillors would consider all submissions before making a decision. “Our priority is to ensure the Reserve Road area is as safe as possible for students, families and other pedestrians,” he said.



“We know the community holds a range of views on the future of Reserve Road, and we’re carefully considering all feedback.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Fans condemned for throwing bottles at umpires after prelim heartbreak
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaAFL 2026 Fans condemned for throwing bottles at umpires after prelim heartbreak Alexander Darling Updated September 20, 2026 — 10:03am ,first published September 20, 2026 — 8:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ugly scenes erupted at the MCG on Saturday night when fans threw bottles onto the ground, narrowly missing umpires as they walked off the turf after a pulsating finish to the preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane. Dozens of water bottles and cans rained down on the ground after Brisbane’s nine-point victory, when Hawthorn fans booed the umpires and vented their fury to a series of high-stakes decisions in the match’s dying minutes. Loading Footage showed one field umpire, Jacob Mollison, reacting quickly to protect his colleague from a projectile that appeared to have been thrown from the second level of the stadium. The ugly scenes triggered a blunt reaction from AFL figures: “They should not have things thrown at them. A bottle’s come down from the top tier,” said commentator Luke Hodge, who played for both Hawthorn and Brisbane.



The Lions clawed back the lead moments before the final siren when Hawks defender Jarman Impey was pinged for holding the ball and Lion Hugh McCluggage cooly slotted the resultant set-shot goal. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said he understood the fans’ emotions, but condemned their behaviour. Cans litter the ground after Hawthorn’s loss to Brisbane. Getty Images “The emotion of sport, it’s why we love it so much,” he said in his post-match press conference. “All sports, but ours in particular – the beauty is the emotion it makes you feel. At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears. Part of me wanted to scream with rage. Part of me wanted to throw chairs. “When you’re in the stands, you need to continue to feel that emotion, but we shouldn’t be throwing things on the field.



AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said on Sunday that he was stunned by the spectacle. “I’ve never seen a collective doing what they did like that,” he told this masthead. Cans and bottles on the ground at the MCG. Getty Images “It wasn’t just one or two or five people. It looked like it was a few hundred people around the entire ground throwing stuff onto the ground. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing.” Issko said the sheer number of fans participating in the ugly spectacle made the incident different to previous throwing incidents.



Earlier this year, Hawks star Nick Watson claimed he had a Coke bottle thrown at him in a match against Sydney, while a fan who threw a lemon at Eagles player Reuben Ginbey was banned for five years. “If we can find people that threw it, even though we’re not going to catch everyone, they should face consequences, that’s just not the fans that the AFL fans association represent,” he said. “It’s just not on. If you want to do that to umpires, we won’t have umpires and we won’t have a game of footy.” Issko said the incident would be on the agenda of his group’s next meeting with the AFL, but how to prevent such widespread delinquency happening again he wasn’t sure.



Victorian Premier Ben Carroll also condemned the behaviour on Sunday, telling reporters that throwing projectiles at umpires was “not the Victorian way” and those responsible should be made an example of. “I think this people should be made an example of. This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head,” Carroll said. Umpires dodge projectiles as they exit the ground. AFL Photos via Getty Images “You’ve always got to respect the umpire’s decision. As a North Melbourne supporter, I’ve gone home heartbroken many a time, but that’s just the way it goes.” The MCG said its security team was investigating the incident. “We have zero tolerance for this type of behaviour at our venue,” a spokesperson said.

World.title: The Qantas lounge gave her a dressing down for her ugg boots. I’m with the airline on this one
World.content:
LifestyleFashionStyle Opinion The Qantas lounge gave her a dressing down for her ugg boots. I’m with the airline on this one Melissa Hoyer Writer September 20, 2026 — 9:30am

September 20, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Recently, someone got turfed out of the Qantas lounge in Melbourne. Not for being drunk, obnoxious, for gluttonous plate stacking, food smuggling or overstaying their welcome, but for wearing ugg boots. Cassidy Gaiter, a singer and theatre performer, said she’d worn the same slippers into five lounges in the past month without a blink from staff. This time, apparently, she didn’t look “business” enough, so someone made a beeline for her at the door. Cassidy Gaiter needs to move to Thornton in NSW’s Hunter Valley, the home of the giant ugg boots, situated outside Mortels Sheepskin Factory. Maitland Mercury Cue the outrage cycle. “Make it make sense,” she said. Except it does make sense; it’s just not the sense she wanted it to make. Face it: their house, their rules. Here’s the thing nobody wants to hear: airport style has been in freefall for years, and the ugg boot bouncer moment isn’t some kooky overreach. It’s one of the last places still enforcing the idea that how you show up in public matters even slightly. And I’m absolutely here for it.



While Cassidy – who seems a nice human – has since deleted her initial lounge banishment beef from TikTok, it got me thinking. Once upon a time, flying was an event. Not a ballgown moment but it at least involved presentable humans in public spaces. These days, somewhere between boarding-group chaos, delayed flights and neck-pillow couture, we’ve collectively decided the plane – and now, apparently, the airline lounge – is just an extension of the couch. Nobody’s asking for three-piece suits or cocktail attire at 35,000 feet – we’re not resurrecting Mad Men energy – but there’s a wide, comfortable middle ground between “airport chic” and “I rolled out of bed and emotionally gave up”. And lots of fliers, whether frequent or not, have set up camp firmly at the second address. And even though we try to sleep on a plane (whether you turn left or right on boarding) you should no more arrive in PJs for the flight than you would walk into a restaurant with an apron and a baking dish expecting to make some noise in the kitchen. Athleisure did some of this damage. Leggings, hoodies, slides, sock-and-sandal hybrids are all technically functional but at times worn with the enthusiasm of someone who has accepted defeat before gate allocation. “You don’t need couture but just clothes that are clean and look like they were meant to be worn out of the house.” Getty Images



Sure, comfort is king when you fly but it doesn’t mean a bit of spit and polish should get walked out via the emergency exit. The “wellness comfort” movement of soft fabrics, oversized everything, breathable nothing-in-particular is brilliant and something we all love, but while long-haul flights are hard on circulation, spines and peace of mind, comfort doesn’t have to mean visual and sensory chaos. Tailored track pants exist. Clean sneakers exist. So do clipped toenails, underarm deodorant and pumice stones. Uggs, famously, were designed for the walk from the shower to the couch and are a winter-wardrobe staple at my place but they’re not for an airport lounge with a buffet, a bar and a view of the tarmac. Interestingly, this isn’t the first time uggs have caused an airport lounge brouhaha. Nearly a decade ago a Human League singer was also denied entry to a lounge for wearing the sheepskin beauties. Social media hasn’t helped with our haute flying attire either. Airport dressing aspiration – the oversized sunglasses, chic trench, effortless “I travel well” vibe – has split into two lanes. There’s hyper-styled influencer theatre or unbothered realism and, somewhere in between, some travellers decided opting out entirely was the easiest lane of all. And it’s Qantas and all airline lounge staff who are left holding the dress code (and yes, there is one!) nobody wants to read before they board.



The idea that airports are still shared, public spaces where a baseline of effort is a form of respect should be common sense, and before you come at me for being an absolute sartorial tosser, no, you do not have to spend big money on a special airport ensemble. You don’t need couture, just clothes that are clean and look like they were meant to be worn out of the house. There is no question that when you dress slightly better, you feel slightly better. You move differently. You carry yourself differently. An airline lounge dress code is one of the few remaining nudges telling us that leaving the house, even to sit in an airport eating free cheese and pikelets, is still, in some small way, an occasion. So no, we’re not bringing back hats and gloves, but maybe, just maybe, if an airline has to spell out “no sleepwear” for adults boarding flights, that’s less a “little-known rule” and more a referendum on how far the bar has dropped. None of this requires a trust fund or a stylist. Looking pulled together is still free. The lounge, it turns out, is just one of the places brave enough to say so out loud.



Melissa Hoyer is a social commentator and writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital Menna Alaa El-Din and Timour Azhari September 20, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Riyadh: Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city’s main airport. Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks by the Houthis in the kingdom. Video and photographs showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main

terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks. Loading The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub.



The Houthis said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa. Related Article Middle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh early on Saturday (Riyadh time). In a statement, the coalition also said it had foiled attacks targeting civilians in the Saudi cities of Bish and

Farasan in the south-west and Taif in the west, as well as Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. It did not say whether there was any damage. Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj, east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh’s Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent.



Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation with the Houthis began in July. Houthi warning The Houthis, who ⁠control ​the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, ​have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red ​Sea. A large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Reuters The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, creating new threats to global oil

supplies and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded.



Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia might have military needs due to the ongoing Houthi attacks and Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants It was unclear what kind of support Turkey might provide, but Fidan, in an interview with broadcaster NTV, said Saudi needs could include “some technical issues”. The trilateral agreement signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all of them. On Friday Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response.



The Iran-aligned group, which seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning advance earlier this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it ​in recent days. The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. US President Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera in an interview aired on

Saturday that Tehran wanted the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to end, adding that he believed Yemenis also wanted a settlement with Saudi Arabia. Rezaei also said Iran had conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in stalled negotiations with the

United States, including “ending the war on all fronts”. Consultations were continuing with Qatari and Pakistani mediators and Tehran was awaiting a response from Trump, Rezaei said.



The UN Security Council in a statement on Friday “condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children”. In the statement, the Security Council also condemned “Houthi military escalation in Yemen”. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Sharon Horgan’s five-star comedy is for every woman stuck in the ‘sandwich generation’
World.content:
★★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Sharon Horgan’s five-star comedy is for every woman stuck in the ‘sandwich generation’ Kylie Northover September 20, 2026 — 9:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Youth ★★★★★ If you’re a fan of Sharon Horgan (who isn’t?), as both writer and actor, you’ll almost certainly love her new comedy-drama. Something of a spiritual successor to her 2006 series Pulling, which followed the dating lives of women in their 30s, and the brilliant Catastrophe, about a marriage kick-started by an accidental pregnancy after a wild week-long fling, Youth sees Horgan exploring the specifics of middle-aged womanhood. But if that sounds too earnest, be assured that it’s very, often darkly, funny. Sharon Horgan as Alex in the comedy-drama Youth. Horgan is Alex, a recently divorced 50-year-old who is the embodiment of the “sandwich generation”, the term for those (almost always women) juggling caring for ageing parents, teenaged or young adult kids, holding down a career and the onset of invisibility and waning sex appeal. The series is deeply informed by her own life: Horgan, recently divorced herself, describes it as “auto-fictiony”. She recently told Vanity Fair that she wanted to look “through the lens of a divorced woman who has a very specific amount of time left to find happiness,” while feeling like there’s a “big alarm bell going off”.



The first episode opens as a solemn voiceover over a montage of influential older women – Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Gloria Steinem, Margaret Atwood – intones about ageing, telling us that “no decade moves faster than 50-60. You need to make every single second of your time count”, before cutting to Alex laughing at a TikTok video of a parrot having a haircut and blow-dry. Phew. Horgan as Alex and Aran Murphy as her rebellious teenage son Ruari. HBO Max Her scrolling is interrupted by a text from her boss/best friend Sam (Sharlene Whyte) asking where she is. Alex is a literary agent, and working for her friend is just one of many frustrations. She’s excited though, that her rebellious teenage son Ruari (Aran Murphy, son of Cillian), is about to head off to university, even if he has started dabbling in videos from manosphere influencers. Ruari’s self-absorbed dad Lorcan (Owen McDonnell), isn’t exactly the greatest role model – he’s a jobbing actor about to move to Canada with his younger girlfriend for a role in a B-grade sci-fi series, leaving Alex to deal with Ruari as he grapples with young manhood. Then there are her parents: her mum has diabetes and her dad is showing signs of dementia (“mild-ish Alzheimer’s, like Joe Biden second term-level”). These are problems she’s trying to share with her younger sister, who is busy with a newborn baby.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Patrick Brammall’s home-grown thriller, plus five more picks At once thrilled and terrified at her newly emptied nest, Alex is also anxious about her age, studying older women on the bus, constantly buying new fitness equipment, worried she’ll never have a relationship again. She has an ongoing casual hook-up with Patrick (Rupert Friend), but he is definitely not the settling-down type, although Alex keeps going back there. Sam insists he’s entirely wrong for her, and sets her up on a blind date. But when the date, Michael (Tim McInnerny), reveals he’s 67, he might as well have said 97 by the look on Alex’s face. When Sam texts her to ask how it’s going, Alex’s response is, “he’s old as f--- is how it’s going. I told you how I feel about a new penis, let alone an old penis”. Alex feels like an older version of Catastrophe’s Sharon – perhaps inevitable given both series draw from Horgan’s actual life – and this is a glorious thing. Rupert Friend co-stars as the roguish Patrick, a former boyfriend of Alex’s. HBO Max
