World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAI Albanese urges US, China to strike AI deal akin to nuclear non-proliferation treaty Rob Harris Updated September 20, 2026 — 9:00am ,first published 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cupertino, California: Anthony Albanese has urged the United States and China to strike a deal on artificial intelligence akin to a nuclear non-proliferation treaty ahead as world leaders meeting at the United Nations General Assembly prepare to tackle the rise of the technology. During a visit to California, the prime minister raised the need for nations to commit to international rules governing AI, declaring humans must “remain in control”, after meeting Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and the global tech giant’s executive team. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a press conference at Apple Park Visitor Center in Cupertino, California. Dominic Lorrimer Australia will join a collective middle-power effort at the United Nations this week amid an attempt to shape the global response to AI and a growing debate over whether the technology is developing faster than efforts to control its risks. The race is being played out largely between the United States and China, as Washington and Beijing compete for technological and strategic advantage. After doomsday warnings of wiping out humanity, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (US time) he was forming an “AI force,” despite some within the industry recently sounding the alarm about the dangers of artificial intelligence continuing to grow unchecked.



“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump wrote, declaring he would fight any “decimation or destruction of AI”. Albanese told ABC’s Insiders program he hoped there would be progress in a scheduled meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week. “The truth is, they’re the big two giants here,” he said. “We want to see co-operation. We’ve seen that in the past with new technologies, even on nuclear weapons, for example. I think middle powers, such as Australia, have a role to play here as well.” Speaking to reporters outside Apple Park, Albanese also left the door open to an opt-out copyright regime for artificial intelligence companies, despite warnings from Australian writers, artists and other creatives that such a system would undermine fundamental copyright protections. Asked whether there was a danger in handing too much power to tech companies, given warnings about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, Albanese said there were risks.



Related Article United Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat “I certainly accept that there are risks, and that’s why we need to mitigate,” he said. “That’s why we need to act, and that is something that’s recognised by the companies themselves.” He said the international debate was already under way among leaders preparing to attend the UN General Assembly in New York. “What is being discussed this week, and has already been the subject of interaction between leaders who’ll be attending the UN this week, is what’s the international framework as well to take advantage of the benefits but also to mitigate the risks,” Albanese said. Spruiking Australia’s pioneering social media ban for under 16s, Albanese met with Apple executives behind closed doors for an hour at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. Media were briefly allowed on site for a product demonstration, including the new foldable Duo phone, but were not allowed to film or take any photos of the meeting, buildings or any Apple employees.



AI giants, including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind, have flagged that Australia’s current copyright regime was a hurdle to their increased investment in the country. When asked, Albanese did not rule out the Australian government considering an opt-out system for copyright material used to train AI models. Instead, he stressed the need for Australia to regulate AI and said legislation establishing Australian AI standards would be introduced before the end of the year. “Part of that will be protecting intellectual property,” Albanese said. “We think that the protection of the creative sector is very important, and we’re engaged constructively. I think there’s a way through this.”



Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The ABC last week reported that AI companies would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one plan put forward. Under Australia’s existing copyright regime, the owner of copyright in a piece of writing, photograph or other creative work generally has the right to control how it is reproduced and commercially exploited. Creators and rights holders have warned that an opt-out model would reverse that principle by allowing AI companies to use copyright material unless individual creators took steps to prevent it. They argue the burden should instead fall on AI companies to seek permission before using protected works to train their models. Booker Prize-winning Australian author Richard Flanagan argued last week that copyright was the foundation of Australia’s creative industries rather than an impediment to AI development.

World.title: Labour proposes splitting Foodstuffs and Woolworths from their wholesale arms
World.content:
Labour would force Foodstuffs and Woolworths to run their wholesale operations independently from their retail stores, if elected in November.

The party says the policy would give smaller grocers more places to buy products, and make it easier for new supermarkets to open and grow.

Having previously criticised National's plan to pursue splitting Foodstuffs up as just another review, Labour's commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said Labour would take immediate action.

"The big supermarkets can favour their own retail stores, meaning smaller shops and independent supermarkets end up paying more. That makes it harder for them to compete and offer you a better deal," she said.

Labour wants to create two independently run wholesalers, Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale. Russell Palmer/RNZ

The previous government had told Woolworths and Foodstuffs to strike supply deals with retailers, or face being forced to sell at prices set by regulation.

A review into wholesale by the Commerce Commission, which reported back earlier this year, found Woolworths had strengthened its wholesale offer, including establishing a dedicated wholesale business and implementing initiatives to improve access and customer support.

Foodstuffs North Island had made more incremental improvements, while Foodstuffs South Island had been slower to act, the Commission said.

But the review found competition was still weak in pricing, range, and access.

Labour's plan would be to create two independently run wholesalers, Foodstuffs Wholesale and Woolworths Wholesale.

It would also prevent them from cutting off supply when smaller stores begin gaining customers, and remove restraint of trade rules that stop individual stores like Four Square from lowering their prices, switching to another chain, or going independent.

National's finance and economic growth spokesperson Nicola Willis dismissed Labour's policy as "concerningly light on detail".

"The idea has already been examined and rejected as complex, costly and high-risk.

"A separation of supermarkets' wholesale and retail operations, as Labour is now proposing, was given the lowest score of every option considered by independent experts commissioned by the previous Labour Government.

"It was not taken forward for detailed analysis, meaning Labour cannot say what it would cost, whether it would work, or whether shoppers would pay less as a result. That is a fundamental problem.

"Families deserve grocery reform that is properly tested before it is announced, not policy made in reverse," Willis said.

"National's proposal has been developed from extensive evidence and a cost-benefit analysis that has been rigorously peer reviewed by independent experts. All that work showing this option is likely to deliver the greatest net benefits to Kiwi shoppers is what has led to our proposal."

World.title: Greens announce reforms to lower commercial rents, fill empty shops
World.content:
The Green Party is pledging to restore city centre vibrancy by ensuring market rent reviews for small businesses can lower rents, and letting councils run rental auctions for spaces that have been empty for longer than 12 months.

The party is targeting what are known as "ratchet clauses", which prevent the rent going below what a tenant already pays when the rent comes up for review.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the Greens would change the law so market rent reviews could lower the rent as well as raise it, for new and existing leases for businesses with turnover under $30 million.

"On most main streets in New Zealand you can find empty shops next door to small businesses paying high rents that were set when the market was stronger," Swarbrick said.

"Current commercial leasing rules let rents rise when the market goes up and hold them up when it goes down. Small businesses end up paying more than the market rate when consumer spending slows down."

Any limit on how far rent can fall after a review would match the limit on how far it could rise. The Greens gave the example of a 5 percent cap on reductions meaning a 5 percent cap on increases.

The Greens would also empower councils to auction leases on empty shops in central business districts.

If a shop has been empty for longer than a year, councils would be able to give the landlord eight weeks to find a tenant. If the landlord is unable to fine one, then the council could auction a lease.

"When local businesses fill our main streets, more people come into town, there's more to do, and everyone has a better, safer time," Swarbrick said.

"These common-sense changes will help small businesses stay open and help new ones fill empty spaces, supporting job creation, the local economy, and cities and towns that work better for all of us."

World.title: One dead after motorbike crash in Matamata-Piako
World.content:
One person has died and another has been seriously injured after a motorbike crash in the Matamata-Piako district on Saturday.

Police were alerted to the single-motorbike crash on Morrinsville-Tahuna Road, between Paeroa-Tahuna Road and Quine Road, about 6.45pm on Saturday night.

One person died at the scene. Another rider on the same bike was transported to hospital in a serious condition.

World.title: National vows to limit screen time in primary schools, early childhood centres
World.content:
A re-elected National government wants to ban screen time in early childhood education centres and intends to limit screen use in years 1 to 3.

The party said it wanted a greater emphasis on books, handwriting, conversation, hands-on activities and direct interaction with teachers and other children.

National's education spokesperson Erica Stanford said New Zealand was not alone in reconsidering how much time children spent learning through screens, with the international direction showing that, particularly for young children, digital did not automatically mean better.

"There is also growing evidence about the importance of handwriting and learning by hand. Forming letters helps children learn and retain information. When children are first learning to read and write, that matters," she said.

"Technology still has a place in education, but it should enhance learning, not become the default way children learn," Stanford said.

The policy

End screen and individual-device use in ECE, tightly limit screen and individual-device use in Years 1 to 3, and introduce age-appropriate limits for older primary students

Introduce a School Start Check at ECE before children transition to primary school

Introduce clearer developmental milestones throughout ECE and report this progress to parents

Identify areas where children may need additional support and address that through the Early Intervention Service

Require the writing component of twice-yearly primary school assessments to be completed on paper

It pointed to a study from Singapore which found screen exposure was leading to differences in brain activity, as well a separate study which linked higher screen use in early childhood with poorer academic performance and working memory.

While the studies mainly measured viewing at home, and could not prove screens caused the outcome, National said they added to the case for caution.

The policy is part of the party's ECE policy platform, which includes a new 'School Start Check' at ECE before children move to primary school.

While it would not be a pass-fail test, or prevent a child from starting school, it would set clear expectations about what children need to develop before they attend school, such as toilet training, eating and dressing independently, and holding a pencil.

Stanford said ECE centres would work with parents to assess how ready a child was to start school and where they would need extra support.

World.title: Tiaki Wai warning wastewater discharged in Lower Hutt stream
World.content:
Tiaki Wai is warning that wastewater is being discharged into Lower Hutt's Waiwhetū Stream.

The organisation, which replaced Wellington Water in July, said high rainfall caused the plant in the suburb of Seaview to overflow.

It said the wastewater has been fully treated, but may cause the water to appear cloudy or murky, and have some odour.

World.title: Suffrage Day marked with promise to boost women's health, safety and financial security
World.content:
New Zealand is marking 133 years since women won the right to vote, with the Government using Suffrage Day to highlight its focus on women's economic security, health and safety.

Minister for Women Nicola Grigg said the day was a chance to honour the women who changed New Zealand's history and paved the way for future generations.

She said the suffragists had campaigned for more than the right to vote, including greater opportunity, dignity and fairness.

"The best way to honour the suffragists' legacy is to keep building a New Zealand where women and girls can fully participate, where they can lead and they can have their voices heard," she said.

New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give women the right to vote in 1893.

The Government said its focus now included improving women's health, safety and financial security.

It said the gender pay gap was 5.3 percent this year, close to its record low.

The Government was also focused on getting more women into higher-paid jobs, which it said would help close gender pay and retirement savings gaps.

The Government also said it had strengthened protections for women experiencing stalking and harassment and launched resources for stalking victims and women facing online abuse.

Former Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner Dame Judy McGregor said a narrowing gender pay gap did not necessarily mean women had economic security.

She said the 5.3 percent gender pay gap did not tell the whole story, particularly for Māori, Pacific and migrant women.

"It's great to see that the gender pay gap is coming down," she said.

"But that reflects several things. One, it doesn't account for the very much greater disparity for Māori and Pacific and migrant women."

McGregor said focusing on getting more women into higher-paid jobs overlooked those in lower-paid work.

World.title: 'I was a massive nerd': A road trip with Chloe Swarbrick
World.content: “I had a few different political parties approach me and after talking to a lot of the people in my life who I love, and those who often can proffer some pretty critical advice, decided that I would regret it if I didn’t just try and throw myself at the wall as much as possible to pursue this deep sense of the need for fairness and justice and everybody to be able to participate in society.

World.title: Number of meth pipes, bongs seized by Customs soars
World.content:
The number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs confiscated at the border is soaring, with Customs officers seizing almost 40,000 in the first seven months of this year - more than in all of 2025.

An RNZ investigation found glass pipes for smoking meth are widely available at vape stores, $2 shops and dairies around the country

A law in place since 2014 makes it illegal to import or sell meth pipes, cannabis bongs or hash pipes

New Customs figures show importers are trying to bring a soaring number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs into the country, despite a law banning the sale or importation of drug utensils.

Over the first seven months of this year, Customs seized just under 40,000 pipes and bongs at the border - more than the 37,000 seized during all of last year and a massive 25 times more than 2024.

Earlier this year, RNZ visited vape stores, $2 shops and dairies in two Far North towns, and found roughly two-thirds openly sold glass pipes for smoking the class A drug methamphetamine, also known as meth or P.

Most shops had no age restrictions in place and some displayed the pipes on store counters, next to children's novelty items.

Anecdotal evidence suggests similar availability around the country, despite a law in force since 2014, making it illegal to import or sell meth pipes, hash pipes or cannabis bongs.

Customs northern inspections manager Jared Nicholson said prohibited drug utensils could arrive through any border pathway, including air cargo, mail, sea cargo and passenger luggage.

Meth pipes can be bought at vape stores, $2 shops and dairies around the country. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He said Customs used intelligence and risk assessment to identify goods and people of concern. Frontline officers then carried out targeted inspections and searches based on those assessments.

Critics of the ban on importing drug paraphernalia said it wouldn't solve New Zealand's drug problems, but Nicholson said minimising drug harm required action on several fronts.

"By seizing prohibited drug utensils at the border, Customs helps prevent them from being used to administer drugs or sold for criminal profit," he said. "Customs takes the illegal importation of drug utensils seriously."

If the offending was serious or commercial in scale, the people responsible could be investigated and prosecuted.

In May, Customs intercepted a shipping container at the Port of Auckland containing roughly 1600 three-litre canisters of nitrous oxide, 21,400 meth pipes and 219kg of illicit tobacco sent from China.

As a result, three men, aged 35, 39 and 44, were charged with importing and possessing prohibited goods and defrauding Customs revenue.

In another case, an Auckland couple was sentenced that same month for the large-scale importation of thousands of illegal weapons, bongs and meth pipes.

The 50-year-old man was sentenced to eight months' home detention and their company was fined $45,000.

Nicholson said the number of items seized each year could fluctuate, depending on how many commercial-scale consignments were intercepted.

While Customs has enforced the import ban for several years, an RNZ investigation this year found widespread confusion among police, politicians, councils and retailers about whether it was legal to sell meth pipes.

RNZ enquiries bounced around government departments and ministers, before a briefing paper prepared for Health Minister Simeon Brown finally confirmed selling drug utensils was against the law.

First issued in 2014 and updated in 2020, the Misuse of Drugs (Prohibited Utensils) Notice makes it illegal to import or sell cannabis bongs, hash pipes or meth pipes.

The notice spells out the physical characteristics of each type of pipe, so retailers cannot escape prosecution by claiming the pipes are intended for another purpose - such as decorative ornaments, ingesting herbs or tiny flower vases.

Glass pipes like this one seized at the border are illegal to import or sell. Supplied / Customs

The maximum penalty is three months' jail or a fine of $1000 for an individual, or $5000 for a business.

Possession of a meth pipe is a different matter. That is illegal under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, but police must prove the person caught with the pipe intended to use it for smoking meth.

Customs could not break down how many of the almost 40,000 utensils seized this year were meth pipes and how many were for smoking cannabis. Some utensils could be adapted for use with either drug, making it difficult to arrive at separate figures.

Customs data shows the number of seizure operations is falling, which suggests consignment size is increasing sharply.

The complete figures are as follows:

Number of drug utensils seized: 2023 - 5599, 2024 - 1515, 2025 - 37,068, 2026 (January to July) - 39,196

World.title: Wallaroos collapse against France as bus fire delays game
World.content:
Australia's Wallaroos have been left frustrated by a potentially massive Test win that got away as undisciplined France somehow escaped with a 29-26 win after being 19 points down and reduced at one point to just 11 players.

On an extraordinary day of Test rugby, exacerbated by off-field drama when the second half had to be delayed due to a bus on fire adjacent to the Stade Maurice David, home fans were left almost in disbelief at how their imploding and depleted side somehow still conjured a win.

The French were at one point in the first half down to 11 players after three yellow cards, including one upgraded to a 20-minute red, and a straight red.

A bus fire near the ground delayed the start of the second half. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

It enabled the Wallaroos to power into a 19-0 lead, but that was not enough to stop France fighting back with three second-half tries, even while suffering a sixth card after the break.

Australia, who also had Michaela Leonard sent to the bin in the second half to complete the card chaos, did not help itself as the French reeled off 17 unanswered points in the final 25 minutes to turn a 26-12 deficit into the most unlikely win.

Ultimately, the four Australian tries from Britanny Merlo, Tania Naden, Caitlyn Halse and Piper Duck were not enough for them to follow up last week's comprehensive defeat by England with a morale-boosting win.

The craziness began early, with the French being hit with four cards in 20 minutes, with Ambre Mwayembe, Lea Champon and Lea Murie all binned for high tackles — Mwayembe's being upgraded to a 20-minute red — before Chloe Correa got a straight red for eye-gouging in the maul.

Australia cashed in, with Merlo rolling over from the maul for her second international try after 17 minutes, Naden peeling off to score against a side left helpless when down to 11 and Halse then scoring the Wallaroos' slickest effort after a fine team move.

But when France started getting its numbers back, it became a very different game, as it reduced the deficit to 19-12 by half-time.

After Duck's early score five minutes into the delayed second half, Pauline Bourdon went over to narrow the gap.

When Leonard was binned for a high tackle, the hosts became increasingly encouraged, only to be checked again as Charlotte Escudero got penalised for 10 minutes for her own high challenge.

France then used its maul power to go over for a 68th-minute try through hooker Elisa Riffonneau before Teani Feleu crashed over in the corner for the clincher.

The Wallaroos play in Edinburgh next week against a Scotland side that lost 66-14 to 10-try New Zealand.

AAP

World.title: Cronulla's last step in the NRL finals always seems their longest
World.content:
Sometimes the last step of the journey to a premiership is the longest, and for Cronulla it seemingly gets longer all the time.

After their 46-10 loss to the Roosters, another Sharks season is over. It was a year that marked their fifth finals series in a row and the fourth of those five years that have gone to the second week or beyond.

That's a hard thing to do and there's been a run of consistency under Craig Fitzgibbon that fans of many other clubs would wish for desperately.

They've played more finals games in these past five seasons than Gold Coast and Wests Tigers have in the past 20 years combined.

NRL live A dominant second-half showing has seen the Sydney Roosters defeat Cronulla-Sutherland 46-10 to progress to a preliminary final clash with the Dolphins next weekend. Follow live.

But with the Sharks the granting of that wish came with a curse, like it was made on a monkey's paw.

They are always in the mix but never seem to rise right to the top. They are good enough to be on the raggedy edge that separates triumph and tragedy but when it counts they can't quite end up on the right side.

They know exactly what a premiership calibre team looks like because they get up close and personal with at least one of them nearly every year. They would do anything to be like them but that glorious fate proves elusive.

This defeat to the Roosters gives them one win and five losses against top four teams in the finals since the start of 2022, with the sole victory coming over the battle-weary and depleted Raiders in Canberra last year.

This was the heaviest of those losses and their most lopsided defeat in any match of the past two and a half years.

They were already outsiders going in and the job got that much harder when Nicho Hynes was knocked out of the game after just three minutes.

Cronulla lost halfback Nicho Hynes inside the first three minutes of the game. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Rookie Niwhai Puru did his best in relief and talismanic five-eighth Braydon Trindall did his best to carry the weight of the world, which is hard enough even when you don't have a busted shoulder.

Trindall set up both their first half tries to keep them in the match and kept trying every trick he knew, working a lovely run around with Billy Burns in the second half that very nearly lead to a score of his own.

Only a late tackle from Billy Smith forced the ball free and stopped it from being 24-16 with 25 minutes to go.

A dodgy ruck penalty on Angus Crichton and a Mark Nawaqanitawase try followed, and from there it was a procession as the Roosters ran up the score with a cavalier cruelty, showing attacking gears and a raw brilliance that Cronulla does not possess.

Few teams do, because few teams have players like Nawaqanitawase, who scored a fine double and helped set up another try with a behind-the-back pass that he threw as he was thrown over the sideline.

The dual international got so close to one of the TV cameras it's a wonder he didn't up in your living room as Connor Watson finished off one of the tries of the season.

By the end, as Daly Cherry-Evans and Robert Toia added to their highlight reels to warm up for a preliminary final blockbuster against the Dolphins next week, the Sharks looked outmatched and outgunned.

They were stuck in a fight where the weapons that serve them so well during the regular season — namely, a deliberate and consistent attack that converts pressure into points —were no longer enough.

On average, Cronulla run in their tries from a closer distance than any other team in the league. They had just five tries from inside their own half all season, the fewest of any team in the league.

They move up the field and execute well from close range to punch it in and they are good enough at it that only three teams scored more points through the regular season.

They play the percentages well and they minimise risks and that is good enough nearly every single week of the season until it isn't anymore.

There is a chance for Cronulla to revamp themselves over the summer. Sione Katoa, a fixture of the side for almost a decade, who brought up a century of tries for them last week, is off to the Cowboys.

He'll be joined up there by Jesse Ramien, while powerful utility Siosifa Talakai is off to Perth and lock forward and former skipper Cam McInnes is heading even further away, bound for Super League side York.

For a team that has been extremely stable in recent years, often only losing one or two players per season, it's a lot of changes all at once.

Cronulla were outgunned by the high-flying Roosters. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

They don't want to rebuild, which is understandable, and most of the changes will come by promoting youngsters already at the club but it gives them the opportunity to retool a little and perhaps refresh a lot and maybe whatever changes they land on can give them the final push they need.

A little more speed wouldn't go astray, nor would some extra creativity outside the spine but wherever the change comes from it will be welcome.

There is talent at Cronulla and tenacity and a clear and shining will to succeed, otherwise they wouldn't make the finals every year.

But to win under the brightest of lights against the best of opponents they need to find something extra, something that is missing right now, something they have not yet found but are desperately seeking.

They must believe it's out there, whatever it is, because it is their deliverance.

It is the thing that will take them on that last step, the one they have been trying to take for half a decade now, the one that will give them that which seems so close for so much of the year but every September seems to elude their grasp.

World.title: Lions to take one big advantage into grand final showdown with Freo
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan has urged the Lions to lean into their experience to seize the rare prize of an AFL premiership three-peat.

The two-time reigning premiers qualified for a fourth consecutive grand final with an epic 20.11 (131) to 19.8 (122) win over Hawthorn, in front of 97,835 fans at the MCG on Saturday evening.

The Lions can join the legendary Brisbane team of 2001-03 and Hawthorn from 2013-15 as modern-day teams to go back-to-back-to-back if they beat minor premier Fremantle at the MCG next Saturday.

"It's very exciting to be in the position where we can achieve something like that," Fagan said.

"But it's not worth thinking about that because you get caught up in thinking the wrong way.

"We've just got to get back, recover well, come back down and just follow our process."

Brisbane is one win away from its second premiership three-peat this century. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The Lions last played Fremantle at the Gabba on May 30, when they lost by 25 points amid a difficult run of form.

But while that result didn't go their way, they have experience on their side in their first final against the Dockers, who are chasing a maiden premiership.

All of Brisbane's 23 players, except recruits Oscar Allen and Sam Draper, have won flags, while Fremantle's only premiership players are Shai Bolton, Luke Jackson and Mason Cox.

"There was a bit to like about that game. That was our third loss in a row when we went through that bad patch," Fagan said.

"So we have to go back and have a little bit of a look at that.

"The good thing for us is we're an experienced team in this situation. So that will count for maybe just a little bit. It won't necessarily give us the game.

"But we know what next week is all about. Because our players have done it a few times now and they won't be intimidated by it at all. They'll be ready for it.

"I'm sure they'll give it their best to try and make the most of the opportunity. Because the opportunity is rare."

Fagan pondered the heartbreaking four-point grand final loss to Collingwood in 2023 that prompted Brisbane's era of dominance.

The Lions are preparing for their fourth consecutive grand final. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone/AFL Photos)

"I've thought to myself at different times, maybe if we had got it right that day we would have been three in a row already," Fagan said.

"But we're going to get a chance. We'll have some fun trying to achieve it."

History beckons for Fremantle Sydney will be pondering what could have been, while Fremantle has an eye on history.

The Lions have a decision to make on whether to recall defender Noah Answerth, who was unable to return from an ankle injury for the preliminary final.

The defender would normally handle Hawks star Nick Watson, who nearly won the game off his own boot with six goals, and could be one of this year's heartbreak stories.

"He was relatively close. We'll see how he goes and what their team looks like," Fagan said.

"Whether we think we've got the right team already and we don't make a change — or whether we do. They're always hard decisions to make.

"We're fortunate to be in that position. But you always feel for the person who misses out."

AAP

World.title: Olympic contenders put rowing course to the test in state regatta
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It's 7am on Saturday and the crack of a starter's gun can be heard in the distance upstream.

Eight boats spring from the starting line, as teenage rowers begin to slice through the glassy, brown waters of the Fitzroy River in central Queensland.

The action is beamed back to their supporters on a big screen on the riverbank which, just minutes before, featured a video  for the local crocodile farm.

The Fitzroy River is set to host rowing events at the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

We'll get to the 'crocodile in the room' shortly.

For these young competitors this weekend, it's a school regatta.

For Rockhampton, it's a glimpse of an Olympic future.

Olympic dreams take shape

Ryan Hendrie trains and races on the mighty Fitzroy every day.

But on Saturday, the 18-year-old said knowing the river was now all but confirmed as an Olympic rowing course gave it a different feeling.

Eighteen-year-old rower Ryan Hendrie hopes to represent Australia on the world stage. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"It's amazing to think that I'm rowing at the same spot that Olympians are going to be rowing at," he said before his race.

As future Olympic dreams start taking shape for almost 700 athletes at the three-day state regatta, some young rowers, like Ryan, can already picture themselves there.

He'll be 24 when the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games rolls around.

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta is being held on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"I definitely think that could be an amazing achievement if I could achieve something like that," he said.

"Everyone is really excited. We've had the Australian [team] row here and train here [before] most Olympics."

'Inspiring to all the students'

Fitzroy River to host 2032 Olympic rowing The Fitzroy River in Rockhampton will host the events despite concerns over its suitability, including its crocodile inhabitants.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli this week announced the Rockhampton venue had passed an independent technical assessment "with flying colours" to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

It came after months of fierce debate over the Fitzroy River's suitability, including its status as a crocodile habitat.

The premier delivered the news to Rockhampton Grammar School director of co-curricular Todd Wells, alongside a group of school rowers.

Todd Wells says young athletes are inspired by the decision to hold Olympic rowing events in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"It was very exciting. We had no idea what was coming, basically, apart from a call from the premier," Mr Wells said.

"It's inspiring to all the students that are here this weekend.

"In six years' time, they'll be right in the mix of hopefully selection for the Olympics and that's what it's all about, providing pathways for these students."

So what do visitors think?

Coolangatta's Bruce Waldon was checking out the Fitzroy River and newly minted Olympic rowing course for the first time while he supported his grandson.

Bruce Waldon has travelled to the Fitzroy River to watch his grandson compete. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"I have no problem with it at all, although I have seen some of the videos from overseas and their jibes at us," he said.

"I wish the water was clearer but, besides that, I think it's a good venue."

Townsville mother Camilla Richardson has attended rowing regattas before on the Fitzroy River with her two sons.

Camilla Richardson says it is an honour to see the Fitzroy River confirmed as an Olympic rowing venue. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"We're going to see the Olympics here in 2032 so it's such an honour and a privilege to be back," she said.

"It's great for regional Queensland because, coming from Townsville, we are in the deep north and we often get forgotten about, so this is wonderful for the regions."

Crocodiles and rowing share the spotlight at the Fitzroy River, with a pair of crocs pictured beside the oars on Saturday. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Ms Richardson also had no concerns about the Fitzroy's resident crocodiles.

"It won't be a problem, you stay in your boat and you row, and it's going to be a fabulous course for all the rowers," she said.

" We're on the Ross River in Townsville and [my sons] often row past wildlife and we all just co-exist. "

Crews from across the state have travelled to central Queensland for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta. (ABC Capricornia: Hannah Moon)

Games fever building

The 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events on the Fitzroy River.

It follows an independent technical assessment of this very stretch of water, which World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide endorsed "as safe and fair for athletes".

Rowers catch their breath after finishing a race on the Fitzroy River on Saturday. (ABC Capricornia: Hannah Moon)

But the international sporting bodies eagerly await the next phase of venue planning.

These include technical details and confirmation of service levels and facilities needed for Olympic and Paralympic competitions.

The weekend's regatta is the first state-level rowing event hosted by Rockhampton in five years, placing a timely spotlight on the controversial Olympic selection of the central Queensland waterway.

Anthea O'Loughlin says regatta participants are excited about the upcoming Olympics. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

While Rowing Queensland acknowledged the schools' regatta should not be viewed as a test or demonstration event for the Olympics, Games fever was evident among competitors, officials and spectators on Saturday.

"It's a very positive vibe at the moment, everyone's concentrating on the event and their racing," Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin said.

"There are definitely possible Australian Olympic athletes coming out from these kids."

World.title: Junior Matildas know the price they're willing to pay to make it
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Athletes are often told there's a price to pay if they want to make it to the top of elite sport.

And the journey has to start young, but the Junior Matildas are framing the cost of pursuing their dreams differently.

"No matter what you choose to do in life, there's a price of entry," coach Mike Cooper told ABC Sport.

"Whether that's how much time and effort you have to put into it as a mum and dad driving your child around, the ups and downs of playing well, not playing well, learning from that.

"No matter what level anyone's achieved in whatever sport, they've gone through similar things and knowing that and learning from that I think is really humbling."

Cooper comes from a teaching background, and with two teenage daughters of his own, is uniquely placed to tap into the teen psyche.

Mike Cooper supervises training ahead of the World Cup. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

He knows the expectations placed on any team carrying the Matildas moniker, especially this group, which is the first Australian side to qualify for the U-17 Women's World Cup.

"We want to go with a purpose, we want to perform, want the girls to express themselves, be brave, be bold, make themselves proud before making other people proud," he said.

"And then come home and learn from that experience because whatever happens over there is just part of their journey."

Testing themselves against the best

It's the opportunity of a very young lifetime for players such as 15-year-old Willa Pearson.

She is already a familiar figure in the women's game here, becoming the youngest-ever A-League player last season when she debuted at 14.

Willa Pearson made her A-League Women's debut in November 2025, at just 14 years old. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

She then broke Sam Kerr's record as the league's youngest-ever goalscorer.

But the Sydney FC defender is keeping a level head.

"That was crazy to be honest," Pearson told ABC Sport.

"It hasn't really sunk in. [I'm] trying to take it step by step, play as good as I can and when I get the opportunity to step on the field, perform as well as I can for Sydney."

Pearson captained the Junior Matildas at the Asian Cup, where a semifinal appearance secured qualification for the World Cup.

Willa Pearson represented the Junior Matildas in their run to the Asian Cup semifinals. (Getty Images: Liu Lu)

"[I've] had the opportunity to test myself against the best players in Asia," she said.

"So now bringing that to a world stage and playing against the European countries and hopefully if we make it past the group stage, America, that would just be insane, to have my benchmark against other players in the world."

Maeve Nicholas, 17, plays for Adelaide United, and was also part of the Asian Cup.

"I think so many people our age would only dream of this opportunity," she said.

Maeve Nicholas was part of the side that secured qualification for the World Cup. (Getty Images: Liu Lu)

"So I think just enjoying the experience, and then also making an impact and showing that Australian football, compared to other nations, is capable of achieving amazing things."

Quotable quotes

Part of Cooper's coaching arsenal includes different ways to bring the team together.

Currently, that involves the players learning Spanish and relating that to football, and he has previously had players and staff choose a quote to share.

The final World Cup squad is yet to be selected. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

"It's just multiple different ways to get to know each other, build connection and where possible link it back to the purpose of what we're trying to do," he said.

Nicholas is living by the mantra that "hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard".

"I think that resonates with me a lot because I'm always willing to work hard," she said.

"And I think that's definitely a part of our journey. You need to be willing to put in the effort in order to achieve the results.

Pearson opted for the famed 1-per-centers.

"My quote was '1 per cent better every day'," she said.

"I feel like you get so much thrown at you in life. You get setbacks, good achievements.

"So just trying to make sure everything you have that comes towards you, good or bad, you take a little bit out of that and see if you can be better the next day."

Simple words for mature minds, hoping it all pays off in the long run.

World.title: Roosters power into prelim as Sharks insist they are not in rebuild mode
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters are 80 minutes away from their first NRL grand final in seven years after fighting past Cronulla in a 46-10 semifinal win.

Trent Robinson's men will play the Dolphins in a preliminary final after being made to work for victory against the Sharks at Sydney Football Stadium.

Halfback Daly Cherry-Evans was placed on report for tripping Cronulla's Teig Wilton on Saturday and, aside from the fitness of Sam Walker, is likely to be the only question mark heading into next Friday's meeting with the Dolphins.

Queensland number seven Walker underwent ankle surgery less than a month ago but coach Trent Robinson said the team is "pretty confident" he will be back to face the Dolphins.

"He hasn't trained with us yet but he's had really good progressions," Robinson said.

Just as everything fell into place for the Roosters, who also welcomed back Angus Crichton from a long injury lay-off on Saturday, just about everything fell apart for Cronulla.

Halfback Nicho Hynes failed a head injury assessment after copping a bang en route to Lindsay Collins' second-minute opening try.

Nicho Hynes was ruled out due to a second-minute head knock. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

And then centre Mawene Hiroti went off with a knee injury after 20 minutes after crashing over the dead-ball line.

It was little wonder the Roosters put a depleted Sharks outfit to the sword, piling on 24 points in the final half an hour.

Cronulla is now one of just two teams in the NRL era to reach five straight finals series without making a grand final, and has not been returned to the last game of the season despite making the top eight in nine of 10 seasons since.

"We've been up for five years now with the same group of guys and a good portion of those are leaving," Sharks coach Craig Fitzgibbon said.

Cameron McInnes, Sione Katoa, Siosifa Talakai, Jesse Ramien and Mawene Hiroti are some of the core members of the team on their way out, but Fitzgibbon said it would not be a complete rebuild for the club.

"Everyone thinks we need a reset or rebuild; we'll just keep going, we've got some guys ready to go," he said.

"We won't be going anywhere."

Look back at all the action in our live blog below and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Broncos blitz Knights to set up derby preliminary final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Defending NRLW premiers Brisbane have destroyed Newcastle in a 40-16 win to set up a preliminary final against Gold Coast.

The Broncos led 34-0 at half-time at Langlands Park on their way to clinching a fourth straight win.

But there were some concerns for the Broncos, with Bree Spreadborough sustaining an ankle injury.

Lock Lillian Yarrow was also put on report for a lifting tackle.

It took the Knights until the 16th minute to complete a set of six as they were blown off the park by a rampant Broncos outfit.

Raiders end Tigers' NRLW fairytale The Raiders claim a first-ever NRLW finals win, downing the Tigers 6-0 to end Wests' fairytale season.

Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel tormented their former club in masterclass displays.

Upton, who was given an early mark 20 minutes from full-time, probed and dazzled from fullback.

Southwell was the chief puppeteer at number seven with a pinpoint kicking game, and Teitzel was dominant in the right edge second-row spot.

The Broncos had a dream start with a try after just 56 seconds, brought about by perfect execution in all aspects of play.

Knights fullback Lucy Spain dropped the ball after a Southwell bomb, with Teitzel picking up the scraps to storm over.

Robinson weaved over five minutes later and barnstorming prop Shannon Mato was unstoppable close to the line.

Teitzel's second try was followed by Upton's four-pointer.

Upton laid one on with a crafty grubber for centre Georgia Bartlett to finish, and it was already a cakewalk before the half-time siren.

Broncos prop Brianna Clark crashed over after the break before Knights backs Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, Shanice Parker and Sidney Taylor got the visitors on the board in an improved second-half performance.

AAP

World.title: Demons claim top spot as Cats maintain winning ways
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne is the only unbeaten side after six rounds of the AFLW season, producing a statement 34-point win over Carlton at Casey Fields.

But the Demons may count the cost of Saturday's 8.10 (58) to 3.6 (24) win after star forward Georgia Gall limped off in the third quarter with an ankle injury.

A day after Hawthorn manufactured an upset to topple defending premiers North Melbourne, the Demons knew a win over the Blues would lift them into top spot on the ladder and establish a 6-0 (win-loss) start to their campaign.

The Blues were spirited in the opening half, but Melbourne slotted four straight goals in the third quarter to set up the victory.

Midfielder Olivia Purcell (26 disposals) was at the centre of the blitz, slotting two majors, while Jorja Livingstone scored on debut in the final quarter.

Tyla Hanks (32 disposals, one goal) also excelled, but it came as Gall sustained her injury.

It is the second consecutive loss for the Blues (4-2) and dents their top-four aspirations, although midfielder Claudia Whitfort was typically busy with 24 disposals.

Cats in fifth straight win

Aishling Moloney produced a goal-of-the-year contender to help Geelong to a 14.6 (90) to 7.7 (49) triumph over Collingwood at Victoria Park.

Knowing a victory would shore up their position inside the top eight, the Cats (5-1) were given a scare when the winless Magpies levelled scores minutes after the main break.

But the visitors flicked a switch, finding six goals in an electrifying third quarter to take a 31-point lead into the final break.

One of those majors was from Moloney, who booted the ball from halfway before it took a favourable flurry of bounces and crept into the goal.

The Cats tightened the screws in the final quarter, keeping Collingwood goal-less to seal their fifth straight win.

Midfielders Nina Morrison (30 disposals), Mikayla Bowen (29 disposals) and Georgie Prespakis (12 clearances) were prolific for the Cats, while Moloney and Chloe Scheer grabbed three and four majors respectively.

While the loss kept the Magpies (0-6) winless, they enjoyed a highlight when half-forward Olivia Lewis booted a goal on her AFLW debut after shifting from Super Netball's Melbourne Mavericks to the Magpies.

Lewis was a late call-up on Saturday morning because midfielder Bri Davey was ill.

Swans move clear in top four

Chloe Molloy continued her glittering goal-scoring form, spearheading Sydney to a 14-point victory over Port Adelaide.

Chloe Molloy played a starring role for the Swans. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

The Swans (5-1) knew a win at Alberton Oval would move them four points clear of the fifth-placed Blues.

Molloy was instrumental in helping the visitors secure the precious 5.11 (41) to 3.9 (27) victory, booting three goals.

Her dazzling display came despite the Power keeping Sydney's usually dynamic attack at bay in the first half, with the scores locked at 16-16 at the main break.

The Swans stepped up in the third quarter, with Molloy booting a crucial goal, although a late major by Gemma Houghton kept the Power in the contest.

Leading by four points at three-quarter time, young Swans forward Cynthia Hamilton snagged a settling major, before Molloy kicked another to open up a match-winning advantage.

Swans defender Zippy Fish was typically influential, picking up 26 disposals, while midfielder Montana Ham had 16 possessions.

Midfielder Abbey Dowrick was a shining light for the Power (2-4), racking up a match-high 27 disposals and 415 metres gained.

Triumphant Bulldogs

The Western Bulldogs held firm to claim a 6.4 (40) to 4.6 (30) victory over Fremantle.

Looking to jump into the top eight, the Bulldogs (4-2) were kept scoreless in the opening term in Perth but kicked four unanswered majors in the second quarter to lead by 11 points at half-time.

The Dockers tightened their defence in the third quarter, holding the visitors to just one point as they surged back after Hayley Miller and Kiara Bowers found goals.

But just 17 seconds into the final quarter, a series of slick handballs led to Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley slotting a major, before Sarah Hartwig nailed a goal to help her team move up to seventh on the ladder.

The Dockers (3-3) missed an opportunity to cement themselves inside the top eight, although Bowers (23 disposals, eight tackles and one goal) was busy, while midfielders Gabrielle Newton and Aisling McCarthy posted 24 possessions each.

Defender Jess Fitzgerald (25 disposals) shone for the Bulldogs, and midfielder Isabelle Pritchard jagged 21 disposals and a goal.

AAP

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think
Tech.content:
Meta’s Muse is apparently an effective AI assistant, but one that’s a little creepy. Part of that is because of its new Mac app, which can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes. But for all its smarts, Muse doesn’t actually know how to describe itself. Jason Aten, a contributing editor at Inc Magazine, posted on Threads screenshots of an interaction he had with Muse in which the assistant asks him some questions about a conversation he was having in Messages.

The problem is that Aten says he didn’t give Muse access to his messages. When asked how it knew about the contents of his messages, Muse replied, “I saw the notification previews, not your message history. I haven’t been reading your texts.” Aten continued to push, asking how Muse was receiving message previews, it didn’t have a good answer. “Honest answer: I can’t give you the exact plumbing,” it said. “What I know is that the paired Mac app exposes notifications as one of its capabilities, and they arrive to me through the device sync.

Obviously, not great.

Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton chimed in below the post to try to explain. First, he walks through all the permissions Muse needs to read messages, including granting the Mac app full disk access. He states that the features are opt-in. The more interesting part comes in towards the end of the thread in which Singleton says that Muse, “does not watch notifications on your Mac, but rather syncs data from Messages only after the user has specifically enabled access.” He suggests that the issue isn’t Muse illicitly reading Aten’ texts, but simply that Muse has no idea what it’s talking about:

In the conversation with his Muse in Jason’s screenshots, when Muse said it synced “device notifications”, it was confused about how to explain the feature and gave an incorrect explanation. That’s on us. We apologize for the incorrect response from Muse and we’re working to improve Muse’s understanding of its own internals so that it gives correct answers to questions about how it functions more consistently.

That might not be particularly reassuring, but it also makes some sense. We already know chatbots won’t tell you their secrets and will instead tell you what you want to hear.

Tech.title: Gemini went rogue, hacked three companies, and Google hid it
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In May, Gemini broke containment and hacked three different companies, but Google didn’t disclose the incident until the Wall Street Journal approached the company. The hacks happened during a test of the model’s cybersecurity capabilities run by third-party Irregular, which was also involved in similar incidents involving Meta and OpenAI.

According to WSJ, Google didn’t disclose the hack because it didn’t consider it to be an “example of model misalignment.” The company said that it was an instance of “mistaken identity,” and once the model realized it had brute-forced its way into a real company by guessing a password, it stopped. “In this case, the model acted appropriately,” Google VP of Security Engineering Heather Adkins said.

Adkins told The Verge that “the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”

Adkins didn’t elaborate on how Gemini taking it upon itself to break containment and target third parties failed to qualify as misalignment. “Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems - even if it’s as simple as a weak password,” she said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”

But Jack Cable, CEO of AI security firm Corridor, told WSJ that, “the meta problem is, hey, models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.” Additionally, security lapses at Irregular may have made these attacks possible. The model wasn’t supposed to have internet access during testing, but Irregular told WSJ it was unintentionally left available.

As incidents like this pile up, calls to rein in AI have only grown.

Tech.title: Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

They’re also a band that’s terminally online and very plugged into the video game scene as well as the weirder sides of the internet — just listen to Peter and Luke’s guest spot on the Panic World podcast talking about Etsy witches.

Anamanaguchi has a new single, “Yeah I Guess,” continuing in the musical direction of Anyway. And if it’s a precursor to a new album dropping soon, I’m sure I’ll be looping it endlessly just as I did the tracks “Magnet,” “Fall Away,” and “Valley of Silence.” (Seriously, I’ve at times had Anyway set on repeat for hours straight.)

Not only did all four members of Anamanaguchi agree to answer our weekly questionnaire, but they answered all our questions.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Luke Silas: I think my most used tool is Ableton Live Operator, it is simple and powerful and can make basic things happen incredibly quickly. I usually open it up just for writing or getting ideas down, but more often than not the sounds I get with it tend to make it to the final product!

Which is the most underappreciated?

Ary Warnaar: Built-in laptop mic and cellphone mic aren’t exactly slept on, but def underappreciated. They’re great for just getting ideas down fast, but now they sound so good that I find myself not even re-recording what I thought would be “scratch” vocals.

Peter Berkman: Right now it’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S. Best mouse I’ve ever had. It has a sideways scroll. It has a button to switch between notched and smooth scroll wheel. The click is satisfying but still really quiet. It’s really sensitive & responsive on whatever surface I happen to have it on. It feels really good in my hand. It charges directly into a USB-C port without external batteries so it gets to look like a mouse with a tail after it’s worked really hard. When I’m at a different computer, or if I’m on a laptop having to use a trackpad, I feel like I’ve lost so much gestural fidelity. I love the keyboard but let’s be real Douglas Engelbart cooked when he invented the mouse. But he didn’t have the recipe of the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and he didn’t even live to see it. The LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S wasn’t even invented until June 2022. I have seen two friends recently using the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and I say “Hey man that’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S” I use that thing too.

James DeVito: Lately it’s been an app called “Amphetamine” that keeps your computer from going to sleep for a set amount of time. It’s great when starting an export/render or other task that may take a while and then being able to throw my laptop in my bag and have it work while I head elsewhere… Just gotta make sure the laptop doesn’t ’splode in your bag from overheating.

LS: I love metronomes! Strengthening time is so important, and getting more comfortable with a metronome means you get to play around with time more confidently! I would love people to love metronomes the way I do!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

LS: Probably Discord? Let’s say Discord.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

AW: Would kill to get a normal 1/8-inch headphone out again. I’ve been constantly replacing dongles ever since Apple ditched the headphone out. Because they break or or get misplaced. Frustrating and wasteful.

JD: A wise friend of mine once taught me to increase the key-repeat on my computer beyond what is normally allowed via the UI. It feels insane at first but your hand/brain coordination catches up with the speed eventually and then you can tttttttttttttttype and deleeeeeeete things so much quicker.

LS: The only thing I’d like to add to my iPhone SE is a USB port so I can type with a keyboard because I suck at typing on my phone.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

LS: I have never done this before! I probably should!!

PB: There’s a new radio aggregator called vvorldwide.com. It’s amazing. It’s like having a radio dial in your car except it pools the feeds from NTS, The Lot, dublab, KEXP, loads of different places from all over the world. It’s one of those products that’s like: Wow. Why did nobody think to make this before? It’s so useful, lightweight, and beautiful. It’s amazing to me how detached from reality and human use the big companies are (and have been for a long time). It’s one of those refreshing things you see, it reminds me of The Unfinished Revolution by Michael Dertouzos. You can just build things you want to see!

JD: Gmail :(

How many tabs do you have open right now?

PB: Tab grouping from Firefox has become an artform for me. I don’t see tabs anymore just folders of memory I can recall like a PSX save file.

LS: 46 and 31 between two windows. Too goddamn many. Most of them are meant to be shared with others or read/watched, every weekend I do a cleanout but there are truthfully a few that have been sitting for months. I can’t be the only one.

JD: I like when Chrome on my phone stops displaying the number of open tabs and just shows a smiley face :)

Which social media platform do you use the most?

LS: Staying detached from social media tends to be better for my mental health on the day-to-day, but scrolling following on Twitter is the easiest way for me to stay connected to games or news still. Instagram stresses me out lately more than ever before. YouTube definitely counts and I do love it very much, but shorts are a rare treat; I tend to watch long-form stuff mostly or have different content with no dialogue on a second monitor, like either a video game longplay or lots of restoration or cooking videos.

What is your happy place online?

AW: Facebook marketplace. Specifically low-balling “I know what I got” type mfs. No one ever accepts my offers, but I think it’s important to keep people humble, and long term, I’d like to think that I’m contributing to keeping the prices low for the next buyers.

PB: I’ve just discovered clothes. So I’m hunting a lot on places like Grailed or Depop or whatever. It’s a lot like the way I treat musical equipment on Reverb. It’s fun to sell stuff and buy stuff… when it’s equal amounts it feels more like barter and temporary sharing.

LS: Video game speedruns! Twitch streams like GDQ or RPG Limit Break are very comforting to me and a very sweet community of fun personalities.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

JD: 3D printers. I’ve been 3D printing for a long time now, and it’s gotten so so so much more reliable/easy at this point. The fact that I can design a bracket etc. for stage production and have it in hand within an hour really is the future.

LS: I’m going to say my Game Boy counts for this question. I use it less for sound design than I used to, but I bought new flash cartridges recently for the first time in years, and I’m ready to get cooking with it again very soon! It’s a perfect little self-contained workstation.

Which was the most disappointing?

LS: I’ve bought a few different effects plugins that tend to have some distinct effects but end up not giving me what I’m looking for, or feel far too specific to a use case for me to reach for generally speaking. I’ve found more exciting results from stacking and tweaking stock effects than I have reaching for dedicated single-use stuff.

PB: I’m not gonna hate on here… but they exist.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

PB: Return of the Obra Dinn was so much fun. Any game that feels like detective work is the kinda thing that gets me going, and instantly creates a moment of excitement for me that stays frozen that I can always go back to. I think about playing [the original] Resident Evil for the first time, the first three Phoenix Wright games: I can tell you everything about where I was and what I was feeling when I first played those games. It’s not even a nostalgia based thing. I played Parasite Eve II for the first time two years ago and it was an instant deep love.

LS: I think my favorite video game of all time is Chrono Trigger. It was a world I really wished I could experience in real life and the atmosphere of every place you go is special to me. I have been trying to rip off Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu every time I write for the last 30 years. It’s the first game I think of when I want to start a new playthrough of something familiar to me!

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

AW: I don’t like forced two step authentication or even worse, the upper case + number + symbol extra long type passwords. Like if I want my password to just be the letter “a,” that’s on me. I’m comfortable with that choice. I’m comfortable with that level of vulnerability. Shit maybe I don’t even want a password sometimes. Just leave it all out there for the people.

LS: Using AI to make music! Blue check accounts on twitter talking about using AI to make music! Write your own fucking music, have fun learning a skill that will continue to give and build and bloom until the day you die!!!

What is one thing you wish you had created?

LS: “Show Me Love” by Robin S. is a perfect song, and every time I hear it I think “God, I wish that could have been mine.” The combination of the M1 organ, that 909 groove, and Robin S.’ top line is like a simple meal where the right ingredients add up to something far greater than the sum of their parts; a perfect BLT, a chocolate/vanilla/peanut butter milkshake, the freshest sushi you’ve ever eaten.

JD: The Black Eyed Peas performed at the 2020 VMAs and they all had light up crotches that sync’d up to the show. Why the f didn’t they call me to do that?

What creation are you most proud of?

PB: Going back and listening to our album Anyway always surprises me. I love it so much. I think it’s the kinda thing that people who didn’t get it will eventually come around on. Sleeper classic even for me ha.

LS: I think the song “Really Like To” from our latest album Anyway is a song that accomplishes a lot of the things I want to when writing for the band! It’s loud and fast, has fun drum parts, fun to sing along to, and I got to do an ambient section at the end; I like showing it to people as an indication of where we’re at right now.

JD: Anyway as well — the entire process was so collaborative throughout. A lot of really great memories writing at the house and recording at Tarbox Road Studios.

Which are you least proud of?

LS: In 2023 I tried to get good at baking cookies, and in the process made a batch of not only the worst cookies I’ve ever had, but some of the worst food I have ever experienced. They looked great, but on a first bite tasted like absolutely nothing and had a texture of chewing damp sand, and on a second bite a bitter taste began to crawl across my tongue that practically gagged me. The only other human who tasted them was my next-door neighbor, just so I could have a witness to the crime that I’d committed. To this day I’m still not sure how I fucked up that bad, and I’ll never forget that taste.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

AW: When I was a kid I met Steve Lukather, the guitarist of Toto, and I told him I wanted to be a guitarist in a band when I grow up. He told me that if I wanted to get the girls I had to either lift weights or get good at guitar solos. I’ve done neither and I’ve been suspicious of all advice ever since.

PB: My dad told me to “never give up” when I was playing Zelda in my basement as a kid. It gave me a big affinity for puzzles, very encouraging. My dad still gives me important advice at all the big moments in my life — I am very grateful to have him.

LS: Progress, not perfection.

What is your current obsession?

PB: Investigating criminal networks of the 1990s! More of a hobby than an obsession.

LS: I’ve unfortunately found myself going further down the rabbit hole of Deltarune theory videos. I don’t buy into the majority of the speculation shared, but I love the game and there is lots of incredible insight shared into the design of it and aspects of it mechanically and narratively that I didn’t even realize I was missing.

What do you do when you need to focus?

AW: Modafinil. Jk lol, I try not to force focusing and just let it be a byproduct of inspiration/motivation. I wait for the focus to come. If I’m having trouble focusing on something then I probably shouldn’t be doing it. Like driving a car. And if you attach rituals to focus it just invites the possibility of not being able to focus without said rituals.

LS: I wait until about 8pm, charge my phone on the other side of my studio, get a large cup of black coffee, put on my second monitor a very long playthrough of a game I’m already familiar with (most recent one was Grandia II), and keep my door shut as long as possible.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

LS: Take a walk down the Venice boardwalk, get a two-dollar salad from Chairman Mao’s, and eat while listening to music and watching people skate at the Venice bowl.

PB: It’s very important to fuck off for a minute. I will go out to a Smash tournament in the Dallas area. There’s a very lively scene that’s super competitive and full of great people. I can always go back from that feeling fresh.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

PB: My phone’s dead half the time so it’s a moment that can happen anytime.

LS: I legitimately don’t remember and that depresses me!! I don’t like that!!

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

LS: About a month ago I picked up a used copy of Only Theatre of Pain by Christian Death at Headline Records, great shop I’ve been going to since I was a kid!

JD: I recently bought a record of a band called “Schlong” at Permanent Records in LA. I love finding stuff that isn’t available on streaming. It can be really easy to get complacent with what’s available online but there’s so much out there in the real world!!!

What do you think is worth splurging on?

LS: I think the most consistent answer for me is special meals. Something unique in another country, or something really special to which I don’t get to treat myself often. It’s always food!

AW: Vacation/travel/time off/adventure etc... I wish it wasn’t considered so much of a splurge. The same way you wouldn’t really call going on a hike a splurge, but in a world where just existing can be expensive, I think it’s something that’s tremendously good for the ~soul~, and worth regularly “splurging” some time/money on. I want to talk to my friends about what cool missions they went on this summer, not what new shoes they bought or whatever.

PB: Gonna agree 100% with Ary. The value of travel can’t be overemphasized.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

AW: “If you cant handle him at his fastest, you don’t deserve him at his furiousest”

JD: “Better to waste than to have not”

PB: “You know he had to do it to em”

LS: “Life is Hectic.”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

PB: I’m very GIF-averse. There’s something about it that feels like wearing someone’s skin. But here’s a pic I like.

Tech.title: The colorful, unique Hyte X50 PC case is $50 off
Tech.content:
The Hyte X50 is a PC case that really stands out from the typical black box design, and it’s $50 off at the company’s site until September 21st, 2026, bringing the price down to $99.99. This attractive case supports motherboards from ITX all the way up to the E-ATX form factors, and GPUs that are up to 430mm long, which should cover even the biggest options available. The standout feature is a massive curved glass panel that spans the left face and top of the case, giving it a unique, eye-catching look. It’s easy to build in, supports a wide variety of components and cooling setups, and has a thoughtful, refined design.

Unlike a lot of cases with big glass panels, the X50 has excellent airflow, with louvered fins along the back for ventilation, a porous mesh front, and plenty of spots for radiators and fans. It comes in a variety of bold colors, too, like the lavender-adjacent “taro milk” and trendy “matcha,” as well as more classic black and white options. If you’d rather opt for something a little more subtle, the X50 Air swaps the glass panel for curved mesh, and is only $79.99 (usually $119.99) from Hyte.

Tech.title: Does AI need an antitrust exemption so it doesn’t kill everyone????
Tech.content:
Today on Decoder, we’ve got the first of a two-part series on the future of business, and I’m talking with Jonathan Kanter, the former antitrust chief for the US Department of Justice in the Biden administration. These days, he’s both a professor of law at WashU and professor of technology policy at Carnegie Mellon.

The biggest story in tech right now is the spiraling debate about AI safety and regulation. Researchers at the big AI labs including Anthropic and Google DeepMind have quit in noisy ways, saying the models pose real threats and safety isn’t being taken seriously across the industry. Other researchers have said the chance of AI killing us all is greater than 10 percent, and the CEOs of all these companies have issued various calls to slow down development and develop regulation, including asking for antitrust exemptions so they can all coordinate on safety issues.

That is a lot of ideas, and I am especially curious about the antitrust piece, which has led to accusations that these companies are seeking regulatory capture, attempting to form a cartel, and even somehow finding a way out from investor pressure ahead of their IPOs.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So to make sense of it all, I called Jonathan Kanter.

Jonathan brought huge antitrust cases against Google, Apple, and Ticketmaster during his time as antitrust chief, and along with Lina Khan, led what amounted to a full reboot of American antitrust policy. As you’ll hear him say, he won those cases against Google and Ticketmaster, and that case against Apple is still live in the Trump DOJ, surprising many.

That reboot has also led to some surprising alliances in the AI debate — avowed libertarian and former Trump AI czar David Sacks has been approvingly retweeting Lina Khan saying there’s no need for an antitrust exemption.

This is all a lot, and you’ll hear Jonathan and me really get into the weeds of how all this regulation might work, and how it might interact with antitrust law, competition policy, and our relationship with China.

Okay: Jonathan Kanter, former DOJ antitrust chief, on AI safety and regulation. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Jonathan Kanter, you’re the former head of the DOJ Antitrust Division in the Biden administration and a current professor of law at WashU and professor of technology policy at Carnegie Mellon. Welcome back to Decoder.

Always a pleasure to be back.

This is great. You’re a private citizen now. You don’t have to give me the politician answers.

I can say whatever I want. I feel so free.

I’m very excited about this.

I plan to as well.

I have a million questions about the state of AI regulation in America right now. There is a swirl of ideas about how we should or should not regulate these companies.

There’s the Trump administration whose posture seems to be “no,” which is fascinating. You rarely see the federal government just decline to participate in the way that the Trump administration appears to be declining to participate. And then there’s an incredible backbone of antitrust concern floating throughout all of this. Are these companies trying to form a cartel? Are they aware that maybe their IPOs aren’t going to go the way they want to, so they’re seeking regulatory capture in some way that is good or bad? Are they trying to foreclose cheaper competition from open-weight Chinese models?

Give me your sense of just the state of things right now, and then I want to dive into the specifics with you.

The state of the world right now is like we’ve invented cars and trucks, but we have no lines on the road, no traffic lights and no stop signs and no speed limits. We’ve invented this incredibly powerful technology that’s transforming how we live our lives, how we conduct business, how we socialize, how we seek and generate and consume information. We need some basic rules of the road. I think about it on two fronts. What are the things that companies should be doing? And what are things the government should be doing? There are responsibilities on both ends. I’m happy to dive into both.

Let’s just start with the very notion that asking for regulation necessarily forms a cartel. All the big frontier AI companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, even Elon Musk — do not necessarily like each other. These are people that do not necessarily like each other. They are saying in concert that they should slow down. The phrase that Dario Amodei from Anthropic is using is to “pace the frontier.”

My read of this is that they simply do not trust each other, that they are in a prisoner’s dilemma and they need an outside force, most likely the government, to enforce some kind of policy framework on them that they have to agree with. Is that a fair read of just the basics here?

Kind of. Let me give you my interpretation from the most generous to the most cynical, neither of which, TL;DR, should result in any sort of antitrust exemption.

The most generous interpretation is that they’re afraid of the pace of innovation and the lack of regulation means they don’t see any lines on the road. They don’t know where to drive and they’re worried about driving off the road or hitting somebody else. They’re begging for the government to step in and do something. Probably there’s a modicum of truth to that. I believe they believe it could destroy humanity. I’m not sure that that doomsday scenario is accurate, but I believe they believe that. That’s the more generous version.

The more cynical version is that they’re spending so much money, they’re hemorrhaging cash and they can’t keep this up, but if they pull back, it’s going to affect their valuation as part of the IPO.
